text.original: وَالْمُتَعَدِّي مَا لَا يَتِمُّ فَهْمُهُ بِغَيْرِ مَا وَقَعَ عَلَيْهِ الْفِعْلُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَضْرُبٍ: الْأَوَّلُ مُتَعَدٍّ إِلَى مَفْعُولٍ وَاحِدٍ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُ مَفْعُولِهِ بِقَرِينَةٍ وَبِدُونِهَا. وَالثَّانِي مُتَعَدٍّ إِلَى مَفْعُولَيْنِ، وَهُوَ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْسَامٍ: الْقِسْمُ الْأَوَّلُ مَا كَانَ مَفْعُولُهُ الثَّانِي مُبَايِنًا لِلْأَوَّلِ، نَحْوُ: أَعْطَيْتُ زَيْدًا دِرْهَمًا، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُهُمَا وَحَذْفُ أَحَدِهِمَا مَعَ قَرِينَةٍ وَبِدُونِهَا.
text.en: The transitive is that whose understanding is not complete without what the act falls upon. It is of three sorts. The first is transitive to one object, as ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran “Zayd hit ʿAmr”; its object may be dropped, with a context and without one. The second is transitive to two objects, and it is of three divisions. The first division is one whose second object is distinct from the first, as aʿṭaytu Zaydan dirhaman “I gave Zayd a dirham”; both of them may be dropped, or one of them, with a context and without one.

text.original: وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّانِي أَفْعَالُ الْقُلُوبِ، وَهِيَ أَفْعَالٌ دَالَّةٌ عَلَى فِعْلٍ قَلْبِيٍّ، دَاخِلَةٌ عَلَى الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ، نَاصِبَةٌ إِيَّاهُمَا عَلَى الْمَفْعُولِيَّةِ، نَحْوُ: عَلِمْتُ وَرَأَيْتُ وَوَجَدْتُ وَزَعَمْتُ وَظَنَنْتُ وَخِلْتُ وَحَسِبْتُ، وَهَبْ بِمَعْنَى احْسِبْ غَيْرَ مُتَصَرِّفٍ. وَلَا يَجُوزُ حَذْفُ مَفْعُولَيْهَا مَعًا أَوْ أَحَدِهِمَا بِدُونِ قَرِينَةٍ، وَمَعَ قَرِينَةٍ كَثُرَ حَذْفُهُمَا مَعًا، وَقَلَّ حَذْفُ أَحَدِهِمَا فَقَطْ.
text.en: The second division is the verbs of the heart (afʿāl al-qulūb): verbs that indicate an act of the heart, come upon the mubtadaʾ and the khabar, and put both in naṣb as objects, as ʿalimtu “I knew”, raʾaytu “I saw [that]”, wajadtu “I found”, zaʿamtu “I claimed”, ẓanantu “I thought”, khiltu and ḥasibtu “I supposed”, and hab, in the sense of iḥsib “suppose!”, which is not conjugated. Their two objects may not be dropped together, nor one of them, without a context; with a context, dropping both together is frequent, and dropping only one of them is rare.

lessons.title: Cancelling and suspending; ṣayyara and its kind; three objects
body: The verbs of the heart have properties of their own. Cancelling (ilghāʾ) and governing are both allowed when the verb stands between its two words, Zaydun ʿalimtu munṭaliqun, or after them, Zaydun munṭaliqun ʿalimtu. Their fāʿil and object may be two joined pronouns of one person: ʿalimtunī qāʾiman, “I knew myself standing”; ʿadima and faqada are treated like wajada in this. And anna may come upon their two objects: ʿalimtu anna Zaydan qāʾimun.

Suspending (taʿlīq) is “cancelling the governing necessarily, in the wording but not in the meaning”, by a word of question, by negation, by the lām of beginning, by an oath, or by inna with the lām in its khabar: ʿalimtu a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun; raʾaytu mā Zaydun munṭaliqun; wajadtu la-Zaydun munṭaliqun; ʿalimtu inna Zaydan la-qāʾimun. The sentence is still the object in meaning; only the naṣb cannot reach it. The commentators set it against cancelling, which is a choice, and cancels the verb's hold in meaning as well as in wording.

Suspending reaches further than these verbs: every verb of the heart, shakaktu, nasītu, tabayyantu; every verb by which knowledge is sought, imtaḥantu, saʾaltu; and the verbs of the five senses, lamastu, abṣartu, samiʿtu, shamimtu, dhuqtu.

The third division of two objects is verbs joined to the verbs of the heart only in coming upon a mubtadaʾ and khabar, and in the rules of dropping: ṣayyara, jaʿala, taraka, ittakhadha. And the third sort of transitive takes three objects, aʿlama and arā: the first object as in the class of aʿṭaytu, the last two as in the class of ʿalimtu: aʿlama Zaydun ʿAmran Bakran fāḍilan.

terms.en: cancelling, allowed when the verb is in the middle or at the end
suspending: cancelling necessarily, in wording not in meaning
the verbs joined to the verbs of the heart

examples.en: cancelling: the verb in the middle
fāʿil and object, two pronouns of one person
suspending by a question
a verb of three objects

tasks.prompt: Give both readings of Zaydun ʿalimtu munṭaliqun.
tasks.answer: Cancelled: Zaydun munṭaliqun, mubtadaʾ and khabar in rafʿ. Governing: Zaydan ʿalimtu munṭaliqan, both in naṣb as objects.

tasks.prompt: Why must ʿalimtu be suspended in ʿalimtu a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun?
tasks.answer: The question hamza takes the front of its sentence, and the verb's naṣb cannot pass it. The sentence is still the object in meaning.

tasks.prompt: Name the three objects in aʿlama Zaydun ʿAmran Bakran fāḍilan.
tasks.answer: ʿAmran, as in the class of aʿṭaytu (the one informed); Bakran and fāḍilan, as in the class of ʿalimtu (once Bakrun fāḍilun).

text.original: وَمِنْ خَصَائِصِهَا جَوَازُ الْإِلْغَاءِ وَالْإِعْمَالِ إِذَا تَوَسَّطَتْ بَيْنَ مَعْمُولَيْهَا، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ عَلِمْتُ مُنْطَلِقٌ، أَوْ تَأَخَّرَتْ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ عَلِمْتُ. وَمِنْهَا جَوَازُ أَنْ يَكُونَ فَاعِلُهَا وَمَفْعُولُهَا ضَمِيرَيْنِ مُتَّصِلَيْنِ مُتَّحِدَيِ الْمَعْنَى، نَحْوُ: عَلِمْتُنِي قَائِمًا، وَحُمِلَ عَدِمَ وَفَقَدَ فِي هَذَا الْجَوَازِ عَلَى وَجَدَ. وَمِنْهَا جَوَازُ دُخُولِ أَنَّ عَلَى مَفْعُولَيْهَا، نَحْوُ: عَلِمْتُ أَنَّ زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ.
text.en: Among their properties is that cancelling and governing are both allowed when they stand between their two governed words, as Zaydun ʿalimtu munṭaliqun “Zayd, I knew, is leaving”, or after them, as Zaydun munṭaliqun ʿalimtu “Zayd is leaving, I knew”. Among them is that their fāʿil and their object may be two joined pronouns with one meaning, as ʿalimtunī qāʾiman “I knew myself standing”; and ʿadima “he lacked” and faqada “he lost” are treated like wajada “he found” in being allowed this. Among them is that anna may come upon their two objects, as ʿalimtu anna Zaydan qāʾimun “I knew that Zayd is standing”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا التَّعْلِيقُ بِكَلِمَةِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ أَوِ النَّفْيِ أَوْ لَامِ الِابْتِدَاءِ أَوِ الْقَسَمِ أَوْ إِنَّ الْمَكْسُورَةِ إِذَا دَخَلَ فِي خَبَرِهَا لَامُ الِابْتِدَاءِ، أَيْ إِبْطَالُ الْعَمَلِ عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْوُجُوبِ لَفْظًا لَا مَعْنًى، فَيَعُمُّ هَذِهِ الْأَفْعَالَ، نَحْوُ: عَلِمْتُ أَزَيْدٌ عِنْدَكَ أَمْ عَمْرٌو، وَرَأَيْتُ مَا زَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ، وَوَجَدْتُ لَزَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ، وَعَلِمْتُ إِنَّ زَيْدًا لَقَائِمٌ، وَكُلَّ فِعْلٍ قَلْبِيٍّ غَيْرَهَا، نَحْوُ: شَكَكْتُ وَنَسِيتُ وَتَبَيَّنْتُ، وَكُلَّ فِعْلٍ يُطْلَبُ بِهِ الْعِلْمُ، نَحْوُ: امْتَحَنْتُ وَسَأَلْتُ، وَمِنْهُ أَفْعَالُ الْحَوَاسِّ الْخَمْسِ، كَلَمَسْتُ وَأَبْصَرْتُ وَسَمِعْتُ وَشَمِمْتُ وَذُقْتُ.
text.en: As for suspending (taʿlīq) by an interrogative word, by negation, by the lām of beginning, by an oath, or by inna with kasra when the lām of beginning comes into its khabar, that is, cancelling the governing necessarily in the wording but not in the meaning, it covers these verbs, as ʿalimtu a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun “I know whether Zayd is with you or ʿAmr”, raʾaytu mā Zaydun munṭaliqun “I saw [that] Zayd is not leaving”, wajadtu la-Zaydun munṭaliqun “I found Zayd surely leaving” and ʿalimtu inna Zaydan la-qāʾimun “I knew that Zayd is surely standing”; and every other verb of the heart, as shakaktu “I doubted”, nasītu “I forgot” and tabayyantu “I made sure”; and every verb by which knowledge is sought, as imtaḥantu “I tested” and saʾaltu “I asked”, and to these belong the verbs of the five senses, as lamastu “I touched”, abṣartu “I saw”, samiʿtu “I heard”, shamimtu “I smelt” and dhuqtu “I tasted”.

text.original: وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّالِثُ أَفْعَالٌ مُلْحَقَةٌ بِأَفْعَالِ الْقُلُوبِ فِي مُجَرَّدِ الدُّخُولِ عَلَى الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ، وَعَدَمِ جَوَازِ حَذْفِهِمَا مَعًا أَوْ حَذْفِ أَحَدِهِمَا فَقَطْ بِلَا قَرِينَةٍ، وَقِلَّةِ حَذْفِ أَحَدِهِمَا فَقَطْ بِهَا، نَحْوُ: صَيَّرَ وَجَعَلَ وَتَرَكَ وَاتَّخَذَ. وَالثَّالِثُ مُتَعَدٍّ إِلَى ثَلَاثَةِ مَفَاعِيلَ، نَحْوُ: أَعْلَمَ وَأَرَى، وَهَذِهِ مَفْعُولُهَا الْأَوَّلُ كَمَفْعُولِ بَابِ أَعْطَيْتُ، وَالْأَخِيرَانِ كَمَفْعُولَيْ بَابِ عَلِمْتُ، نَحْوُ: أَعْلَمَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا بَكْرًا فَاضِلًا.
text.en: The third division is verbs joined to the verbs of the heart only in coming upon the mubtadaʾ and the khabar, in not allowing both to be dropped together, or only one of them, without a context, and in dropping only one of them with a context being rare, as ṣayyara “he made [into]”, jaʿala “he made”, taraka “he left” and ittakhadha “he took [as]”. The third [sort] is transitive to three objects, as aʿlama “he informed” and arā “he showed”: the first object of these is like the object of the class of aʿṭaytu, and the last two are like the two objects of the class of ʿalimtu, as aʿlama Zaydun ʿAmran Bakran fāḍilan “Zayd informed ʿAmr that Bakr is excellent”.

lessons.title: The complete and the deficient verb; kāna and its sisters
body: “Every verb must have its marfūʿ.” If the speech is complete with it, the verb is complete (tāmm): its marfūʿ is the fāʿil, and its manṣūb, if it is transitive, the object. If it needs a manṣūb as well, it is deficient (nāqiṣ): its marfūʿ is its ism and its manṣūb its khabar, and it comes only upon what was in origin a mubtadaʾ and a khabar.

The first division does not indicate nearness, and it is what “deficient verb” means when said alone: kāna and ṣāra; āla, rajaʿa, ḥāla, istaḥāla, taḥawwala, irtadda, jāʾa and qaʿada “when they are in the sense of ṣāra”; aṣbaḥa, amsā, aḍḥā, ẓalla, bāta, āḍa, ʿāda, ghadā and rāḥa; mā zāla, mā fatiʾa (with fatḥa or kasra on the tāʾ), mā bariḥa, mā aftaʾa, mā wanā and mā rāma, “all in the sense of mā zāla”; and mā dāma and laysa.

A complete verb may take on the meaning of ṣāra and become deficient: tamma al-tisʿatu bi-hādhā ʿasharatan, “that is, ṣāra ʿasharatan tāmmatan”; kamula Zaydun ʿāliman, “that is, ṣāra ʿāliman kāmilan”. So the list is not closed: what makes a verb deficient is its meaning.

Their khabars may come before the verbs, except those that begin with mā: not qāʾiman mā zāla Zaydun, and the same if the negative in takes the place of mā. With lam or lan in its place it is allowed: qāʾiman lam yazal Zaydun. The commentators give the reason: mā of negation takes the front of the sentence, and nothing after it comes before it.

terms.en: the complete verb: its marfūʿ is a fāʿil
the deficient verb: an ism and a khabar
in the sense of ṣāra, “became”

examples.en: a complete verb become deficient
in the sense of ṣāra ʿāliman kāmilan
the khabar first, allowed with lam

tasks.prompt: Is tamma complete or deficient in tamma al-tisʿatu bi-hādhā ʿasharatan? Parse ʿasharatan.
tasks.answer: Deficient: tamma has taken the meaning of ṣāra. Al-tisʿatu is its ism, ʿasharatan its khabar in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Why is qāʾiman mā zāla Zaydun wrong but qāʾiman lam yazal Zaydun right?
tasks.answer: A khabar may not come before a deficient verb that begins with mā (or the negative in); with lam or lan in its place it may.

tasks.prompt: When is jāʾa a deficient verb?
tasks.answer: When it is in the sense of ṣāra, “became”; then it has an ism and a khabar.

text.original: ثُمَّ اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ لِكُلِّ فِعْلٍ مِنْ مَرْفُوعِهِ؛ فَإِنْ تَمَّ بِهِ كَلَامًا وَلَمْ يَحْتَجْ إِلَى غَيْرِهِ يُسَمَّى فِعْلًا تَامًّا، وَمَرْفُوعُهُ فَاعِلًا، وَمَنْصُوبُهُ مَفْعُولًا إِنْ كَانَ مُتَعَدِّيًا، كَالْأَفْعَالِ السَّابِقَةِ، وَإِنِ احْتَاجَ إِلَى مَعْمُولٍ مَنْصُوبٍ يُسَمَّى فِعْلًا نَاقِصًا، وَمَرْفُوعُهُ اسْمًا لَهُ، وَمَنْصُوبُهُ خَبَرًا لَهُ، وَلَا يَدْخُلُ إِلَّا عَلَى الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ فِي الْأَصْلِ.
text.en: Then know that every verb must have its marfūʿ. If speech is complete with it and it needs nothing else, it is called a complete verb (fiʿl tāmm), its marfūʿ is called the fāʿil, and its manṣūb is called the object if it is transitive, like the verbs above. If it needs a governed manṣūb word, it is called a deficient verb (fiʿl nāqiṣ), its marfūʿ is called its ism and its manṣūb its khabar; it comes only upon what is in origin a mubtadaʾ and a khabar.

text.original: وَهُوَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: الْقِسْمُ الْأَوَّلُ مَا لَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنَى الْمُقَارَبَةِ، فَهُوَ الشَّائِعُ الْمُتَبَادِرُ مِنْ إِطْلَاقِ الْفِعْلِ النَّاقِصِ، نَحْوُ: كَانَ وَصَارَ، وَكَذَا آلَ وَرَجَعَ وَحَالَ وَاسْتَحَالَ وَتَحَوَّلَ وَارْتَدَّ وَجَاءَ وَقَعَدَ إِذَا كُنَّ بِمَعْنَى صَارَ، وَأَصْبَحَ وَأَمْسَى وَأَضْحَى وَظَلَّ وَبَاتَ وَآضَ وَعَادَ وَغَدَا وَرَاحَ، وَمَا زَالَ، وَمَا فَتِئَ بِفَتْحِ التَّاءِ وَكَسْرِهَا، وَمَا بَرِحَ، وَمَا أَفْتَأَ، وَمَا وَنَى، وَمَا رَامَ، كُلُّهَا بِمَعْنَى مَا زَالَ، وَمَا دَامَ، وَلَيْسَ.
text.en: It is of two divisions. The first division is that which does not indicate the meaning of nearness; it is what is commonly meant and first understood when “deficient verb” is said without qualification, as kāna “he was” and ṣāra “he became”; and likewise āla, rajaʿa, ḥāla, istaḥāla, taḥawwala, irtadda, jāʾa and qaʿada, when they are in the sense of ṣāra; and aṣbaḥa, amsā, aḍḥā, ẓalla, bāta, āḍa, ʿāda, ghadā and rāḥa; and mā zāla, mā fatiʾa, with fatḥa or kasra on the tāʾ, mā bariḥa, mā aftaʾa, mā wanā and mā rāma, all of them in the sense of mā zāla “he did not cease”; and mā dāma “as long as” and laysa “he is not”.

text.original: وَقَدْ يَتَضَمَّنُ الْفِعْلُ التَّامُّ مَعْنَى صَارَ فَيَصِيرُ نَاقِصًا، نَحْوُ: تَمَّ التِّسْعَةُ بِهَذَا عَشَرَةً، أَيْ صَارَ عَشَرَةً تَامَّةً، وَكَمُلَ زَيْدٌ عَالِمًا، أَيْ صَارَ عَالِمًا كَامِلًا، وَغَيْرُ ذَلِكَ. وَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُ أَخْبَارِهَا عَلَى أَنْفُسِهَا إِلَّا مَا فِي أَوَّلِهِ مَا، فَلَا يَجُوزُ نَحْوُ: قَائِمًا مَا زَالَ زَيْدٌ، وَكَذَا إِنْ بُدِّلَ مَا بِإِنِ النَّافِيَةِ، وَأَمَّا إِنْ بُدِّلَ بِلَمْ وَلَنْ فَيَجُوزُ، نَحْوُ: قَائِمًا لَمْ يَزَلْ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: A complete verb may contain the meaning of ṣāra and so become deficient, as tamma al-tisʿatu bi-hādhā ʿasharatan “with this the nine were completed as ten”, that is, ṣāra ʿasharatan tāmmatan “it became a complete ten”, and kamula Zaydun ʿāliman “Zayd was perfected as a scholar”, that is, ṣāra ʿāliman kāmilan “he became a perfect scholar”, and others. Their khabars may be put before the verbs themselves, except those that begin with mā; so something like qāʾiman mā zāla Zaydun “standing Zayd did not cease [to be]” is not allowed; likewise if mā is replaced by the negative in. But if it is replaced by lam or lan, it is allowed, as qāʾiman lam yazal Zaydun “standing Zayd has not ceased [to be]”.

lessons.title: The verbs of nearness
body: The second division of the deficient verbs indicates nearness, and they are called the verbs of nearness (afʿāl al-muqāraba). “Their khabars can only be a muḍāriʿ verb.” They differ in whether that muḍāriʿ takes an.

ʿAsā: its khabar is mostly the muḍāriʿ with an, ʿasā Zaydun an yakhruja, “Zayd may go out”; an may be dropped. And ʿasā may be complete, with an and the muḍāriʿ as its fāʿil: ʿasā an yakhruja Zaydun, “it may be that Zayd goes out”.

Kāda: its khabar is mostly a muḍāriʿ without an, kāda Zaydun yakhruju, “Zayd almost went out”, and it may take an. Karaba is like kāda “in both its ways”. Halhala, ṭafiqa, akhadha, anshaʾa, aqbala, habba, jaʿala and ʿaliqa, verbs of beginning, take the muḍāriʿ without an. Awshaka is used as both ʿasā and kāda are used.

Unlike kāna and its kind, “the khabars of the verbs of nearness may not be put before the verbs themselves”. The commentators give the sense of the an: with ʿasā the act is hoped for and still to come, and an points to the future; with kāda and the verbs of beginning the act is near or already begun, so the bare muḍāriʿ fits.

terms.en: the verbs of nearness: their khabar a muḍāriʿ
the complete ʿasā, with an and the muḍāriʿ as fāʿil
the verbs of beginning: ṭafiqa, akhadha, jaʿala…

examples.en: ʿasā with an: the deficient use
the complete ʿasā
kāda without an

tasks.arabic: عَسَى زَيْدٌ أَنْ يَخْرُجَ — عَسَى أَنْ يَخْرُجَ زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: First: ʿasā deficient, Zaydun its ism, an yakhruja its khabar. Second: ʿasā complete, an yakhruja Zaydun its fāʿil (an with the verb as a maṣdar).

tasks.prompt: Which verbs of nearness take the muḍāriʿ without an?
tasks.answer: Mostly kāda and karaba; always halhala, ṭafiqa, akhadha, anshaʾa, aqbala, habba, jaʿala and ʿaliqa.

tasks.prompt: May one say yakhruju kāda Zaydun?
tasks.answer: No: the khabars of the verbs of nearness may not come before the verbs themselves.

text.original: وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّانِي مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنَى الْقُرْبِ، وَيُسَمَّى أَفْعَالَ الْمُقَارَبَةِ، وَلَا يَكُونُ أَخْبَارُهَا إِلَّا فِعْلًا مُضَارِعًا، نَحْوُ: عَسَى، وَخَبَرُهُ الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ مَعَ أَنْ غَالِبًا، نَحْوُ: عَسَى زَيْدٌ أَنْ يَخْرُجَ، وَقَدْ تُحْذَفُ أَنْ، وَقَدْ تَكُونُ تَامَّةً بِأَنْ مَعَ الْمُضَارِعِ، نَحْوُ: عَسَى أَنْ يَخْرُجَ زَيْدٌ. وَكَادَ، وَخَبَرُهُ غَالِبًا مُضَارِعٌ بِلَا أَنْ، نَحْوُ: كَادَ زَيْدٌ يَخْرُجُ، وَقَدْ يَكُونُ مَعَ أَنْ.
text.en: The second division is that which indicates the meaning of nearness; they are called the verbs of nearness (afʿāl al-muqāraba), and their khabars can only be a muḍāriʿ verb, as ʿasā “it may be”, whose khabar is mostly the muḍāriʿ verb with an, as ʿasā Zaydun an yakhruja “Zayd may go out”; an may be dropped; and it may be complete, with an and the muḍāriʿ [as its fāʿil], as ʿasā an yakhruja Zaydun “it may be that Zayd goes out”. And kāda “he almost”, whose khabar is mostly a muḍāriʿ without an, as kāda Zaydun yakhruju “Zayd almost went out”; it may be with an.

text.original: وَكَرَبَ، وَهُوَ مِثْلُ كَادَ فِي وَجْهَيْهِ، وَهَلْهَلَ وَطَفِقَ وَأَخَذَ وَأَنْشَأَ وَأَقْبَلَ وَهَبَّ وَجَعَلَ وَعَلِقَ، وَأَخْبَارُهَا الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ بِلَا أَنْ، وَأَوْشَكَ، وَهُوَ يُسْتَعْمَلُ اسْتِعْمَالَ عَسَى وَكَادَ. وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُ أَخْبَارِ أَفْعَالِ الْمُقَارَبَةِ عَلَى أَنْفُسِهَا.
text.en: And karaba, which is like kāda in both its ways; and halhala, ṭafiqa, akhadha, anshaʾa, aqbala, habba, jaʿala and ʿaliqa “he began”, whose khabars are the muḍāriʿ verb without an; and awshaka, which is used as ʿasā and kāda are used. The khabars of the verbs of nearness may not be put before the verbs themselves.

parts.title: The governors by rule: the nouns; the abstract governor

lessons.title: The active and the passive participle
body: The second governor by rule is the active participle, which governs as its active verb governs; the third is the passive participle, which governs as its passive verb. Governing a separate fāʿil or an object, they must not be diminutives, ḍuwayrib, muḍayrib, nor qualified by an adjective first, jāʾanī ḍāribun shadīdun. An adjective after the governing does not harm it: jāʾanī rajulun ḍāribun ghulāmuhu shadīdun.

With the lām, no other condition is laid down: al-ḍāribu ghulāmuhu ʿAmran amsi ʿindanā, even with amsi, “yesterday”; the commentators explain that the lām is a relative, and the participle stands in place of a verb. Without the lām, the participle must lean on a mubtadaʾ, a qualified noun or the owner of a ḥāl, jāʾanī Zaydun rākiban ghulāmuhu; on a question, a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni; or on a negation, mā qāʾimun al-Zaydāni.

And to put an object in naṣb, the participle without the lām must mean the present or the future. Ḍāribun Zaydan amsi is not said; one says ḍāribu Zaydin amsi, in iḍāfa. The book gives the condition; the example is the commentators'.

The dual and plural govern like the singular, al-Zaydāni ḍāribāni ʿAmran; and so do three intensive patterns, faʿʿāl, faʿūl and mifʿāl, “and for the governing of these three the meaning of present or future is not a condition”.

terms.en: leaning on a word before it
the diminutive and the qualified: they do not govern
the intensive patterns: faʿʿāl, faʿūl, mifʿāl

examples.en: qualified after governing: allowed
with the lām: no further condition
leaning on a question and a negation

tasks.prompt: Why may al-ḍāribu govern ʿAmran with amsi, yesterday?
tasks.answer: With the lām no condition is laid down but those already given; the condition of present or future applies only to the participle without the lām.

tasks.prompt: What does qāʾimun lean on in mā qāʾimun al-Zaydāni, and what does it govern?
tasks.answer: On the negation mā; it puts al-Zaydāni in rafʿ as its fāʿil, which also completes the sentence.

tasks.prompt: Why does ḍāribun not govern in jāʾanī ḍāribun shadīdun?
tasks.answer: It is qualified by an adjective before governing; the adjective takes it away from the verb. Qualified after governing, it would keep its work.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي اسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ، فَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ الْمَعْلُومِ. وَالثَّالِثُ اسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ، فَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ الْمَجْهُولِ. وَشَرْطُ عَمَلِهِمَا فِي الْفَاعِلِ الْمُنْفَصِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَا مُصَغَّرَيْنِ، نَحْوُ ضُوَيْرِبٍ وَمُضَيْرِبٍ، وَلَا مَوْصُوفَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي ضَارِبٌ شَدِيدٌ، وَإِنْ وُصِفَا بَعْدَ الْعَمَلِ لَمْ يَضُرَّ عَمَلَهُمَا السَّابِقَ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ ضَارِبٌ غُلَامُهُ شَدِيدٌ.
text.en: The second is the active participle (ism al-fāʿil): it governs as its active verb governs. The third is the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl): it governs as its passive verb governs. The condition for their governing a separate fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi is that they are not diminutives, as ḍuwayribin and muḍayribin, and not qualified by an adjective, as jāʾanī ḍāribun shadīdun “a hard hitter came to me”; but if they are qualified after governing, this does not harm their governing that came before, as jāʾanī rajulun ḍāribun ghulāmuhu shadīdun “a man came to me whose servant is hitting hard”.

text.original: ثُمَّ إِنْ كَانَا بِاللَّامِ لَا يُشْتَرَطُ لِعَمَلِهِمَا غَيْرُ مَا ذُكِرَ، نَحْوُ: الضَّارِبُ غُلَامُهُ عَمْرًا أَمْسِ عِنْدَنَا، وَإِنْ كَانَا مُجَرَّدَيْنِ مِنْهَا يُشْتَرَطُ مَعَهُ الِاعْتِمَادُ عَلَى الْمُبْتَدَإِ أَوِ الْمَوْصُوفِ أَوْ ذِي الْحَالِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ رَاكِبًا غُلَامُهُ، أَوِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ، نَحْوُ: أَقَائِمٌ الزَّيْدَانِ، أَوِ النَّفْيِ، نَحْوُ: مَا قَائِمٌ الزَّيْدَانِ. وَيُشْتَرَطُ فِي نَصْبِهِمَا الْمَفْعُولَ بِهِ الدَّلَالَةُ عَلَى الْحَالِ أَوِ الِاسْتِقْبَالِ.
text.en: Then, if they have the lām, no condition other than what was said is laid down for their governing, as al-ḍāribu ghulāmuhu ʿAmran amsi ʿindanā “the one whose servant hit ʿAmr yesterday is with us”. If they are free of it, it is a further condition that they lean on a mubtadaʾ, on a qualified noun or on the owner of a ḥāl, as jāʾanī Zaydun rākiban ghulāmuhu “Zayd came to me, his servant riding”; or on an interrogative, as a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni “are the two Zayds standing?”; or on a negation, as mā qāʾimun al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds are not standing”. For their putting the mafʿūl bihi in naṣb it is a condition that they indicate the present or the future.

text.original: وَتَثْنِيَتُهُمَا وَجَمْعُهُمَا كَمُفْرَدِهِمَا، وَكَذَا ثَلَاثَةُ أَوْزَانٍ مِنْ مُبَالَغَةِ الْفَاعِلِ، نَحْوُ فَعَّالٍ وَفَعُولٍ وَمِفْعَالٍ، وَلَا يُشْتَرَطُ فِي عَمَلِ هَذِهِ الثَّلَاثَةِ مَعْنَى الْحَالِ وَالِاسْتِقْبَالِ.
text.en: Their dual and plural are like their singular; and likewise three patterns of the intensive of the active participle, as faʿʿālin, faʿūlin and mifʿālin; and for the governing of these three the meaning of present or future is not a condition.

lessons.title: The resembling adjective, the elative, the maṣdar
body: The fourth governor by rule is the resembling adjective, which governs as its verb governs, under the conditions of the active participle, “except the meaning of present or future, which is not a condition”: Zaydun ḥasanun wajhuhu. The commentators give the reason: it describes a lasting quality, so a condition of time would mean nothing.

The fifth is the elative (ism al-tafḍīl). “By agreement it does not put the mafʿūl bihi in naṣb”, and it does not raise a visible fāʿil unless it has taken the meaning of the verb: when it describes something connected with the noun it follows, preferred as so connected over itself as connected with another, and is negated. The book's example is the famous one: mā raʾaytu rajulan aḥsana fī ʿaynihi al-kuḥlu minhu fī ʿayni Zaydin, “I have not seen a man in whose eye kohl is more beautiful than in the eye of Zayd”. Al-kuḥlu is the fāʿil of aḥsana. Other words, a ḥāl, an adverb, a tamyīz, it governs freely.

The sixth is the maṣdar. To govern a fāʿil and an object it must not be a diminutive, nor qualified, nor joined with the ḥāl, nor, “according to most”, defined by the lām; nor a maṣdar of number, of kind, or of emphasis, when its verb is meant and need not be dropped. If the verb must be dropped, the maṣdar governs in its place: saqyan Zaydan, “[God] water Zayd!”.
Three things are true of the maṣdar alone: its fāʿil may be dropped “without a deputy”, which nothing else allows; its fāʿil is not hidden in it; and what it governs does not come before it.

terms.en: the resembling adjective: no condition of time
the elative: no object; a visible fāʿil only in one case
the question of the kohl: the elative raising a visible fāʿil

examples.en: the resembling adjective raising its fāʿil

examples.arabic: مَا رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا أَحْسَنَ فِي عَيْنِهِ الْكُحْلُ مِنْهُ فِي عَيْنِ زَيْدٍ
examples.en: the elative raising a visible fāʿil
a maṣdar in place of a verb that must be dropped

tasks.prompt: What raises al-kuḥlu in the book's example, and on what three conditions?
tasks.arabic: مَا رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا أَحْسَنَ فِي عَيْنِهِ الْكُحْلُ مِنْهُ فِي عَيْنِ زَيْدٍ
tasks.answer: The elative aḥsana. It describes something connected with rajulan (the kohl in his eye); the kohl is preferred, as in his eye, over itself in Zayd's eye; and the sentence is negated.

tasks.prompt: Why does saqyan govern Zaydan?
tasks.answer: Its verb (saqā) must be dropped in a prayer like this, and the maṣdar stands in the verb's place, so it governs.

tasks.prompt: Name three conditions under which a maṣdar does not govern.
tasks.answer: Any three of: a diminutive; qualified; joined with the ḥāl; defined by the lām (for most); a maṣdar of number, of kind, or of emphasis whose verb is meant and need not be dropped.

quiz.explanation: It stands in the verb's place.

quiz.prompt: Which may drop its fāʿil without a deputy?

text.original: وَالرَّابِعُ الصِّفَةُ الْمُشَبَّهَةُ، فَهِيَ تَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهَا بِالشُّرُوطِ الْمُعْتَبَرَةِ فِي اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ غَيْرَ مَعْنَى الْحَالِ وَالِاسْتِقْبَالِ، فَإِنَّهُ لَا يُشْتَرَطُ فِي عَمَلِهَا، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ حَسَنٌ وَجْهُهُ.
text.en: The fourth is the resembling adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha): it governs as its verb governs, under the conditions laid down for the active participle, except the meaning of present or future, which is not a condition for its governing, as Zaydun ḥasanun wajhuhu “Zayd, his face is handsome”.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ اسْمُ التَّفْضِيلِ، وَهُوَ لَا يَنْصِبُ الْمَفْعُولَ بِهِ بِالِاتِّفَاقِ، وَلَا يَرْفَعُ الْفَاعِلَ الظَّاهِرَ إِلَّا إِذَا صَارَ بِمَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ، بِأَنْ يَكُونَ وَصْفًا لِمُتَعَلَّقِ مَا جَرَى عَلَيْهِ، مُفَضَّلًا بِاعْتِبَارِ التَّعَلُّقِ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ بِاعْتِبَارِ غَيْرِهِ، مَنْفِيًّا، نَحْوُ: مَا رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا أَحْسَنَ فِي عَيْنِهِ الْكُحْلُ مِنْهُ فِي عَيْنِ زَيْدٍ، وَيَعْمَلُ فِي غَيْرِهِمَا.
text.en: The fifth is the noun of preference (ism al-tafḍīl). By agreement it does not put the mafʿūl bihi in naṣb, and it does not put a visible fāʿil in rafʿ, unless it has come to have the meaning of the verb: that is, it is an adjective of something connected with what it is said of, preferred, as so connected, over itself as connected with something else, and it is negated, as mā raʾaytu rajulan aḥsana fī ʿaynihi al-kuḥlu minhu fī ʿayni Zaydin “I have not seen a man in whose eye kohl is more beautiful than it is in the eye of Zayd”. It governs words other than these two.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسُ الْمَصْدَرُ، وَشَرْطُ عَمَلِهِ فِي الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مُصَغَّرًا، وَلَا مَوْصُوفًا، وَلَا مُقْتَرِنًا بِالْحَالِ، وَلَا مُعَرَّفًا بِاللَّامِ عِنْدَ الْأَكْثَرِ، وَلَا عَدَدًا، وَلَا نَوْعًا، وَلَا تَأْكِيدًا مَعَ الْفِعْلِ أَوْ بِدُونِهِ وَالْفِعْلُ مُرَادٌ غَيْرُ لَازِمِ الْحَذْفِ، وَإِنْ كَانَ لَازِمَ الْحَذْفِ فَيَعْمَلُ الْمَصْدَرُ لِقِيَامِهِ مَقَامَ الْفِعْلِ، نَحْوُ: سَقْيًا زَيْدًا. وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُ فَاعِلِهِ بِلَا نَائِبٍ، وَلَا يَجُوزُ هَذَا فِي غَيْرِ الْمَصْدَرِ، وَلَا يُضْمَرُ فِيهِ، وَلَا يَتَقَدَّمُ مَعْمُولُهُ عَلَيْهِ.
text.en: The sixth is the maṣdar. The condition for its governing the fāʿil and the mafʿūl bihi is that it is not a diminutive; not qualified by an adjective; not joined with the ḥāl; according to most, not defined by the lām; and not [a maṣdar] of number, of kind, or of emphasis, with the verb or without it, when the verb is meant and its dropping is not necessary. If its dropping is necessary, the maṣdar governs, because it stands in the place of the verb, as saqyan Zaydan “[God] water Zayd!”. Its fāʿil may be dropped without a deputy, which is not allowed in anything but the maṣdar; [its fāʿil] is not hidden in it; and what it governs does not come before it.

lessons.title: The muḍāf; the two kinds of iḍāfa
body: The seventh governor by rule is the muḍāf, which governs the jarr. It must be a noun free of its tanwīn and of what stands for it (the nūn of the dual and plural), “for the sake of the iḍāfa”; not equal to the muḍāf ilayhi in generality and particularity; and not absolutely more particular than it. The commentators' example of the second: one does not say layth asadin, both meaning “lion”.

The iḍāfa of meaning (maʿnawiyya) is where the muḍāf is not an adjective joined to what it governs: ghulāmu Zaydin, and ḍāribu ʿAmrin amsi, where the participle with amsi governs nothing and is a plain noun. The muḍāf must be free of definiteness. It has the sense of min when the second is a genus that includes the first, khātamu fiḍḍatin; otherwise, “which is more frequent”, the sense of the lām: ghulāmu Zaydin, raʾsu ʿAmrin.

It makes the muḍāf definite when the muḍāf ilayhi is definite, ghulāmu Zaydin, unless the muḍāf is ghayr, shibh or mithl, which iḍāfa does not make definite; and particular when the muḍāf ilayhi is indefinite, ghulāmu rajulin.

The iḍāfa of wording (lafẓiyya) is an adjective joined to what it governs: ḍāribu Zaydin, ḥasanu al-wajhi, maʿmūru al-dāri, al-ḍāribā Zaydin, al-ḍāribū Zaydin. It “gives nothing but lightness in the wording”: a tanwīn or nūn dropped. So al-ḍāribu Zaydin is not allowed, for nothing is lightened; but al-ḍāribu al-rajuli is, “on the model of al-ḥasani al-wajhi”, whose origin is al-ḥasanu wajhuhu.

terms.en: the iḍāfa of meaning: gives definiteness or particularity
the iḍāfa of wording: gives only lightness
in the sense of min, or of the lām

examples.en: the iḍāfa in the sense of min
definiteness and particularity
the iḍāfa of wording
allowed, on the model of al-ḥasani al-wajhi

tasks.prompt: Of which kind is the iḍāfa in ḍāribu ʿAmrin amsi, and why?
tasks.answer: Of meaning: with amsi the participle means the past and does not govern ʿAmr, so it is not an adjective joined to what it governs.

tasks.prompt: Does mithlu Zaydin become definite? Explain.
tasks.answer: No: ghayr, shibh and mithl are not made definite by iḍāfa, even to a definite noun.

tasks.prompt: Why is al-ḍāribā Zaydin allowed but al-ḍāribu Zaydin not?
tasks.answer: The iḍāfa of wording must lighten something. In al-ḍāribā the nūn of the dual is dropped; in al-ḍāribu Zaydin nothing is dropped, since al- already removed the tanwīn.

quiz.explanation: For the sake of the iḍāfa.

quiz.explanation: Silver is a genus that includes the ring.

quiz.explanation: An adjective on what it governs.

quiz.prompt: Al-ḍāribu al-rajuli is allowed on the model of…

text.original: وَالسَّابِعُ الِاسْمُ الْمُضَافُ، وَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ الْجَرَّ، وَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ اسْمًا مُجَرَّدًا عَنْ تَنْوِينِهِ وَنَائِبِهِ لِأَجْلِ الْإِضَافَةِ، وَأَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مُسَاوِيًا لِلْمُضَافِ إِلَيْهِ فِي الْعُمُومِ وَالْخُصُوصِ، وَلَا أَخَصَّ مِنْهُ مُطْلَقًا. وَهِيَ عَلَى نَوْعَيْنِ: مَعْنَوِيَّةٌ وَلَفْظِيَّةٌ. فَالْمَعْنَوِيَّةُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمُضَافُ غَيْرَ صِفَةٍ مُضَافَةٍ إِلَى مَعْمُولِهَا، نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَضَارِبُ عَمْرٍو أَمْسِ، وَشَرْطُهَا تَجْرِيدُ الْمُضَافِ مِنَ التَّعْرِيفِ.
text.en: The seventh is the muḍāf noun: it governs the jarr. Its condition is that it is a noun free of its tanwīn and of what stands in its place, for the sake of the iḍāfa; that it is not equal to the muḍāf ilayhi in generality and particularity; and that it is not absolutely more particular than it. [The iḍāfa] is of two kinds: of meaning (maʿnawiyya) and of wording (lafẓiyya). That of meaning is when the muḍāf is not an adjective made muḍāf to what it governs, as ghulāmu Zaydin “Zayd's servant” and ḍāribu ʿAmrin amsi “the one who hit ʿAmr yesterday”; its condition is that the muḍāf is free of definiteness.

text.original: وَهِيَ إِمَّا بِمَعْنَى مِنْ إِنْ كَانَ الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ جِنْسًا شَامِلًا لِلْمُضَافِ وَغَيْرِهِ، نَحْوُ: خَاتَمُ فِضَّةٍ، أَوْ بِمَعْنَى اللَّامِ فِي غَيْرِهِ، وَهُوَ الْأَكْثَرُ، نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَرَأْسُ عَمْرٍو. وَتُفِيدُ تَعْرِيفًا إِنْ كَانَ الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ مَعْرِفَةً وَالْمُضَافُ غَيْرَ غَيْرٍ وَشِبْهٍ وَمِثْلٍ، فَإِنَّهَا لَا تَتَعَرَّفُ بِالْإِضَافَةِ، نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَتَخْصِيصًا إِنْ كَانَ نَكِرَةً، نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ رَجُلٍ.
text.en: It is in the sense of min “of” if the muḍāf ilayhi is a genus that includes the muḍāf and other things, as khātamu fiḍḍatin “a ring of silver”, or in the sense of the lām otherwise, which is more frequent, as ghulāmu Zaydin “Zayd's servant” and raʾsu ʿAmrin “ʿAmr's head”. It gives definiteness if the muḍāf ilayhi is definite and the muḍāf is not ghayrin “other”, shibhin “likeness” or mithlin “like”, for these are not made definite by the iḍāfa, as ghulāmu Zaydin “Zayd's servant”; and particularity if it is indefinite, as ghulāmu rajulin “a man's servant”.

text.original: وَاللَّفْظِيَّةُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمُضَافُ صِفَةً مُضَافَةً إِلَى مَعْمُولِهَا، وَلَا تُفِيدُ إِلَّا تَخْفِيفًا فِي اللَّفْظِ، نَحْوُ: ضَارِبُ زَيْدٍ، وَحَسَنُ الْوَجْهِ، وَمَعْمُورُ الدَّارِ، وَالضَّارِبَا زَيْدٍ، وَالضَّارِبُو زَيْدٍ. وَامْتَنَعَ نَحْوُ: الضَّارِبُ زَيْدٍ؛ لِعَدَمِ التَّخْفِيفِ، وَجَازَ نَحْوُ: الضَّارِبُ الرَّجُلِ؛ حَمْلًا عَلَى الْحَسَنِ الْوَجْهِ، أَصْلُهُ: الْحَسَنُ وَجْهُهُ.
text.en: That of wording is when the muḍāf is an adjective made muḍāf to what it governs; it gives nothing but lightness in the wording, as ḍāribu Zaydin “hitting Zayd”, ḥasanu al-wajhi “handsome of face”, maʿmūru al-dāri “whose house is lived in”, al-ḍāribā Zaydin “the two hitting Zayd” and al-ḍāribū Zaydin “those hitting Zayd”. Something like al-ḍāribu Zaydin is not allowed, because there is no lightening; and something like al-ḍāribu al-rajuli “the one hitting the man” is allowed, on the model of al-ḥasani al-wajhi “the handsome of face”, whose origin is al-ḥasanu wajhuhu “the one whose face is handsome”.

lessons.title: The complete vague noun and its tamyīz; the tamyīz of number
body: The eighth is the complete vague noun, which puts an indefinite noun in naṣb as a tamyīz. Its completeness is “its being in a state in which it cannot be made muḍāf”, by one of five things. By itself: the vague pronoun, rubbahu rajulan, yā lahu rajulan, niʿma rajulan, and the demonstrative, mādhā arāda llāhu bi-hādhā mathalan (Q 2:26). By tanwīn, said, riṭlun zaytan, or understood, mathāqīlu dhahaban, aḥada ʿashara rajulan.

By the nūn of the dual, manawāni samnan; and with some of these two kinds the iḍāfa is allowed instead, riṭlu zaytin, manawā samnin, but not with others. By the nūn that resembles the plural, “which is twenty to ninety”, ʿishrūna dirhaman. And by iḍāfa, milʾuhu ʿasalan. What the complete noun governs does not come before it.

The numbers each have their rule. Three to ten do not take a tamyīz in naṣb: it is majrūr and plural, thalāthatu rijālin, except in three hundred to nine hundred. Eleven to ninety-nine take it “manṣūb and singular, always”. A hundred and a thousand, their duals and plurals, take it singular and majrūr: miʾatu rajulin, alfu dirhamin.
So the counted noun follows a pattern worth learning by heart: three to ten, plural in jarr; eleven to ninety-nine, singular in naṣb; a hundred and a thousand, singular in jarr.

terms.en: the complete vague noun: it cannot be made muḍāf
the tamyīz: an indefinite in naṣb that removes vagueness
the nūn that resembles the plural: ʿishrūna to tisʿūna

examples.en: complete by itself: the vague pronoun
by tanwīn, or in iḍāfa
three to ten: plural in jarr
a hundred and a thousand: singular in jarr

tasks.answer: Aḥada ʿashara: an understood tanwīn. Manawāni: the nūn of the dual. Milʾuhu: iḍāfa (to the pronoun).

tasks.prompt: Give the case and number of the counted noun after three, after fifteen, and after a thousand.
tasks.answer: After three: plural, in jarr (thalāthatu rijālin). After fifteen: singular, in naṣb. After a thousand: singular, in jarr (alfu dirhamin).

text.original: وَالثَّامِنُ الِاسْمُ الْمُبْهَمُ التَّامُّ، فَإِنَّهُ يَنْصِبُ اسْمًا نَكِرَةً عَلَى التَّمْيِيزِ. وَتَمَامُهُ، أَيْ كَوْنُهُ عَلَى حَالَةٍ يَمْتَنِعُ إِضَافَتُهُ مَعَهَا، بِأَحَدِ خَمْسَةِ أَشْيَاءَ: بِنَفْسِهِ، وَذَلِكَ فِي الضَّمِيرِ الْمُبْهَمِ، نَحْوُ: رُبَّهُ رَجُلًا، وَيَا لَهُ رَجُلًا، وَنِعْمَ رَجُلًا، وَفِي اسْمِ الْإِشَارَةِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: مَاذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ بِهَذَا مَثَلًا. وَبِالتَّنْوِينِ، إِمَّا لَفْظًا، نَحْوُ: رِطْلٌ زَيْتًا، أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، نَحْوُ: مَثَاقِيلُ ذَهَبًا، وَأَحَدَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا.
text.en: The eighth is the complete vague noun (al-ism al-mubham al-tāmm): it puts an indefinite noun in naṣb as a tamyīz. Its completeness, that is, its being in a state in which it cannot be made muḍāf, is by one of five things. By itself, and that is in the vague pronoun, as rubbahu rajulan “many a man!”, yā lahu rajulan “what a man he is!” and niʿma rajulan “an excellent man”, and in the demonstrative, as His saying, Most High: mādhā arāda Allāhu bi-hādhā mathalan “what does God mean by this as a parable?” [2:26]. By the tanwīn, either in the wording, as riṭlun zaytan “a raṭl of oil”, or understood, as mathāqīlu dhahaban “mithqāls of gold” and aḥada ʿashara rajulan “eleven men”.

text.original: وَمُمَيِّزُ ثَلَاثَةٍ إِلَى عَشَرَةٍ لَا يُنْصَبُ، بَلْ هُوَ مَجْرُورٌ وَمَجْمُوعٌ، نَحْوُ: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ، إِلَّا فِي ثَلَاثِمِائَةٍ إِلَى تِسْعِمِائَةٍ. وَمُمَيِّزُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ إِلَى تِسْعَةٍ وَتِسْعِينَ مَنْصُوبٌ مُفْرَدٌ دَائِمًا. وَمُمَيِّزُ مِائَةٍ وَأَلْفٍ وَتَثْنِيَتِهِمَا وَجَمْعِهِمَا لَا يُنْصَبُ، بَلْ هُوَ مُفْرَدٌ مَجْرُورٌ، نَحْوُ: مِائَةُ رَجُلٍ، وَأَلْفُ دِرْهَمٍ.
text.en: The tamyīz of three to ten is not put in naṣb: it is majrūr and plural, as thalāthatu rijālin “three men”, except in thalāthimiʾatin “three hundred” to tisʿimiʾatin “nine hundred”. The tamyīz of eleven to ninety-nine is always manṣūb and singular. The tamyīz of a hundred and a thousand, of their duals and of their plurals is not put in naṣb: it is singular and majrūr, as miʾatu rajulin “a hundred men” and alfu dirhamin “a thousand dirhams”.

text.original: وَبِنُونِ التَّثْنِيَةِ، نَحْوُ: مَنَوَانِ سَمْنًا، وَيَجُوزُ فِي بَعْضِ هَذَيْنِ الْقِسْمَيْنِ الْإِضَافَةُ، نَحْوُ: رِطْلُ زَيْتٍ، وَمَنَوَا سَمْنٍ، وَلَا يَجُوزُ فِي غَيْرِهِمَا. وَبِنُونِ شِبْهِ الْجَمْعِ، وَهُوَ عِشْرُونَ إِلَى تِسْعِينَ، نَحْوُ: عِشْرُونَ دِرْهَمًا. وَبِالْإِضَافَةِ، نَحْوُ: مِلْؤُهُ عَسَلًا. وَلَا يَتَقَدَّمُ مَعْمُولُ الِاسْمِ التَّامِّ عَلَيْهِ.
text.en: By the nūn of the dual, as manawāni samnan “two manās of clarified butter”; in some of these two divisions the iḍāfa is allowed, as riṭlu zaytin “a raṭl of oil” and manawā samnin “two manās of clarified butter”, and it is not allowed in others. By the nūn that resembles the plural, which is twenty to ninety, as ʿishrūna dirhaman “twenty dirhams”. And by the iḍāfa, as milʾuhu ʿasalan “its fill of honey”. What the complete noun governs does not come before it.

lessons.title: The meaning of the verb: the nouns of verbs; the settled adverb
lessons.arabic: مَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ: أَسْمَاءُ الْأَفْعَالِ وَالظَّرْفُ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ
lessons.transliteration: maʿnā al-fiʿl: asmāʾ al-afʿāl wa-l-ẓarf al-mustaqarr
body: The ninth governor by rule is “the meaning of the verb”: “every word from which the meaning of a verb is understood”. First among them are the nouns of verbs (asmāʾ al-afʿāl), in the sense of the imperative or of the past. They govern as the verb they name governs, and what they govern does not come before them.

In the sense of the imperative: hā Zaydan, “that is, khudhhu”; ruwayda Zaydan, amhilhu; halumma Zaydan, aḥḍirhu; hāti shayʾan, aʿṭihi; ḥayyahali al-tharīda, iʾtihi; balha Zaydan, daʿhu; ʿalayka Zaydan, ilzamhu; dūnaka ʿAmran, khudhhu; tarāki Zaydan, utrukhu. In the sense of the past: hayhāta al-amru, baʿuda; shattāna Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, iftaraqā; sarʿāna Zaydun and washkāna ʿAmrun, qarubā, “they were near”.

The settled adverb (lesson 5) also has the meaning of a verb. “By agreement it does not govern the mafʿūl bihi”, and it raises a visible fāʿil only when it leans on what was named for the participle, or on a relative: Zaydun fī al-dāri abūhu; mā fī al-dāri aḥadun; jāʾanī alladhī fī al-dāri abūhu. It may also be a khabar put first.

When it raises no visible noun, “its fāʿil is a pronoun hidden in it, moved over from the dropped word it is attached to”: in Zaydun fī al-dāri, the pronoun of ḥaṣala has passed into fī al-dāri. And it governs a ḥāl or an adverb without any condition.

terms.en: the meaning of the verb: any word that gives it
the nouns of verbs: of the imperative or the past
the pronoun moved into the adverb from its dropped verb

examples.en: a noun of a verb in the sense of the imperative
a noun of a verb in the sense of the past
the settled adverb raising a visible fāʿil

tasks.prompt: Give the verb named by each and parse the noun after it: balha Zaydan; hayhāta al-amru.
tasks.answer: Balha = daʿ, “leave”: Zaydan is its object in naṣb. Hayhāta = baʿuda, “it was far”: al-amru is its fāʿil in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: What does fī al-dāri raise in Zaydun fī al-dāri abūhu, and what does it lean on?
tasks.answer: It raises abūhu as its fāʿil; it leans on the mubtadaʾ Zaydun, of which it is the khabar.

tasks.prompt: In Zaydun fī al-dāri, where is the fāʿil of the adverb?
tasks.answer: A pronoun hidden in fī al-dāri, moved over from the dropped verb (ḥaṣala) it is attached to.

text.original: وَالتَّاسِعُ مَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ، وَالْمُرَادُ مِنْهُ كُلُّ لَفْظٍ يُفْهَمُ مِنْهُ مَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ. فَمِنْهُ أَسْمَاءُ الْأَفْعَالِ، وَهُوَ مَا كَانَ بِمَعْنَى الْأَمْرِ أَوِ الْمَاضِي، وَيَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ مُسَمَّاهُ، وَلَا يَتَقَدَّمُ مَعْمُولُهُ عَلَيْهِ.
text.en: The ninth is the meaning of the verb; by it is meant every word from which the meaning of a verb is understood. To it belong the verb-nouns (asmāʾ al-afʿāl), which are those in the sense of the imperative or of the past; they govern as what they name governs, and what they govern does not come before them.

text.original: وَالْأَوَّلُ نَحْوُ: هَا زَيْدًا، أَيْ خُذْهُ، وَرُوَيْدَ زَيْدًا، أَيْ أَمْهِلْهُ، وَهَلُمَّ زَيْدًا، أَيْ أَحْضِرْهُ، وَهَاتِ شَيْئًا، أَيْ أَعْطِهِ، وَحَيَّهَلِ الثَّرِيدَ، أَيِ ائْتِهِ، وَبَلْهَ زَيْدًا، أَيْ دَعْهُ، وَعَلَيْكَ زَيْدًا، أَيِ الْزَمْهُ، وَدُونَكَ عَمْرًا، أَيْ خُذْهُ، وَتَرَاكِ زَيْدًا، أَيِ اتْرُكْهُ، وَغَيْرُ ذَلِكَ. وَالثَّانِي نَحْوُ: هَيْهَاتَ الْأَمْرُ، أَيْ بَعُدَ، وَشَتَّانَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو، أَيِ افْتَرَقَا، وَسَرْعَانَ زَيْدٌ، وَوَشْكَانَ عَمْرٌو، أَيْ قَرُبَا.
text.en: The first [kind] is as hā Zaydan “here, Zayd!”, that is, khudhhu “take him”; ruwayda Zaydan “gently with Zayd!”, that is, amhilhu “give him time”; halumma Zaydan “bring Zayd!”, that is, aḥḍirhu “bring him”; hāti shayʾan “give something!”, that is, aʿṭihi “give it”; ḥayyahali al-tharīda “come to the tharīd!”, that is, iʾtihi “come to it”; balha Zaydan “leave Zayd!”, that is, daʿhu “leave him”; ʿalayka Zaydan “keep to Zayd!”, that is, ilzamhu “keep to him”; dūnaka ʿAmran “take ʿAmr!”, that is, khudhhu “take him”; tarāki Zaydan “let Zayd be!”, that is, utrukʹhu “let him be”; and others. The second is as hayhāta al-amru “how far the matter is!”, that is, baʿuda “it was far”; shattāna Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun “how different Zayd and ʿAmr are!”, that is, iftaraqā “they differed”; and sarʿāna Zaydun “how quick Zayd was!” and washkāna ʿAmrun “how quick ʿAmr was!”, that is, qarubā “they were near”.

text.original: وَمِنْهُ الظَّرْفُ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ، وَقَدْ مَرَّ تَفْسِيرُهُ، وَهُوَ لَا يَعْمَلُ فِي الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ بِالِاتِّفَاقِ، وَلَا فِي الْفَاعِلِ الظَّاهِرِ إِلَّا بِشَرْطِ الِاعْتِمَادِ عَلَى مَا ذُكِرَ أَوِ الْمَوْصُولِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ أَبُوهُ، وَمَا فِي الدَّارِ أَحَدٌ، وَجَاءَنِي الَّذِي فِي الدَّارِ أَبُوهُ. وَيَجُوزُ كَوْنُ الظَّرْفِ خَبَرًا مُقَدَّمًا. وَإِذَا لَمْ يَرْفَعْ ظَاهِرًا فَفَاعِلُهُ ضَمِيرٌ مُسْتَتِرٌ فِيهِ مُنْتَقِلٌ مِنْ مُتَعَلَّقِهِ الْمَحْذُوفِ، وَيَعْمَلُ فِي غَيْرِهِمَا كَالْحَالِ وَالظَّرْفِ بِلَا شَرْطٍ.
text.en: To it belongs the settled adverb, whose explanation has gone before. By agreement it does not govern the mafʿūl bihi, nor a visible fāʿil, except on the condition that it leans on what was mentioned or on a relative noun, as Zaydun fī al-dāri abūhu “Zayd, his father is in the house”, mā fī al-dāri aḥadun “no one is in the house” and jāʾanī alladhī fī al-dāri abūhu “the one whose father is in the house came to me”. The adverb may be a khabar put first. When it does not put a visible [noun] in rafʿ, its fāʿil is a pronoun hidden in it, moved over from the dropped word it is attached to. It governs words other than these two, as the ḥāl and the adverb, without condition.

lessons.title: More words with the meaning of a verb; the abstract governor; sixty governors
body: Also with the meaning of a verb: the relative adjective (al-mansūb), which governs as the passive participle does, on its conditions: marartu bi-rajulin hāshimiyyin akhūhu, “a man whose brother is a Hāshimite”. The borrowed noun: marartu bi-rajulin asadin ghulāmuhu, “whose servant is a lion”, and asadun ʿalayya, “that is, mujtariʾun”, bold against me, “and for that reason it governs as that does”.

And every noun from which the meaning of an adjective is understood, as the name Allāh in wa-huwa llāhu fī al-samāwāti (Q 6:3), “that is, al-maʿbūdu fīhā”, the One worshipped in them: so fī al-samāwāti is attached to the meaning of the name, not to a place for God.

Last of the ninth: the demonstrative, layta and laʿalla, the particles of calling, likening, drawing attention and negation, and others. These govern “those words governed by the verb that are other than the fāʿil and the mafʿūl bihi, as the ḥāl and the adverb”; the commentators' example is hādhā Zaydun qāʾiman, the ḥāl governed by the sense of “I point to” in hādhā.

The abstract governor is “a meaning known by the heart”, in which the tongue has no share, and it is two: being free of the verbal governors for the sake of attribution, which raises the mubtadaʾ and khabar, Zaydun qāʾimun; and the muḍāriʿ's standing by itself in the place of a noun, Zaydun yaḍribu, where yaḍribu stands in the place of ḍāribun; that standing is only when it is free of the particles of naṣb and jazm. The grammarians call this the Baṣran view; Naḥw-i Mīr names the other, the muḍāriʿ's being free of naṣb and jazm, which Birgivī makes the condition of the standing. “So the total of the governors we have mentioned is sixty.”

the borrowed noun: asad in the sense of mujtariʾ

text.original: وَمِنْهُ الْمَنْسُوبُ، فَإِنَّهُ يَعْمَلُ كَعَمَلِ اسْمِ الْمَفْعُولِ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ هَاشِمِيٍّ أَخُوهُ، وَيُشْتَرَطُ فِي عَمَلِهِ مَا يُشْتَرَطُ فِيهِ. وَمِنْهُ الِاسْمُ الْمُسْتَعَارُ، نَحْوُ: أَسَدٍ فِي قَوْلِكَ: مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ أَسَدٍ غُلَامُهُ، وَأَسَدٌ عَلَيَّ، أَيْ مُجْتَرِئٌ، فَلِذَا عَمِلَ عَمَلَهُ. وَمِنْهُ كُلُّ اسْمٍ يُفْهَمُ مِنْهُ مَعْنَى الصِّفَةِ، نَحْوُ لَفْظَةِ اللَّهِ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَهُوَ اللَّهُ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ، أَيِ الْمَعْبُودُ فِيهَا.
text.en: To it belongs the relative adjective (al-mansūb): it governs as the passive participle governs, as marartu bi-rajulin hāshimiyyin akhūhu “I passed by a man whose brother is a Hāshimite”, and for its governing the same is a condition as for [the passive participle]. To it belongs the borrowed noun, as asadin “lion” in your saying marartu bi-rajulin asadin ghulāmuhu “I passed by a man whose servant is a lion”, and asadun ʿalayya “a lion against me”, that is, mujtariʾun “bold”; for that reason it governs as that does. To it belongs every noun from which the meaning of an adjective is understood, as the word Allāh in His saying, Most High: wa-huwa Allāhu fī al-samāwāti “and He is God in the heavens” [6:3], that is, al-maʿbūdu fīhā “the One worshipped in them”.

text.original: وَمِنْهُ اسْمُ الْإِشَارَةِ، وَلَيْتَ وَلَعَلَّ، وَحَرْفُ النِّدَاءِ وَالتَّشْبِيهِ وَالتَّنْبِيهِ وَالنَّفْيِ، وَغَيْرُهَا؛ فَهَذِهِ تَعْمَلُ فِي غَيْرِ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ مِنْ مَعْمُولَاتِ الْفِعْلِ، كَالْحَالِ وَالظَّرْفِ.
text.en: To it belong the demonstrative, layta and laʿalla, the particle of calling, of likening, of drawing attention and of negation, and others: these govern those words governed by the verb that are other than the fāʿil and the mafʿūl bihi, as the ḥāl and the adverb.

text.original: وَالْعَامِلُ الْمَعْنَوِيُّ مَا لَا يَكُونُ لِلِّسَانِ فِيهِ حَظٌّ، وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ مَعْنًى يُعْرَفُ بِالْقَلْبِ، وَهُوَ اثْنَانِ: الْأَوَّلُ رَافِعُ الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ، وَهُوَ التَّجْرِيدُ عَنِ الْعَوَامِلِ اللَّفْظِيَّةِ لِأَجْلِ الْإِسْنَادِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ. وَالثَّانِي رَافِعُ الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ، وَهُوَ وُقُوعُهُ بِنَفْسِهِ مَوْقِعَ الِاسْمِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ يَضْرِبُ، فَيَضْرِبُ وَاقِعٌ مَوْقِعَ ضَارِبٍ، وَذَلِكَ الْوُقُوعُ إِنَّمَا يَكُونُ إِذَا تَجَرَّدَ عَنِ النَّوَاصِبِ وَالْجَوَازِمِ. فَمَجْمُوعُ مَا ذَكَرْنَا مِنَ الْعَوَامِلِ سِتُّونَ.
text.en: The abstract governor (al-ʿāmil al-maʿnawī) is one in which the tongue has no share: it is only a meaning known by the heart. It is two. The first is what puts the mubtadaʾ and the khabar in rafʿ, which is being free of the verbal governors for the sake of attribution, as Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”. The second is what puts the muḍāriʿ verb in rafʿ, which is its standing by itself in the place of the noun, as Zaydun yaḍribu “Zayd hits”, where yaḍribu stands in the place of ḍāribin “hitting”; and that standing is only when it is free of the particles of naṣb and of jazm. So the total of the governors we have mentioned is sixty.

parts.title: Chapter two: the governed word and the sentence

lessons.title: What can be governed: the three divisions of words
body: The second chapter turns from the governor to the governed (maʿmūl). Before any rule Birgivī sorts all words. A word laid down for a meaning but not put into a construction (tarkīb), as when words are counted out one by one, “is not governed, just as it does not govern”. Inside a construction words fall into three divisions: those never governed, those always governed, and those that are not governed in origin but are governed when they stand in the place of the second division.

Never governed are two. The particle, without exception. And the imperative made without the lām, as iḍrib, in the view of the Baṣrans: the muḍāriʿ was given iʿrāb because its letter of the muḍāriʿ made it resemble the noun; when that letter was dropped to make the imperative, the resemblance went, and the word “returned to its origin, which is binā”. The Kūfans say it is muʿrab, in jazm by an understood lām, as if iḍrib were li-taḍrib. Birgivī reports both and follows the Baṣrans.

Always governed are the noun and the muḍāriʿ. The noun is governed without exception, so firmly that the grammarians found a place in iʿrāb even for the nouns of verbs (lesson 22): in rafʿ in their place as a mubtadaʾ whose fāʿil stands in the place of the khabar, or in naṣb in their place as a maṣdar, though some give them no place. To keep the rule whole, the pronoun of separation in kāna Zaydun huwa al-qāʾima is judged a particle; those who call it a noun must say it is a noun without a place in iʿrāb.

The lām on an adjective, as in al-ḍārib, is a relative noun in the sense of alladhī for most grammarians. Al-ḍāribu Zaydan comes from alladhī ḍaraba Zaydan, where alladhī is governed and the verb is not; when the speech was changed, the relative took the form of a particle and the verb the form of a noun, so the iʿrāb moved onto ḍārib. Wording wins over meaning here, “in the iʿrāb, which is a rule of wording”.

The third division is the past verb and the sentence (the next lesson). The past verb is governed in two places only: after the maṣdar-making an its place is in naṣb, and after a particle of jazm, as condition or response, its place is in jazm. Its own form never changes; the proof is a muḍāriʿ joined to it, which shows the iʿrāb openly: wa-taqtula in naṣb, wa-taqtul in jazm. This is what “in its place” (maḥallan) means: an iʿrāb the word cannot show, but which is there and shows on what follows it.

terms.en: the governed word, which takes the governor's effect
the construction: words put together in speech
the pronoun of separation, here judged a particle
in naṣb in its place, though the form does not show it

examples.en: kāna Zaydun huwa al-qāʾima: huwa, the pronoun of separation, judged a particle
the lām of al-ḍārib is a relative noun, for most grammarians
its origin: alladhī governed, ḍaraba not
ḍarabta in naṣb in its place: wa-taqtula shows it
ḍarabta and ḍarabtuka in jazm in their place: wa-taqtul and wa-aqtul show it

tasks.prompt: Put each word into one of the three divisions: min, iḍrib, Zaydun, yaḍribu, ḍaraba.
tasks.answer: Never governed: min (a particle) and iḍrib (the imperative without the lām, for the Baṣrans). Always governed: Zaydun (a noun) and yaḍribu (a muḍāriʿ). Governed only in some places: ḍaraba (a past verb), after the maṣdar-making an or a particle of jazm.

tasks.prompt: Why is iḍrib mabnī for the Baṣrans, and what do the Kūfans say?
tasks.answer: The muḍāriʿ has iʿrāb because its letter of the muḍāriʿ makes it resemble the noun. The imperative drops that letter, so the resemblance is gone and it returns to the verb's origin, binā. The Kūfans say it is muʿrab, in jazm by an understood lām of command.

tasks.prompt: In aʿjabanī an ḍarabta wa-taqtula, how do we know that ḍarabta is in naṣb?
tasks.answer: Ḍarabta is a past verb and cannot show naṣb, but it stands after the maṣdar-making an, so its place is in naṣb. The muḍāriʿ joined to it, wa-taqtula, shows that naṣb with its fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Explain, as most grammarians do, why the iʿrāb falls on ḍārib in jāʾanī al-ḍāribu Zaydan.
tasks.answer: The phrase comes from jāʾanī alladhī ḍaraba Zaydan. The lām is the relative alladhī, which was governed, and the verb after it was not. When the speech was changed, the relative took the form of a particle and the verb the form of a noun, so the iʿrāb, a rule of wording, was given to the word that looks like a noun: al-ḍāribu.

quiz.prompt: A word that is not put into a construction is…
quiz.explanation: Words counted out one by one have no governor and govern nothing.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is never governed?
quiz.explanation: The particle, without exception, with the imperative without the lām for the Baṣrans.

quiz.prompt: For the Baṣrans the imperative iḍrib is…
options: in jazm by an understood lām
mabnī, having lost the letter of the muḍāriʿ
quiz.explanation: Without that letter it no longer resembles the noun and returns to binā.

quiz.prompt: In kāna Zaydun huwa al-qāʾima, the book judges huwa to be…
quiz.explanation: The pronoun of separation is a particle, so the rule that every noun is governed stays whole.

quiz.prompt: Most grammarians take the lām of al-ḍārib to be…
options: a relative noun in the sense of alladhī
quiz.explanation: Al-ḍāribu Zaydan comes from alladhī ḍaraba Zaydan.

quiz.prompt: Where is a past verb governed?
options: after the maṣdar-making an, and after a particle of jazm
quiz.explanation: Naṣb in its place after an; jazm in its place as condition or response.

quiz.prompt: In in ḍarabta wa-taqtul ḍarabtuka wa-aqtul, what shows the jazm of ḍarabta?
options: the jazm of wa-taqtul, joined to it
quiz.explanation: The iʿrāb appears in the muḍāriʿ joined to it by ʿaṭf.

text.original: اعْلَمْ أَوَّلًا أَنَّ الْأَلْفَاظَ الْمَوْضُوعَةَ إِذَا لَمْ تَقَعْ فِي التَّرْكِيبِ لَمْ تَكُنْ مَعْمُولَةً، كَمَا لَا تَكُونُ عَامِلَةً، وَإِنْ وَقَعَتْ فِيهِ فَعَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْسَامٍ. الْقِسْمُ الْأَوَّلُ مَا لَا يَكُونُ مَعْمُولًا أَصْلًا، وَهُوَ اثْنَانِ: الْأَوَّلُ الْحَرْفُ مُطْلَقًا، وَالثَّانِي الْأَمْرُ بِغَيْرِ اللَّامِ عِنْدَ الْبَصْرِيِّينَ؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا حُذِفَ عَنْهُ حَرْفُ الْمُضَارَعَةِ الَّتِي بِسَبَبِهَا صَارَ الْمُضَارِعُ مُشَابِهًا لِلِاسْمِ فَأُعْرِبَ وَعُمِلَ فِيهِ، خَرَجَ عَنِ الْمُشَابَهَةِ فَعَادَ إِلَى أَصْلِهِ، وَهُوَ الْبِنَاءُ. وَقَالَ الْكُوفِيُّونَ: هُوَ مُعْرَبٌ مَجْزُومٌ بِلَامٍ مُقَدَّرَةٍ.
text.en: Know first that the words laid down [for meanings], when they do not stand in a construction, are not governed, just as they do not govern; and if they stand in one, they are of three divisions. The first division is that which is never governed, and it is two. The first is the particle, without exception. The second is the imperative without the lām, according to the Baṣrans: for when the letter of the muḍāriʿ was dropped from it, by which the muḍāriʿ had come to resemble the noun and so was given iʿrāb and was governed, it went out of the resemblance and returned to its origin, which is binā. The Kūfans said: it has iʿrāb and is majzūm by an understood lām.

text.original: وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّانِي مَا يَكُونُ مَعْمُولًا دَائِمًا، وَهُوَ اثْنَانِ أَيْضًا: الْأَوَّلُ الِاسْمُ مُطْلَقًا، حَتَّى حُكِمَ عَلَى أَسْمَاءِ الْأَفْعَالِ بِأَنَّهَا مَرْفُوعَةُ الْمَحَلِّ عَلَى الِابْتِدَاءِ وَفَاعِلُهَا سَادٌّ مَسَدَّ الْخَبَرِ، أَوْ مَنْصُوبَةُ الْمَحَلِّ عَلَى الْمَصْدَرِيَّةِ، وَإِنْ قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ: لَا مَحَلَّ لَهَا مِنَ الْإِعْرَابِ لِكَوْنِهَا بِمَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ، وَعَلَى ضَمِيرِ الْفَصْلِ، نَحْوُ: كَانَ زَيْدٌ هُوَ الْقَائِمَ، بِالْحَرْفِيَّةِ، خِلَافًا لِبَعْضِهِمْ؛ يَقُولُ: إِنَّهُ اسْمٌ لَا مَحَلَّ لَهُ مِنَ الْإِعْرَابِ.
text.en: The second division is that which is always governed, and it too is two. The first is the noun, without exception; so much so that the verb-nouns were judged to be marfūʿ in their place as mubtadaʾ, with their fāʿil standing in the place of the khabar, or manṣūb in their place as a maṣdar, even though some said they have no place in iʿrāb, because they have the meaning of the verb; and that the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), as in kāna Zaydun huwa al-qāʾima “Zayd was the one standing”, was judged a particle, against some who say it is a noun that has no place in iʿrāb.

text.original: وَأَمَّا اللَّامُ الدَّاخِلَةُ عَلَى الصِّفَاتِ فَقَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ: إِنَّهَا حَرْفٌ كَغَيْرِهَا، وَقَالَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ: هِيَ اسْمٌ مَوْصُولٌ بِمَعْنَى الَّذِي أَوِ الَّتِي، أُعْطِيَ إِعْرَابُهَا لِمَا بَعْدَهَا لَمَّا انْتَقَلَ مِنَ الْفِعْلِيَّةِ إِلَى الِاسْمِيَّةِ؛ فَأَصْلُ: جَاءَنِي الضَّارِبُ زَيْدًا: جَاءَنِي الَّذِي ضَرَبَ زَيْدًا، فَالْأَوَّلُ مَعْمُولٌ وَالثَّانِي غَيْرُ مَعْمُولٍ، فَلَمَّا غُيِّرَ هَذَا الْكَلَامُ صَارَ الْأَوَّلُ فِي صُورَةِ الْحَرْفِ وَالثَّانِي فِي صُورَةِ الِاسْمِ، فَانْعَكَسَ الْحُكْمُ؛ تَرْجِيحًا لِجَانِبِ اللَّفْظِ عَلَى جَانِبِ الْمَعْنَى فِي الْإِعْرَابِ الَّذِي هُوَ حُكْمٌ لَفْظِيٌّ. وَالثَّانِي الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ.
text.en: As for the lām that comes upon adjectives, some said it is a particle like the others; most said it is a relative noun in the sense of alladhī or allatī “who, which”, whose iʿrāb was given to what comes after it when that passed from being a verb to being a noun. So the origin of jāʾanī al-ḍāribu Zaydan “the one hitting Zayd came to me” is jāʾanī alladhī ḍaraba Zaydan “the one who hit Zayd came to me”: the first is governed and the second is not governed; when this speech was changed, the first took the form of a particle and the second the form of a noun, and the rule was reversed, giving the side of the wording precedence over the side of the meaning in the iʿrāb, which is a rule of wording. The second [that is always governed] is the muḍāriʿ verb.

text.original: وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّالِثُ مَا كَانَ الْأَصْلُ فِيهِ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مَعْمُولًا، لَكِنْ قَدْ يَقَعُ مَوْقِعَ الْقِسْمِ الثَّانِي فَيَكُونُ مَعْمُولًا، وَهُوَ اثْنَانِ أَيْضًا: الْأَوَّلُ الْمَاضِي؛ فَإِنَّهُ إِذَا وَقَعَ بَعْدَ أَنِ الْمَصْدَرِيَّةِ يُحْكَمُ عَلَى مَحَلِّهِ بِالنَّصْبِ، وَإِذَا وَقَعَ بَعْدَ الْجَازِمِ شَرْطًا أَوْ جَزَاءً يُحْكَمُ عَلَى مَحَلِّهِ بِالْجَزْمِ؛ لِظُهُورِ ذَلِكَ الْإِعْرَابِ فِي الْمَعْطُوفِ، نَحْوُ: أَعْجَبَنِي أَنْ ضَرَبْتَ وَتَقْتُلَ، وَإِنْ ضَرَبْتَ وَتَقْتُلْ ضَرَبْتُكَ وَأَقْتُلْ. وَفِي غَيْرِ هَذَيْنِ الْمَوْضِعَيْنِ لَا يَكُونُ مَعْمُولًا.
text.en: The third division is that whose origin is not to be governed, but which may stand in the place of the second division and so be governed; it too is two. The first is the past [verb]: when it stands after the maṣdar-making an, its place is judged to be in naṣb, and when it stands after a particle of jazm as condition or response, its place is judged to be in jazm, because that iʿrāb appears in what is joined to it by ʿaṭf, as aʿjabanī an ḍarabta wa-taqtula “it pleased me that you hit and kill” and in ḍarabta wa-taqtul ḍarabtuka wa-aqtul “if you hit and kill, I hit you and kill”. Outside these two places it is not governed.

lessons.title: The sentence, verbal and nominal; sentences taken as a single word
body: The second word of the third division is the sentence (jumla). It is verbal when it is made of a verb “in wording or in meaning” and its fāʿil. So ḍaraba Zaydun is verbal, and so is the whole conditional in tukrimnī ukrimka; but so too are hayhāta Zaydun, where a noun of a verb raises its fāʿil, a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni, where a participle leaning on the question raises al-Zaydāni, and a-fī al-dāri Zaydun, where the adverb leaning on the question raises Zaydun (lessons 18 and 22). What makes a sentence verbal is a governor with a verb's meaning and its fāʿil, not the look of its first word.

It is nominal when it is made of the mubtadaʾ and khabar, “or of the ism of a governing particle and its khabar”: Zaydun qāʾimun, and inna Zaydan qāʾimun. Inna does not turn the sentence into anything new; it is still a nominal sentence, now with a governor in front.

Some sentences are “treated as a single noun” and so always have iʿrāb. First, the sentence whose wording is meant. In Zaydun qāʾimun jumlatun ismiyyatun, “‘Zayd is standing’ is a nominal sentence”, the whole of Zaydun qāʾimun is the mubtadaʾ, “that is, this wording”, and jumlatun is its khabar. To this kind belongs what is said after a verb of saying: in wa-idhā qīla lahum āminū (Q 2:13), the words āminū are what was said, and the sentence stands where the verb's governed noun would stand.

Second, the sentence that gives a maṣdar meaning. With anna, an or the maṣdar-making mā this is plain: balaghanī annaka qāʾimun is “your standing reached me”, so annaka qāʾimun is the fāʿil; wa-an taṣūmū khayrun lakum (Q 2:184) is “your fasting is better for you”, so an taṣūmū is the mubtadaʾ. Without such a particle it is the sentence a noun is muḍāf to: yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum (Q 5:119), “the day of the profiting of their truthfulness”.

Two more sentences are read as maṣdars without a particle. In sawāʾun ʿalayhim a-andhartahum am lam tundhirhum (Q 2:6) the question is read as “your warning and your not warning” are the same to them. And in the proverb tasmaʿu bi-l-muʿaydiyyi khayrun min an tarāhu, “that you hear of the little Maʿaddī is better than that you see him”, tasmaʿu is read as samāʿuka. Birgivī adds that this last “is limited to what is heard”: a student may not make any verb a maṣdar without an.

the nominal sentence: mubtadaʾ and khabar, or ism and khabar of a particle

understood as a single word

tasks.prompt: Why is a-fī al-dāri Zaydun a verbal sentence, though it has no verb?
tasks.answer: The adverb fī al-dāri has the meaning of a verb (ḥaṣala), and leaning on the question it raises Zaydun as its fāʿil. A verbal sentence is a verb in wording or in meaning with its fāʿil.

tasks.prompt: Parse the whole of Zaydun qāʾimun jumlatun ismiyyatun.
tasks.answer: Zaydun qāʾimun, its wording meant, is the mubtadaʾ, in rafʿ in its place (it is treated as one noun). Jumlatun is its khabar, in rafʿ, and ismiyyatun is an adjective of jumlatun, in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Turn wa-an taṣūmū khayrun lakum into a maṣdar and give the place of an taṣūmū.
tasks.answer: Ṣiyāmukum khayrun lakum, “your fasting is better for you”. An taṣūmū is the mubtadaʾ, in rafʿ in its place; khayrun is its khabar.

tasks.prompt: What is the fāʿil of balagha in balaghanī annaka qāʾimun?
tasks.answer: Annaka qāʾimun, understood as the maṣdar qiyāmuka, “your standing”: it is the fāʿil, in rafʿ in its place.

quiz.prompt: The verbal sentence is made of…
options: a verb, in wording or meaning, and its fāʿil
quiz.explanation: So hayhāta Zaydun and a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni are verbal.

quiz.prompt: Hayhāta Zaydun is…
quiz.explanation: A noun of a verb with its fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: In this book inna Zaydan qāʾimun is…
quiz.explanation: The ism of a governing particle and its khabar.

quiz.prompt: When the wording of a sentence is meant, the sentence…
options: has iʿrāb, like a single noun
quiz.explanation: It can stand as mubtadaʾ, fāʿil, deputy and the rest.

quiz.prompt: Balaghanī annaka qāʾimun means…
options: I stood when you reached me
quiz.explanation: Anna with its sentence gives the maṣdar qiyāmuka, the fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: Yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum is understood as…
quiz.explanation: The sentence a noun is made muḍāf to is read as a maṣdar.

quiz.prompt: Reading tasmaʿu as samāʿuka, without an, is…
options: limited to what is heard from the Arabs
quiz.explanation: The proverb is kept as it was heard, not taken as a rule.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي الْجُمْلَةُ، وَهِيَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: فِعْلِيَّةٌ، وَهِيَ الْمُرَكَّبَةُ مِنَ الْفِعْلِ لَفْظًا أَوْ مَعْنًى وَفَاعِلِهِ، مِثْلُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ، وَإِنْ تُكْرِمْنِي أُكْرِمْكَ، وَهَيْهَاتَ زَيْدٌ، وَأَقَائِمٌ الزَّيْدَانِ، وَأَفِي الدَّارِ زَيْدٌ؛ وَاسْمِيَّةٌ، وَهِيَ الْمُرَكَّبَةُ مِنَ الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ، أَوْ مِنِ اسْمِ الْحَرْفِ الْعَامِلِ وَخَبَرِهِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَإِنَّ زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ.
text.en: The second is the sentence (jumla), and it is of two divisions. Verbal (fiʿliyya), which is made up of a verb, in wording or in meaning, and its fāʿil, as ḍaraba Zaydun “Zayd hit”, in tukrimnī ukrimka “if you honour me, I will honour you”, hayhāta Zaydun “how far Zayd is!”, a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni “are the two Zayds standing?” and a-fī al-dāri Zaydun “is Zayd in the house?”. Nominal (ismiyya), which is made up of the mubtadaʾ and the khabar, or of the ism of a governing particle and its khabar, as Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing” and inna Zaydan qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”.

text.original: فَإِنْ أُرِيدَ بِالْجُمْلَةِ لَفْظُهَا فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ إِعْرَابٍ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ فِي حُكْمِ الِاسْمِ الْمُفْرَدِ، حَتَّى يَجُوزُ وُقُوعُهَا فِي كُلِّ مَا وَقَعَ فِيهِ، فَتَقَعُ مُبْتَدَأً وَفَاعِلًا وَنَائِبَهُ وَغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ جُمْلَةٌ اسْمِيَّةٌ، أَيْ هَذَا اللَّفْظُ. وَمِنْهُ مَقُولُ الْقَوْلِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ آمِنُوا.
text.en: If by the sentence its wording is meant, it must have iʿrāb, because it is treated as a single noun, so much so that it can stand wherever that stands: it stands as mubtadaʾ, as fāʿil, as its deputy and so on, as Zaydun qāʾimun jumlatun ismiyyatun “‘Zayd is standing’ is a nominal sentence”, that is, hādhā al-lafẓu “this wording”. To it belongs what is said after saying, as His saying, Most High: wa-idhā qīla lahum āminū “and when it is said to them: believe” [2:13].

text.original: وَكَذَا إِنْ أُرِيدَ بِهَا مَعْنًى مَصْدَرِيٌّ، إِمَّا بِوَاسِطَةِ أَنَّ وَأَنْ وَمَا الْمَصْدَرِيَّتَيْنِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: بَلَغَنِي أَنَّكَ قَائِمٌ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ، أَوْ بِغَيْرِهَا، نَحْوُ الْجُمْلَةِ الَّتِي أُضِيفَ إِلَيْهَا، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: يَوْمَ يَنْفَعُ الصَّادِقِينَ صِدْقُهُمْ، أَيْ يَوْمَ نَفْعِ صِدْقِ الصَّادِقِينَ، وَنَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: سَوَاءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَأَنْذَرْتَهُمْ أَمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهُمْ، أَيْ إِنْذَارُكَ وَعَدَمُ إِنْذَارِكَ، وَنَحْوُ: تَسْمَعُ بِالْمُعَيْدِيِّ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَنْ تَرَاهُ، أَيْ سَمَاعُكَ؛ وَهَذَا الْأَخِيرُ مَقْصُورٌ عَلَى السَّمَاعِ.
text.en: Likewise if a maṣdar meaning is meant by it, either by means of anna, or of the two maṣdar-making an and mā, as your saying balaghanī annaka qāʾimun “it has reached me that you are standing”, and as His saying, Most High: wa-an taṣūmū khayrun lakum “and that you fast is better for you” [2:184]; or without them, as the sentence to which [a noun] is made muḍāf, as His saying, Most High: yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum “the day their truthfulness profits the truthful” [5:119], that is, yawma nafʿi ṣidqi al-ṣādiqīna “the day of the profiting of the truthfulness of the truthful”; and as His saying, Most High: sawāʾun ʿalayhim a-andhartahum am lam tundhirhum “it is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them” [2:6], that is, indhāruka wa-ʿadamu indhārika “your warning and your not warning”; and as tasmaʿu bi-al-muʿaydiyyi khayrun min an tarāhu “that you hear of the little Maʿaddī is better than that you see him”, that is, samāʿuka “your hearing”; and this last is limited to what is heard [from the Arabs].

lessons.title: Sentences that have a place in iʿrāb
lessons.arabic: الْجُمَلُ الَّتِي لَهَا مَحَلٌّ مِنَ الْإِعْرَابِ
lessons.transliteration: al-jumal allatī lahā maḥallun min al-iʿrāb
body: Every other sentence, one not taken as a single word, “has no iʿrāb” of its own, unless it stands where a single word would stand and be governed. Then it has an iʿrāb in its place (maḥallan): no vowel shows, because a sentence has no last letter to carry one, but the place it fills is in rafʿ, naṣb or jazm. Birgivī gathers these places at the end: “a khabar, an object, the response of a condition that puts in jazm, with the fāʾ or idhā, a ḥāl, and a follower.”

As a khabar it is in rafʿ in its place after a mubtadaʾ, Zaydun abūhu qāʾimun, and after inna, inna Zaydan qāma abūhu; in naṣb in its place after kāna, kāna Zaydun abūhu ʿālimun, and after kāda, kāda Zaydun yakhruju. Notice that every one of these khabar sentences holds a pronoun going back to the noun before it, the hā of abūhu, or the pronoun hidden in yakhruju: without that link the sentence would not be about Zayd.

As an object it is in naṣb in its place: the second object of ʿalima, ʿalima Zaydun ʿAmran abūhu qāʾimun; the third of aʿlama; or the sentence a verb of the heart is suspended from (lesson 15), ʿalimtu a-qāʾimun Zaydun, where the question stops ʿalima from working on the words but not from taking the whole as its object. As a ḥāl it is in naṣb in its place too: jāʾanī Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun.

As the response of a condition that puts in jazm it is in jazm in its place, but only when it comes after the fāʾ or after idhā, the idhā of surprise, as in Q 30:36, idhā hum yaqnaṭūna: in tukrimnī fa-anta mukramun. Without the fāʾ the response is a muḍāriʿ in jazm by its own form, and the question of a place does not arise (lesson 39).

As a follower its iʿrāb is that of what it follows: an adjective of an indefinite, jāʾanī rajulun abūhu qāʾimun, in rafʿ because rajulun is in rafʿ; a sentence joined to a single word, Zaydun ḍāribun wa-yaqtulu, or to a sentence that has a place; a badal; an emphasis; or, “in one view”, an explanation (bayān). The madrasa learns a short rule with this: a sentence after an indefinite is an adjective, after a definite it is a ḥāl, as in jāʾanī Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun.
