tasks.prompt: Give the place in iʿrāb of the sentence in kāna Zaydun abūhu ʿālimun and in inna Zaydan qāma abūhu.
tasks.arabic: كَانَ زَيْدٌ أَبُوهُ عَالِمٌ — إِنَّ زَيْدًا قَامَ أَبُوهُ
tasks.answer: Abūhu ʿālimun is the khabar of kāna, in naṣb in its place. Qāma abūhu is the khabar of inna, in rafʿ in its place.

tasks.prompt: Why is abūhu qāʾimun in rafʿ in its place in Zaydun abūhu qāʾimun, but in naṣb in its place in ʿalima Zaydun ʿAmran abūhu qāʾimun?
tasks.answer: In the first it is the khabar of a mubtadaʾ, which is in rafʿ. In the second it is the second object of ʿalima, which is in naṣb. The sentence is the same; the place it fills decides its iʿrāb.

tasks.prompt: Name the five places in which a sentence not taken as a single word is governed.
tasks.answer: As a khabar, as an object, as the response of a condition that puts in jazm (with the fāʾ or idhā), as a ḥāl, and as a follower (adjective, joined word, badal, emphasis, and in one view an explanation).

tasks.prompt: Parse the sentence after rajulun in jāʾanī rajulun abūhu qāʾimun.
tasks.answer: Abūhu is a mubtadaʾ and qāʾimun its khabar; the whole sentence is an adjective of the indefinite rajulun and follows it: in rafʿ in its place, as rajulun, the fāʿil of jāʾa, is in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: A sentence not taken as a single word is governed in…
quiz.explanation: Khabar, object, response with fāʾ or idhā, ḥāl and follower.

quiz.prompt: In inna Zaydan qāma abūhu, the sentence qāma abūhu is…
quiz.explanation: It is the khabar of inna.

quiz.prompt: In kāda Zaydun yakhruju, yakhruju is…
options: the khabar of kāda, in naṣb in its place
quiz.explanation: A sentence as the khabar of kāna or kāda is in naṣb in its place.

quiz.prompt: In ʿalimtu a-qāʾimun Zaydun, the sentence after ʿalimtu is…
options: in naṣb in its place, the verb suspended from it
quiz.explanation: The question suspends the verb from the words, not from the whole.

quiz.prompt: In in tukrimnī fa-anta mukramun, fa-anta mukramun is…
quiz.explanation: The response of a jāzim after the fāʾ is in jazm in its place.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾanī Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun, wa-huwa rākibun is…
options: a ḥāl, in naṣb in its place
quiz.explanation: After the definite Zayd the sentence is a ḥāl.

quiz.prompt: A sentence that is an adjective, badal or joined word takes…
options: the iʿrāb of what it follows
quiz.explanation: Its iʿrāb is on the measure of the iʿrāb of what it follows.

text.original: وَفِي غَيْرِ هَذَيْنِ لَا يَكُونُ لَهُ إِعْرَابٌ إِلَّا أَنْ تَقَعَ خَبَرَ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ لِبَابِ إِنَّ، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ زَيْدًا قَامَ أَبُوهُ، فَتَكُونُ مَرْفُوعَةَ الْمَحَلِّ؛ أَوْ لِبَابِ كَانَ، نَحْوُ: كَانَ زَيْدٌ أَبُوهُ عَالِمٌ، أَوْ لِبَابِ كَادَ، نَحْوُ: كَادَ زَيْدٌ يَخْرُجُ، أَوْ مَفْعُولًا ثَانِيًا لِبَابِ عَلِمَ، نَحْوُ: عَلِمَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ ثَالِثًا لِبَابِ أَعْلَمَ، نَحْوُ: أَعْلَمَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا بَكْرًا أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ مُعَلَّقًا عَنْهَا، نَحْوُ: عَلِمْتُ أَقَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ، أَوْ حَالًا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وَهُوَ رَاكِبٌ، فَتَكُونُ مَنْصُوبَةَ الْمَحَلِّ.
text.en: Outside these two it has no iʿrāb, unless it stands as the khabar of a mubtadaʾ, as Zaydun abūhu qāʾimun “Zayd, his father is standing”, or of the class of inna, as inna Zaydan qāma abūhu “Zayd, his father stood”, and then it is marfūʿ in its place; or of the class of kāna, as kāna Zaydun abūhu ʿālimun “Zayd was [one whose] father is a scholar”, or of the class of kāda, as kāda Zaydun yakhruju “Zayd almost went out”; or as the second object of the class of ʿalima, as ʿalima Zaydun ʿAmran abūhu qāʾimun “Zayd knew ʿAmr [to be one whose] father is standing”, or the third of the class of aʿlama, as aʿlama Zaydun ʿAmran Bakran abūhu qāʾimun “Zayd informed ʿAmr that Bakr's father is standing”; or [the verb] is suspended from it, as ʿalimtu a-qāʾimun Zaydun “I know whether Zayd is standing”; or as a ḥāl, as jāʾanī Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun “Zayd came to me while he was riding”; and then it is manṣūb in its place.

text.original: أَوْ جَوَابًا لِشَرْطٍ جَازِمٍ بَعْدَ الْفَاءِ أَوْ إِذَا، نَحْوُ: إِنْ تُكْرِمْنِي فَأَنْتَ مُكْرَمٌ، فَتَكُونُ مَجْزُومَةَ الْمَحَلِّ؛ أَوْ صِفَةً لِنَكِرَةٍ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ مَعْطُوفَةً عَلَى مُفْرَدٍ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ ضَارِبٌ وَيَقْتُلُ، أَوْ جُمْلَةٍ لَهَا مَحَلٌّ مِنَ الْإِعْرَابِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ وَابْنُهُ قَاعِدٌ، أَوْ بَدَلًا مِنْ أَحَدِهِمَا، أَوْ تَأْكِيدًا لِلثَّانِيَةِ، أَوْ بَيَانًا لَهَا عَلَى رَأْيٍ، فَيَكُونُ إِعْرَابُهَا عَلَى حَسَبِ إِعْرَابِ الْمَتْبُوعِ.
text.en: Or as the answer of a condition that puts in jazm, after the fāʾ or idhā, as in tukrimnī fa-anta mukramun “if you honour me, you are honoured”, and then it is majzūm in its place; or as an adjective of an indefinite, as jāʾanī rajulun abūhu qāʾimun “a man whose father is standing came to me”; or joined by ʿaṭf to a single word, as Zaydun ḍāribun wa-yaqtulu “Zayd is hitting and kills”, or to a sentence that has a place in iʿrāb, as Zaydun abūhu qāʾimun wa-ibnuhu qāʿidun “Zayd, his father is standing and his son is sitting”; or as a badal of either of them, or as an emphasis of the second, or as an explanation of it in one view; and then its iʿrāb follows the iʿrāb of what it follows.

text.original: فَظَهَرَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْجُمْلَةِ أَنَّ الْجُمْلَةَ قِسْمَانِ: قِسْمٌ فِي تَأْوِيلِ الْمُفْرَدِ، فَيَكُونُ لَهُ إِعْرَابٌ فِي كُلِّ مَوْضِعٍ، وَذَلِكَ أَيْضًا قِسْمَانِ: مَا أُرِيدَ بِهِ لَفْظُهُ، وَمَا أُرِيدَ بِهِ مَعْنًى مَصْدَرِيٌّ؛ وَقِسْمٌ مِنَ الْجُمْلَةِ لَا يَكُونُ فِي تَأْوِيلِ الْمُفْرَدِ، فَلَا تَكُونُ مَعْمُولَةً إِلَّا فِي خَمْسَةِ مَوَاضِعَ: خَبَرٍ، وَمَفْعُولٍ، وَجَوَابِ شَرْطٍ جَازِمٍ مَعَ الْفَاءِ أَوْ إِذَا، وَحَالٍ، وَتَابِعٍ.
text.en: So it has become clear from all this that the sentence is of two divisions. One division is understood as a single word, and it has iʿrāb in every place; and that too is of two divisions: that by which its wording is meant, and that by which a maṣdar meaning is meant. The other division of the sentence is not understood as a single word, and it is governed only in five places: as a khabar, as an object, as the answer of a condition that puts in jazm, with the fāʾ or idhā, as a ḥāl, and as a follower.

lessons.title: The two kinds of governed word; the fāʿil and its deputy
body: The governed word is of two kinds. It is governed “in its own right” (bi-l-aṣāla) when a governor reaches it directly, and “by following” (bi-l-tabaʿiyya) when it only takes the iʿrāb of a word before it, as the followers do (lessons 40–43). The first kind is of four divisions, by the iʿrāb it takes: marfūʿ, manṣūb, majrūr and majzūm. The book counts nine marfūʿ and takes them one by one, beginning with the fāʿil.

The fāʿil is “that to which a complete active verb, or what has its meaning, is attributed”. Every word of the definition does work. “Attributed” (usnida): the verb is said of it. “Complete” (tāmm) leaves out the ism of kāna, to which a deficient verb is attributed (lesson 16). “Active” (maʿlūm) leaves out the deputy. “Or what has its meaning” brings in a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni and hayhāta Zaydun (lessons 18 and 22). So the fāʿil is a matter of attribution, not of who acts: in māta Zaydun, “Zayd died”, Zayd did nothing, and he is the fāʿil.

The deputy of the fāʿil (nāʾib al-fāʿil) is the same with a passive verb: ḍuriba Zaydun, or with what has its meaning, the passive participle: maḍrūbun al-Zaydāni. Both are always nouns, “or understood as a noun”, as a sentence with an (lesson 25). The deputy alone may also be a preposition with its majrūr, murra bi-Zaydin, “Zayd was passed by”; then the verb stays singular and masculine whatever follows the bāʾ.

Two rules hold for both. They do not come before their governor: in Zaydun ḍaraba, Zaydun is not a fāʿil put first but a mubtadaʾ, and the fāʿil is a pronoun in ḍaraba (next lesson). And they are not dropped, “except from the maṣdar, as has gone before”: only the maṣdar may leave its fāʿil unsaid (lesson 19).

Each of them is either a pronoun (muḍmar) or a visible noun (muẓhar). The pronoun is hidden (mustatir), with no letter of its own, or showing (bāriz). The hidden pronoun is necessarily hidden when it may never be shown and the governor is attributed only to it, or possibly hidden when the same governor is attributed sometimes to it and sometimes to a visible noun. A beginner who sees aḍribu anā should know that anā is only an emphasis: the fāʿil is still the pronoun hidden in aḍribu.

terms.en: governed in its own right, reached by its governor directly
that to which a complete active verb, or its like, is attributed
the deputy of the fāʿil, with a passive verb or its like
the hidden and the showing pronoun
necessarily hidden: its governor is attributed only to it

examples.en: ḍaraba Zaydun: the fāʿil of a complete active verb
the fāʿil of what has a verb's meaning
the deputy of the fāʿil of a passive verb
the deputy of the fāʿil of a passive participle
a preposition and its majrūr as the deputy: the verb singular and masculine

tasks.prompt: Name the fāʿil in each and say which words of the definition admit it.
tasks.arabic: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ — هَيْهَاتَ زَيْدٌ — أَقَائِمٌ الزَّيْدَانِ
tasks.answer: Zaydun is the fāʿil of ḍaraba, a complete active verb. Zaydun is the fāʿil of hayhāta, and al-Zaydāni of qāʾimun: both governors are “what has the verb's meaning”, a noun of a verb and an active participle leaning on the question.

tasks.prompt: Why is the ism of kāna not a fāʿil by this definition?
tasks.answer: The definition says a “complete” verb. Kāna is a deficient verb: it needs a khabar to complete it. So what it is attributed to is called its ism, not a fāʿil.

tasks.prompt: In murra bi-Zaydin, what is the deputy of the fāʿil, and what form must the verb take?
tasks.answer: The deputy is bi-Zaydin, the preposition with its majrūr. With such a deputy the verb must be singular and masculine.

tasks.prompt: Parse Zaydun ḍaraba as the book does, and say why Zaydun is not the fāʿil.
tasks.answer: Zaydun is a mubtadaʾ in rafʿ. Ḍaraba is a past verb whose fāʿil is a pronoun hidden in it, going back to Zayd; the sentence ḍaraba is the khabar. Zaydun cannot be the fāʿil, because the fāʿil does not come before its governor.

quiz.prompt: A word governed by following takes its iʿrāb…
options: from a governor of its own
quiz.explanation: The followers take the iʿrāb of what they follow.

quiz.prompt: How many marfūʿ does the book count?
quiz.explanation: The fāʿil is the first of nine.

quiz.prompt: The word “complete” in the definition of the fāʿil leaves out…
quiz.explanation: Kāna is deficient; what it is attributed to is its ism.

quiz.prompt: In hayhāta Zaydun, Zaydun is…
options: the fāʿil of what has a verb's meaning
quiz.explanation: Hayhāta is a noun of a verb, in the sense of baʿuda.

quiz.prompt: In murra bi-Zaydin, the deputy of the fāʿil is…
options: bi-Zaydin, the preposition and its majrūr
quiz.explanation: Only the deputy may be a preposition with its majrūr.

quiz.prompt: From which word alone may the fāʿil be dropped?
quiz.explanation: As lesson 19 showed, only the maṣdar may leave its fāʿil unsaid.

quiz.prompt: A necessarily hidden pronoun is one that…
options: is sometimes replaced by a visible noun
may not be shown, its governor attributed only to it
always has a letter of its own
quiz.explanation: Its governor is never attributed to a visible noun.

text.original: ثُمَّ الْمَعْمُولُ عَلَى نَوْعَيْنِ: مَعْمُولٌ بِالْأَصَالَةِ، وَمَعْمُولٌ بِالتَّبَعِيَّةِ. الْأَوَّلُ أَرْبَعَةُ أَقْسَامٍ: مَرْفُوعٌ وَمَنْصُوبٌ وَمَجْرُورٌ وَمَجْزُومٌ. أَمَّا الْمَرْفُوعُ فَتِسْعَةٌ: الْأَوَّلُ الْفَاعِلُ، وَهُوَ مَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ الْفِعْلُ التَّامُّ الْمَعْلُومُ أَوْ مَا بِمَعْنَاهُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ، وَأَقَائِمٌ الزَّيْدَانِ، وَهَيْهَاتَ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: Then the governed is of two kinds: governed in its own right (bi-l-aṣāla), and governed by following (bi-l-tabaʿiyya). The first is of four divisions: marfūʿ, manṣūb, majrūr and majzūm. As for the marfūʿ, it is nine. The first is the fāʿil, which is that to which a complete active verb, or what has its meaning, is attributed, as ḍaraba Zaydun “Zayd hit”, a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni “are the two Zayds standing?” and hayhāta Zaydun “how far Zayd is!”.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ، وَهُوَ مَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ الْفِعْلُ التَّامُّ الْمَجْهُولُ أَوْ مَا بِمَعْنَاهُ، نَحْوُ: ضُرِبَ زَيْدٌ، أَوْ مَضْرُوبٌ الزَّيْدَانِ. وَلَا يَكُونَانِ إِلَّا اسْمَيْنِ أَوْ فِي تَأْوِيلِهِ، غَيْرَ أَنَّ النَّائِبَ قَدْ يَكُونُ جَارًّا وَمَجْرُورًا، نَحْوُ: مُرَّ بِزَيْدٍ، فَيَجِبُ إِفْرَادُ عَامِلِهِ وَتَذْكِيرُهُ. وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُمَا عَلَى عَامِلِهِمَا، وَلَا حَذْفُهُمَا مَعًا إِلَّا مِنَ الْمَصْدَرِ، وَقَدْ مَرَّ.
text.en: The second is the deputy of the fāʿil (nāʾib al-fāʿil), which is that to which a complete passive verb, or what has its meaning, is attributed, as ḍuriba Zaydun “Zayd was hit” or maḍrūbun al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds are hit”. They are only nouns, or understood as a noun, except that the deputy may be a preposition and its majrūr, as murra bi-Zaydin “Zayd was passed by”, and then its governor must be singular and masculine. They may not be put before their governor, nor may both be dropped together, except from the maṣdar, as has gone before.

text.original: وَكُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا قِسْمَانِ: مُضْمَرٌ وَمُظْهَرٌ. فَالْمُضْمَرُ أَيْضًا عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: مُسْتَتِرٌ وَبَارِزٌ. فَالْمُسْتَتِرُ أَيْضًا قِسْمَانِ: وَاجِبُ الِاسْتِتَارِ، بِحَيْثُ لَا يَجُوزُ إِبْرَازُهُ وَلَا يُسْنَدُ عَامِلُهُ إِلَّا إِلَيْهِ، وَجَائِزُ الِاسْتِتَارِ، بِحَيْثُ يُسْنَدُ عَامِلُهُ تَارَةً إِلَيْهِ وَتَارَةً إِلَى اسْمٍ ظَاهِرٍ.
text.en: Each of them is of two divisions: a pronoun (muḍmar) and a visible noun (muẓhar). The pronoun too is of two divisions: hidden (mustatir) and showing (bāriz). The hidden too is of two divisions: necessarily hidden, in that it may not be shown and its governor is attributed only to it; and possibly hidden, in that its governor is attributed sometimes to it and sometimes to a visible noun.

lessons.title: Where the pronoun of the fāʿil is hidden
body: The pronoun is necessarily hidden, first, in the speakers and in the single masculine one addressed, outside the past: aḍribu, naḍribu, taḍribu. The test is the definition of the last lesson: one cannot attribute aḍribu to a visible noun, so its fāʿil can only be the hidden anā. It is hidden too in the noun of a verb of command, nazāli, “come down!”, ṣah, “hush!”, mah, “stop!”; and in the elative outside the question of the kohl (lesson 19), Zaydun afḍalu min ʿAmrin, where the fāʿil of afḍalu is a pronoun going back to Zayd.

It is necessarily hidden also in the participles, the words with their meaning, the resembling adjective and the settled adverb, when the condition for governing a visible fāʿil is missing (lessons 18–22): jāʾanī ḍāribun, “one hitting came to me”, where ḍāribun leans on nothing. And it is always hidden in the duals and sound plurals of the participles, ḍāribāni, maḍrūbūna: the alif and wāw there are not pronouns, as they are in yaḍribāni and yaḍribūna, but signs of number, and the fāʿil is hidden behind them.

One more place: ʿadā and khalā used as verbs, and mā ʿadā, mā khalā, laysa and lā yakūnu in exception. In jāʾanī al-qawmu ʿadā Zaydan, “the people came to me except Zayd”, Zaydan is the object, and the fāʿil of ʿadā is a pronoun that is never shown; the commentators say it goes back to “some of them”, understood from al-qawm.

The pronoun is possibly hidden in the single absent masculine and feminine: Zaydun ḍaraba, yaḍribu, li-yaḍrib, lā yaḍrib, and Hindun ḍarabat, taḍribu, li-taḍrib, lā taḍrib. It is only “possibly” hidden because the same verb is also attributed to a visible noun, ḍaraba Zaydun, “and then no pronoun is hidden in it”. Note the trap: taḍribu said to a man is necessarily hidden, taḍribu said of Hind only possibly.

So too in the words that resemble the verb when the condition of their governing is found, except the duals and plurals already named: Zaydun ḍāribun has a pronoun hidden in ḍāribun, but in Zaydun ḍāribun ghulāmuhu the participle raises ghulāmuhu, “and then it is not hidden”. The same word may have a hidden fāʿil in one sentence and a visible one in the next; that is what “possibly” means.

terms.en: possibly hidden: the governor may also be attributed to a visible noun
the noun of a verb of command: nazāli, ṣah, mah
the question of the kohl: where the elative raises a visible noun

examples.en: the speakers and the one man addressed: necessarily hidden
the elative: necessarily hidden
the fāʿil of ʿadā: never shown
possibly hidden: one also says ḍaraba Zaydun
the participle raising a visible fāʿil: nothing hidden

tasks.prompt: Is the pronoun necessarily or possibly hidden? naḍribu; taḍribu said to a man; Hindun taḍribu; ṣah.
tasks.answer: Naḍribu: necessarily (the speakers). Taḍribu to a man: necessarily (the single masculine addressed, outside the past). Hindun taḍribu: possibly (the single absent feminine; one also says taḍribu Hindun). Ṣah: necessarily (a noun of a verb of command).

tasks.prompt: Why is the pronoun of aḍribu necessarily hidden, while that of yaḍribu is only possibly hidden?
tasks.answer: Aḍribu is never attributed to a visible noun: its fāʿil can only be the hidden anā. Yaḍribu may be attributed to a visible noun, as yaḍribu Zaydun, and then no pronoun is hidden in it.

tasks.prompt: In jāʾanī al-qawmu laysa Zaydan, give the fāʿil and the khabar of laysa.
tasks.answer: The ism (fāʿil) of laysa is a pronoun necessarily hidden, which the commentators refer to “some of them”, understood from al-qawm; Zaydan is its khabar, in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Compare Zaydun ḍāribun and Zaydun ḍāribun ghulāmuhu.
tasks.answer: In both ḍāribun is the khabar of Zaydun and leans on it, so it may govern. In the first its fāʿil is a pronoun hidden in it, going back to Zayd; in the second its fāʿil is the visible ghulāmuhu, and nothing is hidden.

quiz.prompt: In aḍribu the pronoun of the fāʿil is…
In Hindun taḍribu the pronoun is…
quiz.explanation: The single absent feminine: one also says taḍribu Hindun.

quiz.prompt: Nazāli, ṣah and mah have as their fāʿil…
The pronoun in the elative is necessarily hidden except in…
In rijālun ḍāribūna, the fāʿil of ḍāribūna is…
quiz.explanation: In the duals and sound plurals of participles the pronoun is always hidden.

quiz.prompt: Why is the pronoun in yaḍribu only possibly hidden?
options: because one also says yaḍribu Zaydun
because it may be shown as huwa
quiz.explanation: Its governor may be attributed to a visible noun.

quiz.prompt: In Zaydun ḍāribun ghulāmuhu the fāʿil of ḍāribun is…
quiz.explanation: The condition is found, so it raises a visible noun and nothing is hidden.

text.original: الْأَوَّلُ فِي الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ وَالْمُخَاطَبِ الْمُفْرَدِ الْمُذَكَّرِ مِنْ غَيْرِ الْمَاضِي، نَحْوُ: أَضْرِبُ وَنَضْرِبُ وَتَضْرِبُ، وَاسْمِ فِعْلِ الْأَمْرِ، نَحْوُ: نَزَالِ وَصَهْ وَمَهْ، وَأَفْعَلِ التَّفْضِيلِ فِي غَيْرِ مَسْأَلَةِ الْكُحْلِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ عَمْرٍو، وَاسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ وَاسْمِ الْمَفْعُولِ وَمَا كَانَ بِمَعْنَاهُمَا وَالصِّفَةِ الْمُشَبَّهَةِ وَالظَّرْفِ الْمُسْتَقَرِّ إِذَا لَمْ يُوجَدْ شَرْطُ عَمَلِهِنَّ فِي الْفَاعِلِ الظَّاهِرِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي ضَارِبٌ، أَوْ مَضْرُوبٌ، أَوْ أَسَدٌ نَاطِقٌ، أَوْ هَاشِمِيٌّ، أَوْ حَسَنٌ، أَوْ فِي الدَّارِ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: The first is in the speakers and the single masculine one addressed, outside the past, as aḍribu “I hit”, naḍribu “we hit” and taḍribu “you hit”; in the verb-noun of command, as nazāli “come down!”, ṣah “hush!” and mah “stop!”; in afʿal of preference outside the question of the kohl, as Zaydun afḍalu min ʿAmrin “Zayd is better than ʿAmr”; and in the active participle, the passive participle and what has their meaning, the resembling adjective and the settled adverb, when the condition for their governing a visible fāʿil is not found, as jāʾanī ḍāribun “one hitting came to me”, or maḍrūbun “one hit”, or asadun nāṭiqun “a speaking lion”, or hāshimiyyun “a Hāshimite”, or ḥasanun “a handsome one”, or fī al-dāri Zaydun “in the house is Zayd”.

text.original: وَفِي تَثْنِيَتَيِ اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ وَجَمْعِهِمَا السَّالِمِ مُطْلَقًا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلَانِ ضَارِبَانِ أَوْ مَضْرُوبَانِ، أَوْ رِجَالٌ ضَارِبُونَ أَوْ مَضْرُوبُونَ، وَفِي عَدَا وَخَلَا فِعْلَيْنِ، وَفِي مَا عَدَا وَمَا خَلَا وَلَيْسَ وَلَا يَكُونُ فِي بَابِ الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ عَدَا زَيْدًا، أَوْ لَيْسَ زَيْدًا، أَوْ لَا يَكُونُ زَيْدًا.
text.en: And in the duals of the active and passive participles and their sound plurals, without exception, as jāʾanī rajulāni ḍāribāni aw maḍrūbāni “two men came to me, hitting or hit” or rijālun ḍāribūna aw maḍrūbūna “men hitting or hit”; in ʿadā and khalā as verbs; and in mā ʿadā, mā khalā, laysa and lā yakūnu in the chapter of exception, as jāʾanī al-qawmu ʿadā Zaydan “the people came to me except Zayd”, or laysa Zaydan, or lā yakūnu Zaydan.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي فِي الْغَائِبِ الْمُفْرَدِ وَالْغَائِبَةِ الْمُفْرَدَةِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ ضَرَبَ، أَوْ يَضْرِبُ، أَوْ لِيَضْرِبْ، أَوْ لَا يَضْرِبْ، وَهِنْدٌ ضَرَبَتْ، أَوْ تَضْرِبُ، أَوْ لِتَضْرِبْ، أَوْ لَا تَضْرِبْ، وَيُقَالُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ، وَكَذَا الْبَوَاقِي، فَلَا يَسْتَتِرُ فِيهِ ضَمِيرٌ؛ وَفِي شِبْهِ الْفِعْلِ مِمَّا ذُكِرَ إِذَا وُجِدَ شَرْطُ عَمَلِهِ غَيْرَ التَّثْنِيَةِ وَالْجَمْعِ الْمَذْكُورَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: ضَارِبٌ، أَوْ مَضْرُوبٌ، أَوْ أَسَدٌ نَاطِقٌ، أَوْ هَاشِمِيٌّ، أَوْ حَسَنٌ، أَوْ فِي الدَّارِ، وَيُقَالُ: زَيْدٌ ضَارِبٌ غُلَامُهُ، وَكَذَا الْبَوَاقِي، فَلَا يَسْتَتِرُ.
text.en: The second is in the single absent masculine and the single absent feminine, as Zaydun ḍaraba “Zayd, he hit”, or yaḍribu “he hits”, or li-yaḍrib “let him hit”, or lā yaḍrib “let him not hit”, and Hindun ḍarabat “Hind, she hit”, or taḍribu “she hits”, or li-taḍrib “let her hit”, or lā taḍrib “let her not hit”; for one also says ḍaraba Zaydun “Zayd hit”, and so the rest, and then no pronoun is hidden in it. And in what resembles the verb among those mentioned, when the condition for its governing is found, other than the dual and plural just mentioned, as ḍāribun, or maḍrūbun, or asadun nāṭiqun, or hāshimiyyun, or ḥasanun, or fī al-dāri; for one also says Zaydun ḍāribun ghulāmuhu “Zayd, his servant is hitting”, and so the rest, and then it is not hidden.

lessons.title: The showing pronoun of the fāʿil; the visible fāʿil and its verb
body: The showing pronoun joined to the verb is a letter you can see. In the duals it is the alif: ḍarabā, ḍarabtumā, yaḍribāni, iḍribā. In the masculine plurals the wāw: ḍarabū, yaḍribūna, li-yaḍribū, and ḍarabtum too, “since its origin is ḍarabtumū”. In the feminine plurals the nūn: ḍarabna, ḍarabtunna, yaḍribna, iḍribna. In the past, the tāʾ for the one addressed and the speaker, ḍarabtu, ḍarabta, ḍarabti, “with the vowels of the tāʾ”, and nā for the speaker with others, ḍarabnā. Outside the past, the yāʾ for the woman addressed: taḍribīna, iḍribī.

Two letters are often mistaken for pronouns. The tāʾ of ḍarabat, “she hit”, is not a pronoun but the sign of the feminine, which is why the verb can still take a visible fāʿil: ḍarabat Hindun. And the nūn of yaḍribāni and yaḍribūna is not the pronoun but the sign of rafʿ, which falls away in naṣb and jazm, lan yaḍribā; the pronoun there is the alif or the wāw.

With a visible fāʿil, the verb “must be singular and of the third person, even if it is dual or plural”: ḍaraba al-Zaydāni, ḍaraba al-Zaydūna, not ḍarabā al-Zaydāni. The reason is the last lessons' rule: the verb already has its fāʿil in the visible noun, so it takes no pronoun as a second fāʿil.

The verb must be feminine in two cases. When the fāʿil is a real feminine “among human beings”, singular or dual, joined to its governor, and the governor is conjugated: ḍarabat Hindun, ḍarabat al-Hindāni, and with a participle, Zaydun ḍāribatun jāriyatuhu. The word “conjugated” leaves out a verb like niʿma (lesson 13). And when the verb is attributed to a feminine pronoun, unless it stands for a broken plural of rational males: Hindun ḍarabat, and even al-shamsu ṭalaʿat, though the sun is not a real feminine.

Everywhere else both are allowed: ṭalaʿat or ṭalaʿa al-shamsu, a feminine that is not real; sārat or sāra al-nāqatu, real but not human; jāʾat or jāʾa al-muʾminātu, a plural; jāʾat or jāʾa al-qāḍiya al-yawma imraʾatun, a real feminine separated from its verb; al-rijālu jāʾat or jāʾū, a pronoun of a broken plural of rational males; and jāʾat or jāʾa al-rijālu.

terms.en: the showing pronoun joined to the verb
a real feminine: a female being
the tāʾ of the feminine on the verb: a sign, not a pronoun
a broken plural of rational males, as al-rijāl

examples.en: a visible dual fāʿil: the verb singular
a real human feminine joined to its verb: the feminine required
a feminine pronoun: the feminine required

examples.arabic: جَاءَتْ أَوْ جَاءَ الْقَاضِيَ الْيَوْمَ امْرَأَةٌ
examples.en: separated from its verb: both allowed
a pronoun of a broken plural of rational males: both allowed

tasks.prompt: Name the pronoun of the fāʿil in each: ḍarabtumā, yaḍribna, iḍribī, ḍarabnā.
tasks.answer: Ḍarabtumā: the alif (the dual). Yaḍribna: the nūn (feminine plural). Iḍribī: the yāʾ (the woman addressed, outside the past). Ḍarabnā: nā (the speaker with others, in the past).

tasks.prompt: Someone writes ḍarabā al-Zaydāni. Correct it and give the rule.
tasks.answer: Ḍaraba al-Zaydāni. When the fāʿil is a visible noun, the verb is singular and of the third person even if the fāʿil is dual or plural, because the visible noun is already its fāʿil.

tasks.prompt: Must the verb be feminine? ṭalaʿa al-shamsu; ḍaraba Hindun; sāra al-nāqatu; jāʾa al-qāḍiya al-yawma imraʾatun.
tasks.answer: Only ḍaraba Hindun must become ḍarabat Hindun: Hind is a real human feminine, singular, joined to a conjugated verb. Ṭalaʿa al-shamsu (not a real feminine), sāra al-nāqatu (not human) and jāʾa al-qāḍiya al-yawma imraʾatun (separated) may be masculine or feminine.

tasks.prompt: Why must one say al-shamsu ṭalaʿat, when ṭalaʿa al-shamsu is allowed?
tasks.answer: In al-shamsu ṭalaʿat the verb is attributed to a pronoun going back to the feminine al-shams, and a verb attributed to a feminine pronoun must be feminine. In ṭalaʿa al-shamsu the fāʿil is a visible noun that is not a real feminine, so either is allowed.

quiz.prompt: In ḍarabā, the alif is…
options: only the sign of the dual
the fāʿil, a showing joined pronoun
quiz.explanation: The alif in the duals of the verbs is the pronoun.

quiz.prompt: The book says ḍarabtum comes from…
quiz.explanation: So the wāw of the plural is its pronoun, dropped in use.

quiz.prompt: The yāʾ of taḍribīna is the pronoun of…
quiz.explanation: Outside the past, for the single feminine addressed.

quiz.prompt: With a visible dual or plural fāʿil, the verb is…
In which must the verb be feminine?
quiz.explanation: A real human feminine, singular, joined to a conjugated verb.

quiz.prompt: Al-rijālu jāʾat or jāʾū are both allowed because the pronoun stands for…
options: a broken plural of rational males
quiz.explanation: The one exception to the feminine pronoun.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾa al-qāḍiya al-yawma imraʾatun, the masculine verb is allowed because…
options: imraʾa is not a real feminine
the fāʿil is separated from its verb
quiz.explanation: The rule of the feminine needs the fāʿil joined to its governor.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْبَارِزُ الْمُتَّصِلُ فَفِي تَثَانِي الْأَفْعَالِ، وَهُوَ الْأَلِفُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَا، وَضَرَبَتَا، وَضَرَبْتُمَا، وَيَضْرِبَانِ، وَتَضْرِبَانِ، وَلِيَضْرِبَا، وَلِتَضْرِبَا، وَاضْرِبَا، وَلَا يَضْرِبَا، وَلَا تَضْرِبَا؛ وَجَمْعِهَا الْمُذَكَّرِ، وَهُوَ الْوَاوُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبُوا، وَضَرَبْتُمْ، إِذْ أَصْلُهُ ضَرَبْتُمُوا، وَيَضْرِبُونَ، وَتَضْرِبُونَ، وَلِيَضْرِبُوا؛ وَجَمْعِهَا الْمُؤَنَّثِ، وَهُوَ النُّونُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْنَ، وَضَرَبْتُنَّ، وَيَضْرِبْنَ، وَتَضْرِبْنَ، وَلِيَضْرِبْنَ، وَاضْرِبْنَ، وَلَا يَضْرِبْنَ، وَلَا تَضْرِبْنَ.
text.en: As for the showing pronoun that is joined, it is in the duals of the verbs, and it is the alif, as ḍarabā, ḍarabatā, ḍarabtumā, yaḍribāni, taḍribāni, li-yaḍribā, li-taḍribā, iḍribā, lā yaḍribā and lā taḍribā; in their masculine plural, and it is the wāw, as ḍarabū, and ḍarabtum, since its origin is ḍarabtumū, yaḍribūna, taḍribūna and li-yaḍribū; and in their feminine plural, and it is the nūn, as ḍarabna, ḍarabtunna, yaḍribna, taḍribna, li-yaḍribna, iḍribna, lā yaḍribna and lā taḍribna.

text.original: وَفِي الْمُخَاطَبِ الْمُفْرَدِ، مُذَكَّرًا كَانَ أَوْ مُؤَنَّثًا، وَالْمُتَكَلِّمِ وَحْدَهُ فِي الْمَاضِي، وَهُوَ التَّاءُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتَ، بِحَرَكَاتِ التَّاءِ، وَالْمُتَكَلِّمِ مَعَهُ غَيْرُهُ فِي الْمَاضِي، وَهُوَ نَا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْنَا، وَالْمُخَاطَبَةِ الْمُفْرَدَةِ فِي غَيْرِ الْمَاضِي، وَهُوَ الْيَاءُ، نَحْوُ: تَضْرِبِينَ، وَاضْرِبِي، وَلَا تَضْرِبِي.
text.en: And in the single one addressed, masculine or feminine, and the speaker alone, in the past, and it is the tāʾ, as ḍarabta, with the [different] vowels of the tāʾ; in the speaker with others, in the past, and it is nā, as ḍarabnā “we hit”; and in the single feminine one addressed, outside the past, and it is the yāʾ, as taḍribīna “you hit”, iḍribī “hit!” and lā taḍribī “do not hit!”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُظْهَرُ فَظَاهِرٌ، وَإِذَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ الْعَامِلُ يَجِبُ إِفْرَادُهُ وَغَيْبَتُهُ وَلَوْ كَانَ مُثَنًّى أَوْ مَجْمُوعًا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ الزَّيْدَانِ، أَوِ الزَّيْدُونَ. وَإِنْ كَانَ مُؤَنَّثًا حَقِيقِيًّا مِنَ الْآدَمِيِّينَ، مُفْرَدًا أَوْ مُثَنًّى، مُتَّصِلًا بِعَامِلِهِ، يَجِبُ تَأْنِيثُهُ إِنْ كَانَ مُتَصَرِّفًا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَتْ هِنْدٌ، أَوِ الْهِنْدَانِ، وَزَيْدٌ ضَارِبَةٌ جَارِيَتُهُ، وَكَذَا إِذَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَى ضَمِيرِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ غَيْرِ جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ الْمُكَسَّرِ الْعَاقِلِ، نَحْوُ: هِنْدٌ ضَرَبَتْ أَوْ ضَارِبَةٌ، وَالشَّمْسُ طَلَعَتْ أَوْ طَالِعَةٌ.
text.en: As for the visible noun, it is clear. When the governor is attributed to it, [the governor] must be singular and of the third person, even if [the noun] is dual or plural, as ḍaraba al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds hit”, or al-Zaydūna “the Zayds”. If it is a real feminine among human beings, singular or dual, joined to its governor, [the governor] must be feminine if it is conjugated, as ḍarabat Hindun “Hind hit”, or al-Hindāni “the two Hinds”, and Zaydun ḍāribatun jāriyatuhu “Zayd, his slave-girl is hitting”. So too when it is attributed to a feminine pronoun, other than [one for] a broken plural of rational males, as Hindun ḍarabat aw ḍāribatun “Hind, she hit, or is hitting”, and al-shamsu ṭalaʿat aw ṭāliʿatun “the sun, it rose, or is rising”.

text.original: وَفِي غَيْرِهِمَا يَجُوزُ تَأْنِيثُ عَامِلِهِ وَتَذْكِيرُهُ إِنْ كَانَ مُؤَنَّثًا، نَحْوُ: طَلَعَتْ أَوْ طَلَعَ الشَّمْسُ، وَنَحْوُ: سَارَتْ أَوْ سَارَ النَّاقَةُ، وَنَحْوُ: جَاءَتْ أَوْ جَاءَ الْمُؤْمِنَاتُ، وَجَاءَتْ أَوْ جَاءَ الْقَاضِيَ الْيَوْمَ امْرَأَةٌ، وَالرِّجَالُ جَاءَتْ أَوْ جَاءُوا، وَجَاءَتْ أَوْ جَاءَ الرِّجَالُ.
text.en: Outside these two, its governor may be feminine or masculine, if [the noun] is feminine, as ṭalaʿat aw ṭalaʿa al-shamsu “the sun rose”, and as sārat aw sāra al-nāqatu “the she-camel went”, and as jāʾat aw jāʾa al-muʾminātu “the believing women came”, jāʾat aw jāʾa al-qāḍiya al-yawma imraʾatun “a woman came to the judge today”, al-rijālu jāʾat aw jāʾū “the men, they came” and jāʾat aw jāʾa al-rijālu “the men came”.

lessons.title: The feminine, the plurals and the dual; the verb with a plural
body: The rules of the last lesson turn on the feminine and the plural, so Birgivī now defines them. The feminine is what has a mark of the feminine “in the wording or understood”. The marks are three: the tāʾ that is read as hāʾ in pause, ẓulma, “darkness”, read ẓulmah at the end of a phrase; the short alif, ḥublā, “pregnant”, daʿwā, “claim”; and the long alif, ḥamrāʾ, “red”. Shams, “sun”, has no mark in its wording; its tāʾ is understood, and the grammarians show it in the diminutive, shumaysa.

The numbers three to ten go the other way: the tāʾ is on the number for a masculine noun and dropped for a feminine, thalāthatu rijālin, “three men”, arbaʿu niswatin, “four women”. From thirteen to nineteen the first part keeps this rule and the second part follows the noun: thalāthata ʿashara rajulan, “thirteen men”, with the tāʾ on the first part only; thalātha ʿashrata imraʾatan, “thirteen women”, with the tāʾ on the second only.

A real feminine is one that “has a male facing it among living beings”, as imraʾa, “woman”, and nāqa, “she-camel”; every other feminine is verbal (lafẓī), as ghurfa, “room”, and shams. Notice that the she-camel is a real feminine, yet the rule that made the feminine verb necessary was only for real feminines “among human beings”: so sārat or sāra al-nāqatu (lesson 29). The plurals: the broken plural changes the form of its singular, rijāl; the sound masculine plural adds wāw or yāʾ with a nūn that has fatḥa, muslimūna, muslimīna; the sound feminine plural adds alif and tāʾ, muslimāt; and the dual adds alif or yāʾ with a nūn that has kasra, muslimāni, muslimayni. Both nūns drop in iḍāfa.

“Every plural other than the sound masculine plural is feminine, because it has the meaning of a group (jamāʿa).” The sound masculine plural is the one exception: its governor must be masculine, jāʾa al-muslimūna, rajulun qāʿidun nāṣirūhu; and a verb attributed to its pronoun must be a masculine plural: al-muslimūna jāʾū, or yajīʾūna, or jāʾūna.

The broken plural of rational males, with its pronoun, takes a feminine singular or a masculine plural: al-rijālu jāʾat, jāʾū, jāʾiyatun or jāʾūna. Every other plural, with its pronoun, takes a feminine singular or a feminine plural: al-muslimātu jāʾat or jiʾna; al-ashjāru quṭiʿat or quṭiʿna, maqṭūʿatun or maqṭūʿātun. The beginner's mistake is to give trees a masculine plural: al-ashjāru is not a plural of rational males, so the wāw of the masculine plural has no place in its verb.

terms.en: the mark of the feminine: the tāʾ, the short alif, the long alif
the verbal feminine, with no male facing it
the broken plural: the singular's form changed
the sound masculine plural, with wāw or yāʾ and nūn
the dual, with alif or yāʾ and a nūn with kasra

examples.en: the short alif and the long alif of the feminine
three to ten: the tāʾ with the masculine

examples.arabic: ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا — ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً
examples.en: thirteen: the tāʾ on the first part, or on the second
a sound masculine plural: its governor masculine
another plural with its pronoun: feminine singular or plural

tasks.prompt: Give the mark of the feminine in each, and say whether it is in the wording or understood: ḥublā, ḥamrāʾ, ẓulma, shams.
tasks.answer: Ḥublā: the short alif, in the wording. Ḥamrāʾ: the long alif, in the wording. Ẓulma: the tāʾ read as hāʾ in pause, in the wording. Shams: the tāʾ understood, not written.

tasks.prompt: Write the book's “three men”, “four women”, “thirteen men” and “thirteen women”, and give the rule.
tasks.arabic: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ — أَرْبَعُ نِسْوَةٍ — ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا — ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً
tasks.answer: From three to ten the number has the tāʾ with a masculine noun and drops it with a feminine one. Compounded with ten, the tāʾ stays on the first part only with a masculine noun, and goes on the second part only with a feminine one.

tasks.prompt: Which governors are allowed? al-muslimūna with jāʾat or jāʾū; al-rijālu with jāʾat or jāʾū; al-ashjāru with quṭiʿat or quṭiʿū.
tasks.answer: Al-muslimūna jāʾū only: a sound masculine plural takes a masculine plural. Al-rijālu jāʾat and al-rijālu jāʾū are both right: a broken plural of rational males takes a feminine singular or a masculine plural. Al-ashjāru quṭiʿat only (or quṭiʿna): other plurals take a feminine singular or plural, never quṭiʿū.

tasks.prompt: Why does the book call every plural except the sound masculine plural feminine?
tasks.answer: Because every such plural has the meaning of a group (jamāʿa), and jamāʿa is feminine. The sound masculine plural keeps the form of its masculine singular, so its governor stays masculine.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT a mark of the feminine in this book?
options: the tāʾ read as hāʾ in pause
quiz.explanation: The three marks are the tāʾ, the short alif and the long alif.

quiz.prompt: The mark of the feminine in shams is…
“Four women” in the book is…
quiz.explanation: Three to ten drop the tāʾ with a feminine noun.

quiz.prompt: Nāqa, “she-camel”, is…
quiz.explanation: It has a male facing it among living beings.

quiz.prompt: Which plural is not feminine, in the book's rule?
quiz.explanation: Every other plural has the meaning of a group.

quiz.prompt: Al-rijālu, with its pronoun, takes a governor that is…
quiz.explanation: Al-rijālu jāʾat, or jāʾū, or jāʾiyatun, or jāʾūna.

quiz.prompt: Which is wrong?
quiz.explanation: Only a plural of rational males takes the masculine plural.

text.original: وَالْمُؤَنَّثُ مَا فِيهِ عَلَامَةُ التَّأْنِيثِ لَفْظًا أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، وَهِيَ التَّاءُ الْمَوْقُوفُ عَلَيْهَا هَاءً، نَحْوُ ظُلْمَةٍ وَشَمْسٍ، وَالْأَلِفُ الْمَقْصُورَةُ، نَحْوُ حُبْلَى وَدَعْوَى، وَالْأَلِفُ الْمَمْدُودَةُ، نَحْوُ حَمْرَاءَ. وَهَذَا فِي غَيْرِ ثَلَاثَةٍ إِلَى عَشَرَةٍ، فَإِنَّ مُذَكَّرَهَا بِالتَّاءِ وَمُؤَنَّثَهَا بِحَذْفِهَا، نَحْوُ: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ، وَأَرْبَعُ نِسْوَةٍ. وَإِذَا رُكِّبَتْ ثَلَاثَةٌ إِلَى تِسْعَةٍ مَعَ عَشَرَةٍ أُثْبِتَتِ التَّاءُ فِي الْأَوَّلِ فَقَطْ فِي الْمُذَكَّرِ، نَحْوُ: ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَفِي الثَّانِي فَقَطْ فِي الْمُؤَنَّثِ، نَحْوُ: ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً.
text.en: The feminine is that which has a mark of the feminine, in the wording or understood. [The marks] are the tāʾ that is pronounced as hāʾ in pause, as ẓulmatin “darkness” and shamsin “sun”; the short alif, as ḥublā “pregnant” and daʿwā “claim”; and the long alif, as ḥamrāʾa “red”. This is outside three to ten, for their masculine has the tāʾ and their feminine is without it, as thalāthatu rijālin “three men” and arbaʿu niswatin “four women”. When three to nine are compounded with ten, the tāʾ is kept in the first only in the masculine, as thalāthata ʿashara rajulan “thirteen men”, and in the second only in the feminine, as thalātha ʿashrata imraʾatan “thirteen women”.

text.original: وَالتَّأْنِيثُ الْحَقِيقِيُّ مَا بِإِزَائِهِ ذَكَرٌ مِنَ الْحَيَوَانِ، نَحْوُ امْرَأَةٍ وَنَاقَةٍ، وَاللَّفْظِيُّ بِخِلَافِهِ، نَحْوُ غُرْفَةٍ وَشَمْسٍ. وَجَمْعُ الْمُكَسَّرِ مَا تَغَيَّرَ صِيغَةُ مُفْرَدِهِ، نَحْوُ رِجَالٍ.
text.en: The real feminine is that which has a male facing it among living beings, as imraʾatin “woman” and nāqatin “she-camel”; and the verbal is the opposite, as ghurfatin “room” and shamsin “sun”. The broken plural is that in which the form of its singular has changed, as rijālin “men”.

text.original: وَجَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ مَا لَحِقَ آخِرَ مُفْرَدِهِ وَاوٌ مَضْمُومٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا أَوْ يَاءٌ مَكْسُورٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَنُونٌ مَفْتُوحَةٌ فِي غَيْرِ الْإِضَافَةِ؛ فَإِنَّ النُّونَ تُحْذَفُ فِيهَا، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمُونَ وَمُسْلِمِينَ. وَجَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ مَا لَحِقَ آخِرَ مُفْرَدِهِ أَلِفٌ وَتَاءٌ، نَحْوُ مُسْلِمَاتٍ. وَالتَّثْنِيَةُ مَا لَحِقَ آخِرَ مُفْرَدِهِ أَلِفٌ أَوْ يَاءٌ مَفْتُوحٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَنُونٌ مَكْسُورَةٌ فِي غَيْرِ الْإِضَافَةِ، وَفِيهَا تُحْذَفُ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمَانِ وَمُسْلِمَيْنِ.
text.en: The sound masculine plural is that to the end of whose singular is joined a wāw with a ḍamma before it, or a yāʾ with a kasra before it, and a nūn with a fatḥa, outside the iḍāfa, for in it the nūn is dropped, as muslimūna and muslimīna “Muslims”. The sound feminine plural is that to the end of whose singular an alif and a tāʾ are joined, as muslimātin “Muslim women”. The dual is that to the end of whose singular is joined an alif, or a yāʾ with a fatḥa before it, and a nūn with a kasra, outside the iḍāfa, and in it [the nūn] is dropped, as muslimāni and muslimayni “two Muslims”.

text.original: وَكُلُّ جَمْعٍ غَيْرِ جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ مُؤَنَّثٌ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ بِمَعْنَى الْجَمَاعَةِ. وَأَمَّا جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ فَيَجِبُ تَذْكِيرُ عَامِلِهِ، فَتَقُولُ: جَاءَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ، أَوْ رَجُلٌ قَاعِدٌ نَاصِرُوهُ، وَإِذَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَى ضَمِيرِهِ يَجِبُ كَوْنُهُ جَمْعًا مُذَكَّرًا، نَحْوُ: الْمُسْلِمُونَ جَاءُوا، أَوْ يَجِيئُونَ، أَوْ جَاءُونَ.
text.en: Every plural other than the sound masculine plural is feminine, because it has the meaning of a group (jamāʿa). As for the sound masculine plural, its governor must be masculine, so you say jāʾa al-muslimūna “the Muslims came” or rajulun qāʿidun nāṣirūhu “a man whose helpers are sitting”; and when [the governor] is attributed to its pronoun, it must be a masculine plural, as al-muslimūna jāʾū “the Muslims, they came”, or yajīʾūna “they come”, or jāʾūna “coming”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ الْمُكَسَّرُ الْعَاقِلِ إِذَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَى ضَمِيرِهِ فَيَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ عَامِلُهُ مُفْرَدًا مُؤَنَّثًا أَوْ جَمْعًا مُذَكَّرًا، نَحْوُ: الرِّجَالُ جَاءَتْ، أَوْ جَاءُوا، أَوْ جَائِيَةٌ، أَوْ جَاءُونَ. وَغَيْرُهُمَا مِنَ الْجُمُوعِ إِذَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَى ضَمِيرِهَا يَجِبُ كَوْنُ عَامِلِهَا مُفْرَدًا مُؤَنَّثًا أَوْ جَمْعًا مُؤَنَّثًا، نَحْوُ: الْمُسْلِمَاتُ جَاءَتْ، أَوْ جِئْنَ، أَوْ جَائِيَةٌ، أَوْ جَائِيَاتٌ، وَالْأَشْجَارُ قُطِعَتْ، أَوْ قُطِعْنَ، أَوْ مَقْطُوعَةٌ، أَوْ مَقْطُوعَاتٌ.
text.en: As for the broken masculine plural of rational beings, when [the governor] is attributed to its pronoun, its governor must be feminine singular or masculine plural, as al-rijālu jāʾat “the men, they came”, or jāʾū, or jāʾiyatun “coming”, or jāʾūna. The plurals other than these two, when [the governor] is attributed to their pronoun, their governor must be feminine singular or feminine plural, as al-muslimātu jāʾat “the Muslim women, they came”, or jiʾna, or jāʾiyatun “coming”, or jāʾiyātun; and al-ashjāru quṭiʿat “the trees, they were cut”, or quṭiʿna, or maqṭūʿatun “cut”, or maqṭūʿātun.

lessons.title: The mubtadaʾ: its two kinds and its conditions
body: The third marfūʿ is the mubtadaʾ, of two kinds. The first is “the noun, or what is understood as one, to which something is attributed, free of the verbal governors”: Zaydun qāʾimun. “Free of the verbal governors” means that no word governs it; it is raised by the abstract governor (lesson 23). “Or what is understood as one” brings in ḥaqqun annaka qāʾimun, “that you are standing is true”, where annaka qāʾimun is the mubtadaʾ, as if qiyāmuka, and ḥaqqun is its khabar put first. This kind “must have a khabar”.

The second kind is “the adjective standing after an interrogative word or a negation and putting a visible noun in rafʿ”: a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni, mā qāʾimun al-Zaydūna. It has no khabar, “because it has the meaning of a verb”: like a verb it is completed by its fāʿil, and the fāʿil “stands in the place of the khabar”. Here are the conditions of lessons 18 and 19 at work: the participle leans on a question or a negation, so it governs.

Why does the book choose the dual al-Zaydāni? With a singular, a-qāʾimun Zaydun, the words could also be read the first way, Zaydun a mubtadaʾ put last and qāʾimun its khabar put first. With the dual that reading is shut, because the khabar would have to be qāʾimāni; only the second kind is left. A good example in the madrasa books is chosen so that it can be read only one way.

Three rules follow. The mubtadaʾ is one: one khabar is not said of two mubtadaʾs at once, though, as the next lesson shows, one mubtadaʾ may have several khabars. In origin it comes first. And it is definite, or an indefinite made particular: wa-la-ʿabdun muʾminun khayrun min mushrikin (Q 2:221), where ʿabdun is indefinite but narrowed by its adjective muʾminun. A wholly unknown subject would tell the hearer nothing.

The mubtadaʾ may be dropped when the context shows it: asked mani al-qāʾimu, “who is standing?”, you answer Zaydun, “that is, al-qāʾimu Zaydun”. Notice how Birgivī parses the answer: Zaydun is the khabar, and the dropped mubtadaʾ is al-qāʾimu, the word of the question.

terms.en: the noun attributed to, free of the verbal governors
standing in the place of the khabar: the fāʿil of the second kind
an indefinite made particular, as by an adjective
the context that shows what is dropped

examples.en: a mubtadaʾ understood as a noun: annaka qāʾimun
the second kind: the fāʿil in the place of the khabar
an indefinite made particular (Q 2:221)
the mubtadaʾ dropped: al-qāʾimu Zaydun

tasks.prompt: Parse ḥaqqun annaka qāʾimun.
tasks.answer: Ḥaqqun is the khabar, put first, in rafʿ. Annaka qāʾimun, anna with its ism and khabar, is understood as the maṣdar qiyāmuka and is the mubtadaʾ, in rafʿ in its place.

tasks.prompt: Why has mā qāʾimun al-Zaydūna no khabar?
tasks.answer: Qāʾimun is a mubtadaʾ of the second kind: an adjective after a negation that raises a visible noun. It has the meaning of a verb, so it is completed by its fāʿil al-Zaydūna, which stands in the place of the khabar.

tasks.prompt: ʿAbdun is indefinite. Why may it be the mubtadaʾ in wa-la-ʿabdun muʾminun khayrun min mushrikin?
tasks.answer: An indefinite may be a mubtadaʾ when it is made particular. Here the adjective muʾminun narrows ʿabdun to a believing slave, so the khabar khayrun min mushrikin tells the hearer something.

tasks.prompt: Asked a-qāʾimun Zaydun, a student says only one reading is possible. Is he right?
tasks.answer: No. Qāʾimun can be a mubtadaʾ of the second kind with Zaydun as its fāʿil, or Zaydun can be the mubtadaʾ put last with qāʾimun as its khabar put first. With the dual, a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni, only the first reading is possible.

quiz.prompt: The first kind of mubtadaʾ is free of…
quiz.explanation: It is raised by the abstract governor.

quiz.prompt: In ḥaqqun annaka qāʾimun, the mubtadaʾ is…
quiz.explanation: Understood as qiyāmuka; ḥaqqun is the khabar put first.

quiz.prompt: A mubtadaʾ of the second kind comes after…
quiz.explanation: And puts a visible noun in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: In a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni, what stands in the place of the khabar?
quiz.explanation: The adjective has a verb's meaning and its fāʿil completes it.

quiz.prompt: An indefinite may be a mubtadaʾ when it is…
Which is true in this book?
options: the mubtadaʾ may not be more than one
the mubtadaʾ comes last in origin
quiz.explanation: In origin it comes first, and it may be dropped with a context.

quiz.prompt: Zaydun, in answer to mani al-qāʾimu, is…
options: a mubtadaʾ with a dropped khabar
the khabar of a dropped mubtadaʾ

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ الْمُبْتَدَأُ، وَهُوَ نَوْعَانِ: الْأَوَّلُ الِاسْمُ أَوِ الْمُؤَوَّلُ بِهِ الْمُسْنَدُ إِلَيْهِ الْمُجَرَّدُ عَنِ الْعَوَامِلِ اللَّفْظِيَّةِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَحَقٌّ أَنَّكَ قَائِمٌ، وَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ خَبَرٍ. وَالثَّانِي الصِّفَةُ الْوَاقِعَةُ بَعْدَ كَلِمَةِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ أَوِ النَّفْيِ رَافِعَةً لِظَاهِرٍ، نَحْوُ: أَقَائِمٌ الزَّيْدَانِ، وَمَا قَائِمٌ الزَّيْدُونَ، وَلَا خَبَرَ لِهَذَا الْمُبْتَدَإِ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ بِمَعْنَى الْفِعْلِ، بَلْ فَاعِلُهُ سَادٌّ مَسَدَّ الْخَبَرِ.
text.en: The third is the mubtadaʾ, and it is of two kinds. The first is the noun, or what is understood as one, to which something is attributed, free of the verbal governors, as Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing” and ḥaqqun annaka qāʾimun “that you are standing is true”; it must have a khabar. The second is the adjective standing after an interrogative word or a negation and putting a visible noun in rafʿ, as a-qāʾimun al-Zaydāni “are the two Zayds standing?” and mā qāʾimun al-Zaydūna “the Zayds are not standing”. This mubtadaʾ has no khabar, because it has the meaning of a verb: rather its fāʿil stands in the place of the khabar.

text.original: وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَعَدُّدُ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، وَالْأَصْلُ تَقْدِيمُهُ، وَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَعْرِفَةً أَوْ نَكِرَةً مُخَصَّصَةً، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَلَعَبْدٌ مُؤْمِنٌ خَيْرٌ مِنْ مُشْرِكٍ، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُهُ عِنْدَ قِيَامِ قَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ، فِي جَوَابِ: مَنِ الْقَائِمُ؟ أَيِ الْقَائِمُ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: The mubtadaʾ may not be more than one. In origin it comes first, and its condition is that it is definite, or an indefinite made particular, as His saying, Most High: wa-la-ʿabdun muʾminun khayrun min mushrikin “and a believing slave is better than an idolater” [2:221]. It may be dropped when there is a context, as Zaydun “Zayd” in answer to mani al-qāʾimu “who is the one standing?”, that is, al-qāʾimu Zaydun “the one standing is Zayd”.

lessons.title: The khabar; the fāʾ in the khabar; the other marfūʿ
body: The fourth marfūʿ, the khabar, is “that, free of the verbal governors, by which something is attributed, other than the verb and what has its meaning”. “Other than the verb” leaves out the verb of a verbal sentence; “what has its meaning” leaves out the adjective of the second kind of mubtadaʾ (last lesson). A mubtadaʾ may have more than one khabar, Zaydun qāʾimun qāʿidun. When the khabar is a sentence it needs a word that refers back (ʿāʾid) to the mubtadaʾ (lesson 26), unless the mubtadaʾ is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), a pronoun that stands for “the matter” and is explained by the sentence itself. The referent may be dropped when the context shows it: al-burru al-kurru bi-sittīna, “wheat: the kurr [of it] is for sixty”, that is, minhu.

In origin the khabar is indefinite, as what is told is new, but it may be definite: Allāhu ilāhunā. It may be dropped with a context: Zaydun, said to one who asked a-Zaydun qāʾimun am ʿAmrun. After ammā the fāʾ must come into the khabar: ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliqun. Two exceptions: the necessity of verse, ammā al-qitālu lā qitāla ladaykumu, and a dropped verb of saying: fa-ammā alladhīna iswaddat wujūhuhum a-kafartum (Q 3:106), “that is, fa-yuqālu lahum a-kafartum”, where the fāʾ belongs to the dropped saying.

Elsewhere the fāʾ is allowed, not required, when the mubtadaʾ looks like a condition: a relative joined to a verb or an adverb, alladhī yaʾtīnī aw fī al-dāri fa-lahu dirhamun, “whoever comes to me, or is in the house, has a dirham”; an indefinite qualified by them, or muḍāf to such an indefinite; and kull muḍāf to an indefinite: kullu rajulin fa-lahu dirhamun. The commentators give the reason: these words have the general sense of a condition, and their khabar is earned by it as a requital is earned. Inna, anna and lākinna do not take the fāʾ away: qul inna al-mawta alladhī tafirrūna minhu fa-innahu mulāqīkum (Q 62:8); the other cancellers of the mubtadaʾ do.

The remaining marfūʿ are named briefly, since each follows a rule already learned. The fifth, the ism of kāna and its class, is “like the fāʿil”. The sixth, the khabar of inna and its class, is like the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, but it may not come before its ism “unless it is an adverb”: inna fī al-dāri rajulan. The seventh, the khabar of the lā that denies the genus, is like the khabar of the mubtadaʾ: lā ghulāma rajulin ʿindanā. The eighth, the ism of mā and lā like laysa, is like the mubtadaʾ.

The ninth is the muḍāriʿ “free of the particles of naṣb and jazm”: yaḍribu, yaḍribāni. It is the only verb among the nine: eight nouns and one verb, all of them governed in their own right, and all of them in rafʿ, whatever governor raises them.

terms.en: what is attributed to the mubtadaʾ, other than the verb and its like
the word in a khabar sentence that refers back to the mubtadaʾ
the pronoun of the matter, explained by the sentence after it
the fāʾ in the khabar: required after ammā, allowed after a condition-like mubtadaʾ

examples.en: one mubtadaʾ, two khabars
the referent dropped: minhu
after ammā the fāʾ is required

examples.arabic: الَّذِي يَأْتِينِي أَوْ فِي الدَّارِ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ
examples.en: a relative joined to a verb or adverb: the fāʾ allowed
the khabar of inna before its ism: only an adverb

tasks.prompt: Give the dropped words and parse al-burru al-kurru bi-sittīna.
tasks.answer: Al-burru is the first mubtadaʾ. Al-kurru is a second mubtadaʾ and bi-sittīna its khabar; the sentence al-kurru bi-sittīna is the khabar of al-burru. Its referent back to al-burru, minhu (“of it”), is dropped because the context shows it: al-kurru minhu bi-sittīna.

tasks.prompt: Why does a-kafartum in Q 3:106 have no fāʾ after ammā?
tasks.answer: A verb of saying is understood: fa-yuqālu lahum a-kafartum. The fāʾ required after ammā goes with that dropped saying, which is the real khabar, and the question a-kafartum is what is said.

tasks.prompt: May the fāʾ come into the khabar? kullu rajulin fa-lahu dirhamun; Zaydun fa-lahu dirhamun.
tasks.arabic: كُلُّ رَجُلٍ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ — زَيْدٌ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ
tasks.answer: In the first, yes: kull is muḍāf to an indefinite, and the mubtadaʾ has the general sense of a condition. In the second, no: Zaydun is a proper name with no sense of a condition, and the book says that outside the cases named the fāʾ is not allowed.

tasks.prompt: Name the nine marfūʿ of the book in order.
tasks.answer: The fāʿil; the deputy of the fāʿil; the mubtadaʾ; the khabar of the mubtadaʾ; the ism of kāna and its class; the khabar of inna and its class; the khabar of the lā that denies the genus; the ism of mā and lā like laysa; the muḍāriʿ free of the particles of naṣb and jazm.

quiz.prompt: May a mubtadaʾ have more than one khabar?
options: only if the khabar is a sentence
quiz.explanation: The khabar may be more than one; the mubtadaʾ may not.

quiz.prompt: A khabar sentence needs no referent when the mubtadaʾ is…
quiz.explanation: The sentence itself explains the pronoun of the matter.

quiz.prompt: After ammā, the fāʾ in the khabar is…
options: required, except in verse or with a dropped saying

quiz.prompt: In alladhī yaʾtīnī fa-lahu dirhamun the fāʾ is…
options: allowed, as the mubtadaʾ is like a condition
quiz.explanation: A relative joined to a verb or adverb.

quiz.prompt: Which canceller leaves the fāʾ in the khabar allowed?
quiz.explanation: Inna, anna and lākinna; not the other cancellers.

quiz.prompt: The khabar of inna may come before its ism only when it is…
Which of the nine marfūʿ is a verb?
options: the muḍāriʿ free of naṣb and jazm

text.original: وَالرَّابِعُ خَبَرُ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، وَهُوَ الْمُجَرَّدُ عَنِ الْعَوَامِلِ اللَّفْظِيَّةِ الْمُسْنَدُ بِهِ، غَيْرُ الْفِعْلِ وَمَعْنَاهُ، نَحْوُ: قَائِمٌ، فِي: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَيَجُوزُ تَعَدُّدُهُ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ قَاعِدٌ. وَقَدْ يَكُونُ جُمْلَةً اسْمِيَّةً أَوْ فِعْلِيَّةً، فَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ عَائِدٍ إِلَى الْمُبْتَدَإِ إِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ خَبَرًا عَنْ ضَمِيرِ الشَّأْنِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ قَامَ أَبُوهُ، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُهُ لِقَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: الْبُرُّ الْكُرُّ بِسِتِّينَ، أَيْ مِنْهُ.
text.en: The fourth is the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, which is that, free of the verbal governors, by which [something] is attributed, other than the verb and what has its meaning, as qāʾimun in Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”. It may be more than one, as Zaydun qāʾimun qāʿidun “Zayd is standing [and] sitting”. It may be a nominal or a verbal sentence, and then there must be something referring back to the mubtadaʾ, if it is not the khabar of the pronoun of the matter, as Zaydun abūhu qāʾimun “Zayd, his father is standing”, or qāma abūhu “his father stood”; [this referent] may be dropped because of a context, as al-burru al-kurru bi-sittīna “wheat, the kurr is for sixty”, that is, minhu “of it”.

text.original: وَأَصْلُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ نَكِرَةً، وَقَدْ يَكُونُ مَعْرِفَةً، نَحْوُ: اللَّهُ إِلَهُنَا. وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُهُ عِنْدَ قَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ، لِمَنْ قَالَ: أَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ أَمْ عَمْرٌو. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْمُبْتَدَأُ بَعْدَ أَمَّا وَجَبَ دُخُولُ الْفَاءِ فِي خَبَرِهِ، نَحْوُ: أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَمُنْطَلِقٌ، إِلَّا لِضَرُورَةِ الشِّعْرِ، كَقَوْلِهِ: أَمَّا الْقِتَالُ لَا قِتَالَ لَدَيْكُمُ، أَوْ لِإِضْمَارِ الْقَوْلِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: فَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ اسْوَدَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ أَكَفَرْتُمْ، أَيْ فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ: أَكَفَرْتُمْ.
text.en: In origin it is indefinite, but it may be definite, as Allāhu ilāhunā “God is our God”. It may be dropped when there is a context, as Zaydun “Zayd”, said to one who said a-Zaydun qāʾimun am ʿAmrun “is Zayd standing, or ʿAmr?”. If the mubtadaʾ comes after ammā, the fāʾ must come into its khabar, as ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliqun “as for Zayd, he is leaving”, except by the necessity of verse, as the poet's saying: ammā al-qitālu lā qitāla ladaykumu “as for fighting, there is no fighting with you”, or because a saying is understood, as His saying, Most High: fa-ammā alladhīna iswaddat wujūhuhum a-kafartum “as for those whose faces are blackened: did you disbelieve?” [3:106], that is, fa-yuqālu lahum “it will be said to them”: a-kafartum “did you disbelieve?”.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ اسْمًا مَوْصُولًا بِفِعْلٍ أَوْ ظَرْفٍ، أَوْ مَوْصُوفًا بِهِ، أَوْ نَكِرَةً مَوْصُوفَةً بِأَحَدِهِمَا، أَوْ مُضَافًا إِلَيْهَا، أَوْ لَفْظَ كُلٍّ مُضَافًا إِلَى نَكِرَةٍ مَوْصُوفَةٍ بِمُفْرَدٍ أَوْ غَيْرِ مَوْصُوفَةٍ أَصْلًا، جَازَ دُخُولُ الْفَاءِ فِي خَبَرِهِ، وَكَذَا إِذَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ إِنَّ وَأَنَّ وَلَكِنَّ، بِخِلَافِ سَائِرِ نَوَاسِخِ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، حَرْفًا كَانَ أَوْ فِعْلًا.
text.en: If it is a relative noun joined [as ṣila] to a verb or an adverb, or qualified by one, or an indefinite qualified by one of them, or muḍāf to such an indefinite, or the word kull made muḍāf to an indefinite qualified by a single word, or not qualified at all, the fāʾ may come into its khabar; likewise when inna, anna and lākinna come upon it, unlike the other words that cancel the mubtadaʾ, whether particle or verb.

text.original: نَحْوُ: الَّذِي يَأْتِينِي أَوْ فِي الدَّارِ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ، وَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: قُلْ إِنَّ الْمَوْتَ الَّذِي تَفِرُّونَ مِنْهُ فَإِنَّهُ مُلَاقِيكُمْ، وَنَحْوُ: رَجُلٌ يَأْتِينِي أَوْ فِي الدَّارِ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ، وَغُلَامُ رَجُلٍ يَأْتِينِي أَوْ فِي الدَّارِ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ، وَكُلُّ رَجُلٍ عَالِمٍ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ، وَكُلُّ رَجُلٍ فَلَهُ دِرْهَمٌ، وَفِي غَيْرِهَا لَا يَجُوزُ.
text.en: As alladhī yaʾtīnī aw fī al-dāri fa-lahu dirhamun “whoever comes to me, or is in the house, has a dirham”; His saying, Most High: qul inna al-mawta alladhī tafirrūna minhu fa-innahu mulāqīkum “say: the death from which you flee will surely meet you” [62:8]; and as rajulun yaʾtīnī aw fī al-dāri fa-lahu dirhamun “a man who comes to me, or is in the house, has a dirham”, ghulāmu rajulin yaʾtīnī aw fī al-dāri fa-lahu dirhamun “the servant of a man who comes to me, or is in the house, has a dirham”, kullu rajulin ʿālimin fa-lahu dirhamun “every learned man has a dirham” and kullu rajulin fa-lahu dirhamun “every man has a dirham”. Outside these it is not allowed.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ اسْمُ بَابِ كَانَ، وَحُكْمُهُ كَحُكْمِ الْفَاعِلِ. وَالسَّادِسُ خَبَرُ بَابِ إِنَّ، وَأَمْرُهُ كَأَمْرِ خَبَرِ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، لَكِنْ لَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ عَلَى اسْمِهِ إِلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ ظَرْفًا، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ فِي الدَّارِ رَجُلًا. وَالسَّابِعُ خَبَرُ لَا لِنَفْيِ الْجِنْسِ، وَحُكْمُهُ أَيْضًا كَحُكْمِ خَبَرِ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، نَحْوُ: لَا غُلَامَ رَجُلٍ عِنْدَنَا. وَالثَّامِنُ اسْمُ مَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَيْنِ بِلَيْسَ، وَحُكْمُهُ كَحُكْمِ الْمُبْتَدَإِ. وَالتَّاسِعُ الْمُضَارِعُ الْخَالِي عَنِ النَّوَاصِبِ وَالْجَوَازِمِ، نَحْوُ: يَضْرِبُ وَيَضْرِبَانِ.
text.en: The fifth is the ism of the class of kāna, and its rule is like the rule of the fāʿil. The sixth is the khabar of the class of inna, and its matter is like the matter of the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, but it may not be put before its ism unless it is an adverb, as inna fī al-dāri rajulan “there is a man in the house”. The seventh is the khabar of the lā that denies the genus, and its rule too is like the rule of the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, as lā ghulāma rajulin ʿindanā “no man's servant is with us”. The eighth is the ism of mā and lā that resemble laysa, and its rule is like the rule of the mubtadaʾ. The ninth is the muḍāriʿ free of the particles of naṣb and of jazm, as yaḍribu “he hits” and yaḍribāni “they both hit”.

lessons.title: The manṣūb: the absolute object and the mafʿūl bihi
body: “As for the manṣūb, it is thirteen”, and the first five are the five objects (mafʿūl). The first is the absolute object, “the name of what was done by the doer of a governor that is mentioned, in wording or understood”: the maṣdar that names the act itself. The commentators explain the name: it is the object without a qualifier, while the others are objects “on whom”, “in which”, “for which” and “with whom”. Birgivī's three examples give its three uses: ḍarabtu ḍarban, “I hit a hitting”, which only strengthens the verb; ḍarbatan, “one hit”, which counts it; and ḍirbatan, “a way of hitting”, which gives its kind.

It may be from another word with the same meaning: qaʿadtu julūsan, “I sat a sitting”, where julūs is not from the root of qaʿada. Its verb may be dropped when the context shows it, and the book's example is one of the commonest words of Arabic: ayḍan, “also”, is the maṣdar of āḍa, “to return”, “that is, āḍa ayḍan”. It may come before its governor, and it is not bound to it: a verb may stand without any absolute object at all.

The second is the mafʿūl bihi, “the name of what the act of the doer falls upon”. It is of two divisions. The general one is the word in jarr by a particle, as Zayd in marartu bi-Zaydin: the act reaches him through the bāʾ (lesson 5). The special one belongs to the transitive verb and is in naṣb, as Zaydan in ḍarabtu Zaydan (lesson 14).

The mafʿūl bihi has three freedoms. It may come before its governor: Zaydan ḍarabtu, “Zayd I hit”, where Zaydan is still the object, in naṣb, and the sentence is still verbal. Compare Zaydun ḍaraba (lesson 27): the fāʿil may never come first, and a noun before the verb becomes a mubtadaʾ. It may be dropped “without condition”: ḍarabtu alone is a complete sentence. And its verb may be dropped with a context: Zaydan, said to one who asked man aḍribu, “whom shall I hit?”, that is, iḍrib Zaydan.

the object on which the act falls
“also”: the maṣdar of āḍa, its verb dropped

tasks.prompt: Say what each absolute object gives: ḍarabtu ḍarban; ḍarabtu ḍarbatan; ḍarabtu ḍirbatan.
tasks.answer: Ḍarban only strengthens the verb (emphasis). Ḍarbatan, on the pattern faʿla, counts it: “one hit”. Ḍirbatan, on the pattern fiʿla, gives its kind: “a way of hitting”.

tasks.prompt: Julūsan is not from the root of qaʿada. Why is it the absolute object in qaʿadtu julūsan?
tasks.answer: The absolute object is the name of what the doer of the governor did. Julūs names the very act of sitting that qaʿadtu speaks of, so it is the absolute object though its word is another.

tasks.prompt: Parse ayḍan as the book does.
tasks.answer: Ayḍan is an absolute object, in naṣb, the maṣdar of āḍa, “to return”; its verb is dropped because the context shows it: āḍa ayḍan.

tasks.prompt: Parse Zaydan ḍarabtu, and say why Zaydun ḍaraba is parsed differently.
tasks.answer: In Zaydan ḍarabtu, Zaydan is the mafʿūl bihi put before its governor, in naṣb; ḍarabtu is the verb with its fāʿil, the tāʾ. The object may come first. In Zaydun ḍaraba the noun cannot be a fāʿil put first, since the fāʿil never precedes its verb; so Zaydun is a mubtadaʾ, and the fāʿil is a pronoun hidden in ḍaraba.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَنْصُوبُ فَثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ: الْأَوَّلُ الْمَفْعُولُ الْمُطْلَقُ، وَهُوَ اسْمُ مَا فَعَلَهُ فَاعِلُ عَامِلٍ مَذْكُورٍ لَفْظًا أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ ضَرْبًا، وَضَرْبَةً، وَضِرْبَةً، وَقَدْ يَكُونُ بِغَيْرِ لَفْظِهِ، نَحْوُ: قَعَدْتُ جُلُوسًا، وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ فِعْلُهُ لِقِيَامِ قَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: أَيْضًا، أَيْ آضَ أَيْضًا، وَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ عَلَى عَامِلِهِ، وَلَا يَلْزَمُ الْعَامِلَ.
text.en: As for the manṣūb, it is thirteen. The first is the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq), which is the name of what was done by the doer of a governor that is mentioned, in wording or understood, as ḍarabtu ḍarban “I hit a hitting”, ḍarbatan “one hit” and ḍirbatan “a way of hitting”. It may be of another word than [its verb], as qaʿadtu julūsan “I sat a sitting”. Its verb may be dropped because there is a context, as ayḍan “also”, that is, āḍa ayḍan “it returned a returning”. It may be put before its governor, and it does not have to go with the governor.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي الْمَفْعُولُ بِهِ، وَهُوَ اسْمُ مَا وَقَعَ عَلَيْهِ فِعْلُ الْفَاعِلِ، وَهُوَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: عَامٌّ، وَهُوَ الْمَجْرُورُ بِالْحَرْفِ، وَخَاصٌّ بِالْمُتَعَدِّي، وَقَدْ مَرَّ. وَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ عَلَى عَامِلِهِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدًا ضَرَبْتُ، وَحَذْفُهُ مُطْلَقًا، وَحَذْفُ فِعْلِهِ لِقِيَامِ قَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدًا، لِمَنْ قَالَ: مَنْ أَضْرِبُ؟
text.en: The second is the mafʿūl bihi, which is the name of what the act of the doer falls upon. It is of two divisions: general, which is the one put in jarr by a particle; and special to the transitive [verb], which has gone before. It may be put before its governor, as Zaydan ḍarabtu “Zayd I hit”; it may be dropped without condition; and its verb may be dropped because there is a context, as Zaydan “Zayd”, said to one who said man aḍribu “whom shall I hit?”.

lessons.title: The mafʿūl fīhi, the mafʿūl lahu and the mafʿūl maʿahu
body: The third object is the mafʿūl fīhi, “the name of the time or place in which the content of its governor was done”: ṣumtu shahran, “I fasted a month”. It is in naṣb “in wording” only when fī is understood; when fī is spoken it puts the noun in jarr. The conditions for understanding fī, all the times and the vague places but not the bounded ones, were given in lesson 6. It may come before its governor, “even if that is the meaning of a verb”, as a settled adverb or a noun of a verb is; it may be dropped without condition; and its governor may be dropped with a context, as when one asked “when did you travel?” answers only with the time.

The fourth is the mafʿūl lahu, “the name of that for whose sake the content of its governor was done”: ḍarabtu Zaydan taʾdīban lahu, “I hit Zayd to discipline him”. It is in naṣb only when the lām is understood, and lesson 7 gave the conditions: an act of the same doer as the verb, at the same time. So akramtuka li-ikrāmika keeps its lām, because the honouring was yours, not mine. It may come first, be left out, or lose its governor with a context.

The fifth is the mafʿūl maʿahu, “what is mentioned after the wāw for keeping company with a word governed by a governor”: jiʾtu wa-Zaydan, “I came with Zayd”. The wāw has the meaning of maʿa, “with”, and Zaydan is in naṣb. It is not joined to the tāʾ of jiʾtu, for then it would be in rafʿ, and the joining of a noun to a pronoun in rafʿ needs the separate pronoun first, jiʾtu anā wa-Zaydun.

Unlike the other four, the mafʿūl maʿahu is bound in its place. It may not come before its governor, nor before the word whose company it keeps (one does not say wa-Zaydan jiʾtu), and there is only one of it in a sentence. The commentators give the reason: the wāw is in origin the wāw of joining, and what is joined never comes before what it is joined to.

terms.en: the time or place of the act, with fī understood
that for whose sake the act was done, with the lām understood
the noun after the wāw of company
the wāw in the sense of “with”

tasks.prompt: Name the object and the particle understood in each: ṣumtu shahran; ḍarabtu Zaydan taʾdīban lahu.
tasks.arabic: صُمْتُ شَهْرًا — ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا تَأْدِيبًا لَهُ
tasks.answer: Shahran is the mafʿūl fīhi, with fī understood (fī shahrin). Taʾdīban is the mafʿūl lahu, with the lām understood (li-taʾdībin); Zaydan is the mafʿūl bihi.

tasks.prompt: Why is the lām kept in akramtuka li-ikrāmika?
tasks.answer: The mafʿūl lahu may drop its lām only when it is the act of the doer of the verb and at the same time. Here the reason is your honouring, while the verb is my honouring: another doer, so the lām must stay.

tasks.prompt: Parse jiʾtu wa-Zaydan, and say why Zaydan is not joined to the tāʾ.
tasks.answer: Jiʾtu: a verb with its fāʿil, the tāʾ. Wa: the wāw of company, meaning “with”. Zaydan: the mafʿūl maʿahu, in naṣb. It is not joined to the tāʾ, since joining to a pronoun in rafʿ needs the separate pronoun first (jiʾtu anā wa-Zaydun), and then it would be in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Which of the five objects may not come before its governor, and why, according to the commentators?
tasks.answer: The mafʿūl maʿahu. Its wāw is in origin the wāw of joining, and what is joined does not come before what it is joined to; so it may come neither before its governor nor before the word whose company it keeps.

quiz.explanation: With fī spoken, the noun is in jarr.

quiz.prompt: How many mafʿūl maʿahu may one sentence have?
quiz.explanation: It may not be more than one.

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ الْمَفْعُولُ فِيهِ، وَهُوَ اسْمُ مَا فُعِلَ فِيهِ مَضْمُونُ عَامِلِهِ مِنْ زَمَانٍ أَوْ مَكَانٍ، وَشَرْطُ نَصْبِهِ لَفْظًا تَقْدِيرُ فِي، وَقَدْ مَرَّ شَرْطُ تَقْدِيرِهِ، وَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ عَلَى عَامِلِهِ وَلَوْ كَانَ مَعْنَى فِعْلٍ، وَحَذْفُهُ مُطْلَقًا، وَحَذْفُ عَامِلِهِ لِقَرِينَةٍ.
text.en: The third is the mafʿūl fīhi, which is the name of the time or place in which the content of its governor was done. The condition for its being manṣūb in wording is that fī “in” is understood, and the condition for understanding it has gone before. It may be put before its governor, even if that is the meaning of a verb; it may be dropped without condition; and its governor may be dropped because of a context.

text.original: وَالرَّابِعُ الْمَفْعُولُ لَهُ، وَهُوَ اسْمُ مَا فُعِلَ لِأَجْلِهِ مَضْمُونُ عَامِلِهِ، وَشَرْطُ نَصْبِهِ لَفْظًا تَقْدِيرُ اللَّامِ، وَقَدْ مَرَّ شَرْطُ تَقْدِيرِهِ، وَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ عَلَى عَامِلِهِ، وَتَرْكُهُ، وَحَذْفُ عَامِلِهِ لِقَرِينَةٍ. وَالْخَامِسُ الْمَفْعُولُ مَعَهُ، وَهُوَ الْمَذْكُورُ بَعْدَ الْوَاوِ لِمُصَاحَبَةِ مَعْمُولِ عَامِلٍ، نَحْوُ: جِئْتُ وَزَيْدًا، وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ عَلَى عَامِلِهِ، وَلَا عَلَى الْمَعْمُولِ الْمُصَاحَبِ، وَلَا تَعَدُّدُهُ.
text.en: The fourth is the mafʿūl lahu, which is the name of that for whose sake the content of its governor was done. The condition for its being manṣūb in wording is that the lām is understood, and the condition for understanding it has gone before. It may be put before its governor, it may be left out, and its governor may be dropped because of a context. The fifth is the mafʿūl maʿahu, which is what is mentioned after the wāw for keeping company with a word governed by a governor, as jiʾtu wa-Zaydan “I came with Zayd”. It may not be put before its governor, nor before the governed word whose company it keeps, and it may not be more than one.

lessons.title: The ḥāl
body: The sixth manṣūb is the ḥāl, “what shows the state of the fāʿil or of the mafʿūl bihi, in wording or in meaning”. In ḍarabtu Zaydan qāʾiman, “I hit Zayd standing”, qāʾiman shows Zayd's state while the act fell on him. In hādhā Zaydun qāʾiman, “this is Zayd, standing”, Zaydun is a khabar in wording, but in meaning it is the object of “I point to”, the sense of hādhā (lesson 23): so it is an object “in meaning”.

Its governor is the verb, what resembles it, as the participles, or a word with its meaning, as hādhā. Its condition is that it is indefinite; the commentators add that a ḥāl that looks definite, as waḥdahu in jāʾa Zaydun waḥdahu, is understood as an indefinite, munfaridan, “alone”. It does not come before an abstract governor such as hādhā, nor before an owner (ṣāḥib) that is in jarr: “one does not say marartu jālisan bi-Zaydin.”

And when its owner is a pure indefinite the ḥāl must come first: jāʾanī rākiban rajulun, “there came to me, riding, a man”. The reason is easy to see: after an indefinite, rākibun would be read as its adjective, rajulun rākibun, “a riding man”; put first, it can only be a ḥāl.

The ḥāl may be a sentence that states something (jumla khabariyya), not a command or a question, and then it needs a link (rābiṭ) to its owner. With an affirmative muḍāriʿ the link is “the pronoun only”: jāʾanī Zaydun yarkabu, with no wāw. Elsewhere it may be the pronoun with the wāw, the wāw alone, or the pronoun alone; in a nominal sentence the wāw is more usual: wa-huwa rākibun. The table gives the book's examples.

The ḥāl may be more than one: jāʾanī Zaydun rākiban ḍāḥikan, “Zayd came to me riding, laughing”. And its governor may be dropped when the context shows it: to one who says urīdu al-safara, “I want to travel”, one says rāshidan mahdiyyan, “rightly guided, well led!”, a verb such as “go” being understood.

terms.en: what shows the state of the fāʿil or the object
the owner of the ḥāl, whose state it shows
a sentence that states something, not a command or question
the link of a ḥāl sentence: the pronoun, the wāw, or both

examples.en: the ḥāl of the object
the owner an object in meaning
the owner a pure indefinite: the ḥāl first
two ḥāls
the governor dropped
