tasks.prompt: Find the ḥāl and its owner in each: ḍarabtu Zaydan qāʾiman; hādhā Zaydun qāʾiman.
tasks.arabic: ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا — هَذَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا
tasks.answer: In the first, qāʾiman is the ḥāl and Zaydan, the mafʿūl bihi in wording, is its owner; the governor is ḍarabtu. In the second, qāʾiman is the ḥāl of Zaydun, a khabar in wording but the object of “I point to” in meaning; its governor is the meaning of the verb in hādhā.

tasks.prompt: Why must the ḥāl come first in jāʾanī rākiban rajulun?
tasks.answer: Its owner rajulun is a pure indefinite. After an indefinite the word would be read as its adjective (rajulun rākibun), so the ḥāl is put first, where it can only be a ḥāl.

tasks.prompt: Say which links are used: jāʾanī Zaydun yarkabu; jāʾanī Zaydun wa-rakiba ʿAmrun; jāʾanī Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ يَرْكَبُ — جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وَرَكِبَ عَمْرٌو — جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وَهُوَ رَاكِبٌ
tasks.answer: Yarkabu: an affirmative muḍāriʿ, linked by the pronoun hidden in it only. Wa-rakiba ʿAmrun: a past sentence with no pronoun of Zayd, linked by the wāw alone. Wa-huwa rākibun: a nominal sentence, linked by the wāw and the pronoun huwa, the more usual way.

tasks.prompt: Why is marartu jālisan bi-Zaydin not said, and how should it be said?
tasks.answer: The owner of the ḥāl, Zayd, is in jarr, and the ḥāl does not come before an owner in jarr. One says marartu bi-Zaydin jālisan.

quiz.prompt: The ḥāl shows the state of…
options: the fāʿil or the mafʿūl bihi

quiz.prompt: The condition of the ḥāl is that it is…
quiz.explanation: A ḥāl that looks definite is understood as indefinite.

quiz.prompt: The ḥāl may not come before…
In jāʾanī rākiban rajulun the ḥāl comes first because…
options: its owner is a pure indefinite
quiz.explanation: Otherwise it would be read as an adjective.

quiz.prompt: A ḥāl sentence with an affirmative muḍāriʿ is linked by…
In a nominal ḥāl sentence the more usual link is…
Rāshidan mahdiyyan, said to one who wants to travel, shows that…
options: the governor of the ḥāl may be dropped
quiz.explanation: A verb such as “go” is understood from the context.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسُ الْحَالُ، وَهُوَ مَا يُبَيِّنُ هَيْئَةَ الْفَاعِلِ أَوِ الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ لَفْظًا أَوْ مَعْنًى، مِثْلُ: ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا، وَهَذَا زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا. وَعَامِلُهَا الْفِعْلُ أَوْ شِبْهُهُ أَوْ مَعْنَاهُ، وَشَرْطُهَا أَنْ تَكُونَ نَكِرَةً، وَلَا تَتَقَدَّمُ عَلَى الْعَامِلِ الْمَعْنَوِيِّ، وَلَا عَلَى ذِي الْحَالِ الْمَجْرُورِ، فَلَا يُقَالُ: مَرَرْتُ جَالِسًا بِزَيْدٍ. وَلَوْ كَانَ صَاحِبُهَا نَكِرَةً مَحْضَةً وَجَبَ تَقْدِيمُ الْحَالِ عَلَيْهَا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَاكِبًا رَجُلٌ.
text.en: The sixth is the ḥāl, which is what shows the state of the fāʿil or of the mafʿūl bihi, in wording or in meaning, as ḍarabtu Zaydan qāʾiman “I hit Zayd [while he was] standing” and hādhā Zaydun qāʾiman “this is Zayd, standing”. Its governor is the verb, what resembles it, or its meaning. Its condition is that it is indefinite. It does not come before an abstract governor, nor before an owner of the ḥāl that is majrūr: one does not say marartu jālisan bi-Zaydin “I passed, sitting, by Zayd”. If its owner is a pure indefinite, the ḥāl must come before it, as jāʾanī rākiban rajulun “there came to me, riding, a man”.

text.original: وَتَكُونُ جُمْلَةً خَبَرِيَّةً، فَلَا بُدَّ فِيهَا مِنْ رَابِطٍ، وَهُوَ الضَّمِيرُ فَقَطْ فِي الْمُضَارِعِ الْمُثْبَتِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ يَرْكَبُ، أَوْ مَعَ الْوَاوِ، أَوِ الْوَاوُ وَحْدَهُ، أَوِ الضَّمِيرُ وَحْدَهُ فِي غَيْرِهِ، لَكِنِ الْغَالِبُ فِي الِاسْمِيَّةِ الْوَاوُ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ لَا يَرْكَبُ، أَوْ وَلَا يَرْكَبُ، أَوْ وَلَا يَرْكَبُ عَمْرٌو، أَوْ رَكِبَ، أَوْ وَرَكِبَ، أَوْ وَرَكِبَ عَمْرٌو، أَوْ هُوَ رَاكِبٌ، أَوْ وَهُوَ رَاكِبٌ.
text.en: It may be a sentence that states [something] (jumla khabariyya), and then it must have a link. In the affirmative muḍāriʿ this is the pronoun only, as jāʾanī Zaydun yarkabu “Zayd came to me riding”; in other [sentences] it is [the pronoun] with the wāw, or the wāw alone, or the pronoun alone, but in the nominal [sentence] the wāw is more usual, as jāʾanī Zaydun lā yarkabu “Zayd came to me not riding”, or wa-lā yarkabu “and he is not riding”, or wa-lā yarkabu ʿAmrun “and ʿAmr is not riding”; or rakiba “having ridden”, or wa-rakiba “and he had ridden”, or wa-rakiba ʿAmrun “and ʿAmr had ridden”; or huwa rākibun “he riding”, or wa-huwa rākibun “while he was riding”.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ تَعَدُّدُ الْحَالِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ رَاكِبًا ضَاحِكًا، وَحَذْفُ عَامِلِهِ بِقَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: رَاشِدًا مَهْدِيًّا، لِمَنْ قَالَ: أُرِيدُ السَّفَرَ.
text.en: The ḥāl may be more than one, as jāʾanī Zaydun rākiban ḍāḥikan “Zayd came to me riding, laughing”; and its governor may be dropped because of a context, as rāshidan mahdiyyan “rightly guided, well led!”, said to one who said urīdu al-safara “I want to travel”.

lessons.title: The tamyīz; the mustathnā
body: The seventh manṣūb is the tamyīz, “what removes vagueness from a thing”. The thing may be a noun “mentioned and complete by one of the five things” of lesson 21, as riṭlun zaytan. Or the vagueness may lie in a whole sentence: in ṭāba Zaydun nafsan, “Zayd was good in soul”, the hearer asks what of Zayd was good, and nafsan answers, “that is, ṭābat nafsu Zaydin”. So too in what resembles a sentence, a participle or adjective with its fāʿil: al-ḥawḍu mumtaliʾun māʾan, “the basin is full of water”; ḥasanun wajhan; afḍalu min ʿAmrin ʿilman; and in an iḍāfa: aʿjabanī ṭībuhu aban.
“This tamyīz is a fāʿil in meaning”: nafs is what was good. For that reason it does not come before what it explains, and nafsan ṭāba Zaydun is not said. And “the tamyīz is only indefinite”.

The eighth is the mustathnā, the excepted noun. It is joined (muttaṣil) when it is taken out of a plurality by illā or one of its sisters: jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan, where Zayd was among the people. It is cut off (munqaṭiʿ) when it is mentioned after them without being taken out: jāʾanī al-qawmu illā ḥimāran, where the donkey was never one of the people. It must be in naṣb after illā in complete affirmative speech; when it is put before what it is excepted from, mā jāʾanī illā Zaydan aḥadun; when it is cut off; and after khalā and ʿadā (mostly), mā khalā, mā ʿadā, laysa and lā yakūnu, whose fāʿil lesson 28 explained.

In speech that is not affirmative, with what it is excepted from named, naṣb is allowed but the badal is preferred: mā jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydun, Zaydun replacing al-qawmu. When that is not named, the word after illā takes whatever iʿrāb the governor needs: in mā jāʾanī illā Zaydun, Zaydun is the fāʿil of jāʾa, and illā only limits the negation. After ghayr, siwā and sawāʾ it is in jarr as a muḍāf ilayhi; after ḥāshā mostly, and after ʿadā and khalā less often, as particles of jarr (lesson 4).

Ghayr and illā borrow each other's work. Ghayr is in origin an adjective; used in exception, it takes on itself the iʿrāb the mustathnā would have after illā: jāʾanī al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin. Illā is in origin exception, and is used as an adjective, like ghayr, “when exception is impossible”: law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā (Q 21:22), “that is, ghayru Allāhi”. The commentators show why exception is impossible here: read as an exception, the verse would say that gods without God would ruin the heavens and earth, as if gods with Him would not. So Allāhu is in rafʿ, an adjective of ālihatun.

terms.en: the word that removes vagueness, always indefinite
the joined exception: taken out of what it was part of
the cut-off exception: never part of it
affirmative speech, with no negation, prohibition or question
what the exception is made from

examples.en: a tamyīz of a sentence: ṭābat nafsu Zaydin
a tamyīz after a participle
the cut-off exception
what it is excepted from not named: Zaydun the fāʿil

tasks.prompt: Give the tamyīz and the fāʿil it stands for: ṭāba Zaydun nafsan; al-arḍu mufajjaratun ʿuyūnan.
tasks.arabic: طَابَ زَيْدٌ نَفْسًا — الْأَرْضُ مُفَجَّرَةٌ عُيُونًا
tasks.answer: Nafsan is the tamyīz of the sentence, a fāʿil in meaning: ṭābat nafsu Zaydin. ʿUyūnan is the tamyīz after the passive participle mufajjaratun, a deputy of the fāʿil in meaning: the springs of the earth are burst open.

tasks.prompt: Is the exception joined or cut off, and what is the iʿrāb? jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan; jāʾanī al-qawmu illā ḥimāran.
tasks.answer: Illā Zaydan is joined: Zayd is taken out of the people; in naṣb, after illā in complete affirmative speech. Illā ḥimāran is cut off: the donkey was never among the people; also in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Give the two readings of mā jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zayd… and say which is preferred.
tasks.arabic: مَا جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا — إِلَّا زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: Illā Zaydan, in naṣb as an exception, or illā Zaydun, in rafʿ as a badal of al-qawmu. The speech is negative and what is excepted from is named, so the badal is preferred.

tasks.prompt: Why is Allāhu in rafʿ in Q 21:22, and what does illā mean there?
tasks.arabic: لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا
tasks.answer: Exception is impossible there, so illā is used as an adjective in the sense of ghayr: “gods other than God”. Allāhu takes the iʿrāb of an adjective of ālihatun, which is in rafʿ as the ism of kāna.

quiz.prompt: The tamyīz in ṭāba Zaydun nafsan is, in meaning…
The tamyīz is always…
In jāʾanī al-qawmu illā ḥimāran, the exception is…
quiz.explanation: The donkey was not one of the people.

quiz.prompt: In mā jāʾanī illā Zaydan aḥadun, Zaydan is in naṣb because…
options: it comes before what it is excepted from
quiz.explanation: Put first, the mustathnā must be in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: In mā jāʾanī illā Zaydun, Zaydun is…
quiz.explanation: What is excepted from is not named, so the governor works on it.

quiz.prompt: After ghayr, the excepted noun is in…
quiz.explanation: As a muḍāf ilayhi; ghayr itself takes the iʿrāb of the mustathnā.

quiz.prompt: Illā is used as an adjective when…
quiz.explanation: Law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu (Q 21:22).

text.original: وَالسَّابِعُ التَّمْيِيزُ، وَهُوَ مَا يَرْفَعُ الْإِبْهَامَ عَنْ ذَاتٍ مَذْكُورَةٍ تَامَّةٍ بِأَحَدِ الْأَشْيَاءِ الْخَمْسَةِ، وَقَدْ سَبَقَ، أَوْ مُقَدَّرَةٍ فِي جُمْلَةٍ، نَحْوُ: طَابَ زَيْدٌ نَفْسًا، أَيْ طَابَتْ نَفْسُ زَيْدٍ، أَوْ مَا ضَاهَاهَا، نَحْوُ: الْحَوْضُ مُمْتَلِئٌ مَاءً، وَالْأَرْضُ مُفَجَّرَةٌ عُيُونًا، وَزَيْدٌ طَيِّبٌ أَبًا وَأُبُوَّةً وَدَارًا، وَحَسَنٌ وَجْهًا، وَأَفْضَلُ مِنْ عَمْرٍو عِلْمًا، أَوْ فِي إِضَافَةٍ، نَحْوُ: أَعْجَبَنِي طِيبُهُ أَبًا وَأُبُوَّةً. وَهَذَا التَّمْيِيزُ فَاعِلٌ فِي الْمَعْنَى، فَلِهَذَا لَا يَتَقَدَّمُ عَلَى فَاعِلِهِ، وَالتَّمْيِيزُ لَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا نَكِرَةً.
text.en: The seventh is the tamyīz, which is what removes vagueness from a thing that is mentioned and complete by one of the five things, which has gone before; or from one understood in a sentence, as ṭāba Zaydun nafsan “Zayd was good in soul”, that is, ṭābat nafsu Zaydin “Zayd's soul was good”, or in what resembles it, as al-ḥawḍu mumtaliʾun māʾan “the basin is full of water”, al-arḍu mufajjaratun ʿuyūnan “the earth is burst open with springs”, Zaydun ṭayyibun aban wa-ubuwwatan wa-dāran “Zayd is good as a father, in fatherhood and in house”, ḥasanun wajhan “handsome of face” and afḍalu min ʿAmrin ʿilman “better than ʿAmr in knowledge”; or in an iḍāfa, as aʿjabanī ṭībuhu aban wa-ubuwwatan “his goodness as a father and in fatherhood pleased me”. This tamyīz is a fāʿil in meaning, and for this reason it does not come before its fāʿil; and the tamyīz is only indefinite.

text.original: وَالثَّامِنُ الْمُسْتَثْنَى، وَهُوَ نَوْعَانِ: مُتَّصِلٌ، وَهُوَ الْمُخْرَجُ عَنْ مُتَعَدِّدٍ بِإِلَّا أَوْ إِحْدَى أَخَوَاتِهَا، وَمُنْقَطِعٌ، وَهُوَ الْمَذْكُورُ بَعْدَهَا غَيْرَ مُخْرَجٍ. وَالْمُسْتَثْنَى مَنْصُوبٌ إِذَا كَانَ بَعْدَ إِلَّا غَيْرِ الصِّفَةِ فِي كَلَامٍ مُوجَبٍ تَامٍّ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا، أَوْ مُقَدَّمًا عَلَى الْمُسْتَثْنَى مِنْهُ، نَحْوُ: مَا جَاءَنِي إِلَّا زَيْدًا أَحَدٌ، أَوْ مُنْقَطِعًا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا حِمَارًا، أَوْ كَانَ بَعْدَ خَلَا أَوْ عَدَا فِي الْأَكْثَرِ، أَوْ مَا خَلَا، أَوْ مَا عَدَا، أَوْ لَيْسَ، أَوْ لَا يَكُونُ.
text.en: The eighth is the mustathnā, and it is of two kinds: joined (muttaṣil), which is what is taken out of a plurality by illā or one of its sisters; and cut off (munqaṭiʿ), which is what is mentioned after them without being taken out. The mustathnā is manṣūb when it comes after an illā that is not an adjective, in complete affirmative speech, as jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan “the people came to me except Zayd”; or when it is put before that from which the exception is made, as mā jāʾanī illā Zaydan aḥadun “no one came to me except Zayd”; or when it is cut off, as jāʾanī al-qawmu illā ḥimāran “the people came to me, except a donkey”; or when it comes after khalā or ʿadā, in most usage, or mā khalā, or mā ʿadā, or laysa, or lā yakūnu.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ فِيهِ النَّصْبُ عَلَى الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ، وَيُخْتَارُ الْبَدَلُ فِي كَلَامٍ غَيْرِ مُوجَبٍ وَالْمُسْتَثْنَى مِنْهُ مَذْكُورٌ، نَحْوُ: مَا جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا، أَوْ إِلَّا زَيْدٌ. وَيُعْرَبُ عَلَى حَسَبِ الْعَوَامِلِ إِذَا كَانَ الْمُسْتَثْنَى مِنْهُ غَيْرَ مَذْكُورٍ، نَحْوُ: مَا جَاءَنِي إِلَّا زَيْدٌ. وَمَخْفُوضٌ بَعْدَ غَيْرٍ وَسِوًى وَسَوَاءٍ، وَحَاشَا فِي الْأَكْثَرِ، وَعَدَا وَخَلَا فِي الْأَقَلِّ.
text.en: In it naṣb as an exception is allowed, and the badal is preferred, in speech that is not affirmative when that from which the exception is made is mentioned, as mā jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan “the people did not come to me, except Zayd”, or illā Zaydun. It takes its iʿrāb according to the governors when that from which the exception is made is not mentioned, as mā jāʾanī illā Zaydun “no one came to me but Zayd”. It is in jarr after ghayrin, siwan and sawāʾin “other than”, after ḥāshā in most usage, and after ʿadā and khalā in less usage.

text.original: وَأَصْلُ غَيْرٍ أَنْ يَكُونَ صِفَةً، وَيُحْمَلُ عَلَى إِلَّا فِي الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ، وَيُعْرَبُ كَإِعْرَابِ الْمُسْتَثْنَى بِإِلَّا عَلَى التَّفْصِيلِ. وَأَصْلُ إِلَّا الِاسْتِثْنَاءُ، وَيُحْمَلُ عَلَى غَيْرٍ فِي الصِّفَةِ إِذَا تَعَذَّرَ الِاسْتِثْنَاءُ، فَيَكُونُ مَا بَعْدَهَا صِفَةً لَا مُسْتَثْنًى، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا، أَيْ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ.
text.en: The origin of ghayr is to be an adjective; it is treated like illā in exception, and it takes the iʿrāb of the mustathnā after illā, in the detail [given above]. The origin of illā is exception; it is treated like ghayr as an adjective when exception is impossible, and then what comes after it is an adjective, not a mustathnā, as His saying, Most High: law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā “were there gods in them other than God, they would both have been ruined” [21:22], that is, ghayru Allāhi “other than God”.

lessons.title: The other manṣūb: from the khabar of kāna to the muḍāriʿ
body: The ninth manṣūb is the khabar of kāna and its sisters; “its matter is like the matter of the khabar of the mubtadaʾ”: it may be a sentence, it may be more than one, and so on (lesson 32), only it is in naṣb. Kāna alone of its class may be dropped when the context shows it. The book's example is a well-known one of the grammarians: al-nāsu majziyyūna bi-aʿmālihim, in khayran fa-khayrun wa-in sharran fa-sharrun, “people are requited for their deeds: if [the deed was] good, then good, and if evil, then evil”. Khayran is the khabar of a dropped kāna: in kāna ʿamaluhum khayran.

“In such a case four ways are allowed.” The commentators give them and their rank. Naṣb of the first and rafʿ of the second, as in the book, is the best: the second is the khabar of a dropped mubtadaʾ after the fāʾ, fa-jazāʾuhum khayrun. Rafʿ of the first and naṣb of the second is the weakest. Naṣb of both and rafʿ of both stand between. A student should know the first well and recognise the others.

The tenth is the ism of inna and its sisters. It is like the mubtadaʾ, “but it may not be dropped”: the mubtadaʾ may be dropped with a context (lesson 31), the ism of inna may not. The eleventh is the ism of the lā that denies the genus: lā ghulāma rajulin jālisun ʿindanā. Here the ism is muḍāf, so it is in naṣb in its wording; a single ism is built on fatḥa (lesson 10). This ism may be dropped when the khabar is there: lā ʿalayka, “that is, lā baʾsa”, no harm on you.

The twelfth is the khabar of mā and lā that resemble laysa, like the khabar of the mubtadaʾ: mā Zaydun qāʾiman (lesson 11). The thirteenth is the muḍāriʿ after one of the particles of naṣb: lan yaḍriba. As with the marfūʿ, the list ends with the one verb. The table gathers the thirteen.

terms.en: the khabar of kāna and its sisters, in naṣb
the ism of inna and its sisters: never dropped
the ism of the lā that denies the genus
dropping kāna, allowed with a context, alone of its class

tasks.prompt: Supply what is dropped in in khayran fa-khayrun, and parse khayran and khayrun.
tasks.answer: In kāna ʿamaluhum khayran fa-jazāʾuhum khayrun. Khayran is the khabar of the dropped kāna, in naṣb; its ism, ʿamaluhum, is dropped with it. Khayrun is the khabar of a dropped mubtadaʾ (jazāʾuhum) after the fāʾ, in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Give the four ways of reading in khayran fa-khayrun, in the commentators' order of strength.
tasks.answer: Best: naṣb of the first and rafʿ of the second (khayran fa-khayrun). Between: naṣb of both (khayran fa-khayran) and rafʿ of both (khayrun fa-khayrun). Weakest: rafʿ of the first and naṣb of the second (khayrun fa-khayran).

tasks.prompt: What is dropped in lā ʿalayka, and why may it be dropped?
tasks.answer: The ism of lā that denies the genus: lā baʾsa ʿalayka, “no harm on you”. The book allows the ism of lā to be dropped when its khabar, here ʿalayka, is there.

tasks.prompt: The mubtadaʾ may be dropped with a context. May the ism of inna?
tasks.answer: No. The book says the ism of inna is like the mubtadaʾ, “but it may not be dropped”.

text.original: وَالتَّاسِعُ خَبَرُ بَابِ كَانَ، وَأَمْرُهُ كَأَمْرِ خَبَرِ الْمُبْتَدَإِ، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُ كَانَ دُونَ غَيْرِهِ عِنْدَ قَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: النَّاسُ مَجْزِيُّونَ بِأَعْمَالِهِمْ، إِنْ خَيْرًا فَخَيْرٌ، وَإِنْ شَرًّا فَشَرٌّ، وَيَجُوزُ فِي مِثْلِهِ أَرْبَعَةُ أَوْجُهٍ. وَالْعَاشِرُ اسْمُ بَابِ إِنَّ، وَهُوَ كَالْمُبْتَدَإِ، لَكِنْ لَا يَجُوزُ حَذْفُهُ.
text.en: The ninth is the khabar of the class of kāna, and its matter is like the matter of the khabar of the mubtadaʾ. Kāna, and not the others, may be dropped when there is a context, as al-nāsu majziyyūna bi-aʿmālihim “people are requited for their deeds”: in khayran fa-khayrun “if [the deed was] good, then good”, wa-in sharran fa-sharrun “and if evil, then evil”; in such a case four ways [of reading] are allowed. The tenth is the ism of the class of inna; it is like the mubtadaʾ, but it may not be dropped.

text.original: وَالْحَادِي عَشَرَ اسْمُ لَا الَّتِي لِنَفْيِ الْجِنْسِ، نَحْوُ: لَا غُلَامَ رَجُلٍ جَالِسٌ عِنْدَنَا، وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ عِنْدَ وُجُودِ الْخَبَرِ، نَحْوُ: لَا عَلَيْكَ، أَيْ لَا بَأْسَ. وَالثَّانِي عَشَرَ خَبَرُ مَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَيْنِ بِلَيْسَ، وَهُوَ مِثْلُ خَبَرِ الْمُبْتَدَإِ. وَالثَّالِثَ عَشَرَ الْمُضَارِعُ الدَّاخِلُ عَلَيْهِ إِحْدَى النَّوَاصِبِ، نَحْوُ: لَنْ يَضْرِبَ.
text.en: The eleventh is the ism of the lā that denies the genus, as lā ghulāma rajulin jālisun ʿindanā “no man's servant is sitting with us”; it may be dropped when the khabar is there, as lā ʿalayka “no [harm] upon you”, that is, lā baʾsa “no harm”. The twelfth is the khabar of mā and lā that resemble laysa, and it is like the khabar of the mubtadaʾ. The thirteenth is the muḍāriʿ upon which one of the particles of naṣb comes, as lan yaḍriba “he will not hit”.

lessons.title: The majrūr; dropping in the iḍāfa
body: The majrūr are two: the word in jarr by a particle of jarr, explained in lessons 4–7, and the word in jarr by iḍāfa, the muḍāf ilayhi. Neither the muḍāf ilayhi nor what it governs may come before the muḍāf, with one exception: when the muḍāf is ghayr, what the muḍāf ilayhi governs may come first: anā Zaydan ghayru ḍāribin, “Zayd I am not hitting”. The reason: ghayru ḍāribin has the meaning of lā ḍāribun, and after lā the object of the participle may come first.

Nothing may come between the muḍāf and the muḍāf ilayhi in free speech except “what is heard, and no analogy is drawn from it”; and in verse, under necessity, only an adverb. The two words are held so close that they are almost one word.

The muḍāf may be dropped, and then “its iʿrāb is given to the muḍāf ilayhi, which is the rule”: wa-isʾali al-qaryata (Q 12:82), “ask the town”, that is, the people of the town, so al-qaryata takes the naṣb of the dropped ahla. Rarely the muḍāf ilayhi keeps its jarr: yurīdu al-ākhirati (Q 8:67) “in one reading”, that is, thawāba al-ākhirati; the reading most recite is al-ākhirata.

The muḍāf ilayhi may be dropped and the muḍāf left as it was, without tanwīn, in two cases: when a word made muḍāf to the like of the dropped word is joined to it, bayna dhirāʿay wa-jabhati al-asadi, where dhirāʿay keeps the form it has before al-asadi; and when a muḍāf to the like of it is repeated, yā Tayma Tayma ʿAdiyyin. Otherwise the muḍāf takes tanwīn in place of the dropped word: wa-kullan, “each”, that is, kulla wāḥidin; ḥīnaʾidhin and yawmaʾidhin, where the tanwīn of idh stands for a whole dropped sentence, ḥīna idh kāna kadhā.

The words of limit (ghāya) behave in a third way. They are the six directions, ḥasbu, and lā ghayru and laysa ghayru; when their muḍāf ilayhi is dropped but still meant, they are built on ḍamma. The grammarians' usual example is lillāhi al-amru min qablu wa-min baʿdu (Q 30:4), “the command is God's before and after”, where qablu and baʿdu end in ḍamma after min, because the words they would govern are dropped but intended.

terms.en: the word in jarr by iḍāfa: the muḍāf ilayhi
dropping the muḍāf: its iʿrāb passes to the muḍāf ilayhi
the tanwīn that stands in place of a dropped muḍāf ilayhi
a word of limit, built on ḍamma when its muḍāf ilayhi is dropped but meant

tasks.prompt: Why may Zaydan come before ghayru in anā Zaydan ghayru ḍāribin?
tasks.answer: Zaydan is governed by ḍāribin, the muḍāf ilayhi, and normally what the muḍāf ilayhi governs may not come before the muḍāf. Ghayru ḍāribin has the meaning of lā ḍāribun, and after lā the object may come first; so with ghayr alone it is allowed.

tasks.prompt: Supply the dropped muḍāf and explain the naṣb of al-qaryata in wa-isʾali al-qaryata.
tasks.answer: Wa-isʾal ahla al-qaryati. The muḍāf ahla, the object of isʾal, is dropped, and its naṣb is given to the muḍāf ilayhi, al-qaryata. That is the rule when the muḍāf is dropped.

tasks.prompt: Why has dhirāʿay no nūn and no tanwīn in bayna dhirāʿay wa-jabhati al-asadi?
tasks.answer: It is muḍāf to al-asadi, which is dropped after it because jabhati, joined to it, is muḍāf to the same word. In that case the muḍāf stays as it was before its muḍāf ilayhi: without the nūn of the dual and without tanwīn.

tasks.prompt: What does the tanwīn of ḥīnaʾidhin stand for, and how does it differ from the ḍamma of qablu in min qablu?
tasks.answer: The tanwīn of idh stands in place of a dropped sentence: ḥīna idh kāna kadhā. Qabl is a word of limit: when its muḍāf ilayhi is dropped but meant, it takes no tanwīn but is built on ḍamma.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَجْرُورُ فَاثْنَانِ: الْأَوَّلُ الْمَجْرُورُ بِحَرْفِ الْجَرِّ، وَقَدْ مَرَّ بَيَانُهُ. وَالثَّانِي الْمَجْرُورُ بِالْإِضَافَةِ، وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُهُ وَلَا تَقْدِيمُ مَعْمُولِهِ عَلَى الْمُضَافِ، إِلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمُضَافُ لَفْظَ غَيْرٍ، فَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُ مَعْمُولِ الْمُضَافِ إِلَيْهِ عَلَيْهِ، نَحْوُ: أَنَا زَيْدًا غَيْرُ ضَارِبٍ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ بِمَعْنَى لَا ضَارِبٌ، وَلَا الْفَصْلُ بَيْنَهُمَا بِشَيْءٍ فِي السَّعَةِ غَيْرَ مَا سُمِعَ، وَلَا يُقَاسُ عَلَيْهِ، وَلَا فِي الضَّرُورَةِ إِلَّا بِالظَّرْفِ.
text.en: As for the majrūr, it is two. The first is the one put in jarr by a particle of jarr, which has been explained. The second is the one put in jarr by the iḍāfa. It may not be put before the muḍāf, nor may what it governs, unless the muḍāf is the word ghayr: then what the muḍāf ilayhi governs may be put before it, as anā Zaydan ghayru ḍāribin “Zayd I am not hitting”, because it has the meaning of lā ḍāribun “not hitting”. Nor may anything separate them in free speech, except what is heard, and no analogy is drawn from it; nor in [the necessity of verse], except an adverb.

text.original: وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ الْمُضَافُ فَيُعْطَى إِعْرَابُهُ لِلْمُضَافِ إِلَيْهِ، وَهُوَ الْقِيَاسُ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ، أَيْ أَهْلَ الْقَرْيَةِ، وَقَدْ يَبْقَى مَجْرُورًا عَلَى النُّدُورِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: يُرِيدُ الْآخِرَةِ، بِجَرِّ الْآخِرَةِ عَلَى قِرَاءَةٍ، أَيْ ثَوَابَ الْآخِرَةِ.
text.en: The muḍāf may be dropped, and then its iʿrāb is given to the muḍāf ilayhi, which is the rule, as His saying, Most High: wa-isʾali al-qaryata “and ask the town” [12:82], that is, ahla al-qaryati “the people of the town”. It may stay majrūr, rarely, as His saying, Most High: yurīdu al-ākhirati “He wills the hereafter” [8:67], with al-ākhira in jarr in one reading, that is, thawāba al-ākhirati “the reward of the hereafter”.

text.original: وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ وَيَبْقَى الْمُضَافُ عَلَى حَالِهِ إِنْ عُطِفَ عَلَيْهِ مَا أُضِيفَ إِلَى مِثْلِ الْمَحْذُوفِ، نَحْوُ: بَيْنَ ذِرَاعَيْ وَجَبْهَةِ الْأَسَدِ، أَيْ ذِرَاعَيِ الْأَسَدِ وَجَبْهَةِ الْأَسَدِ، أَوْ كُرِّرَ مُضَافٌ إِلَى مِثْلِ الْمَحْذُوفِ، نَحْوُ: يَا تَيْمَ تَيْمَ عَدِيٍّ.
text.en: The muḍāf ilayhi may be dropped, and the muḍāf stays as it was, if something made muḍāf to the like of what was dropped is joined to it by ʿaṭf, as bayna dhirāʿay wa-jabhati al-asadi “between the two forearms and the brow of the lion”, that is, dhirāʿayi al-asadi wa-jabhati al-asadi “the two forearms of the lion and the brow of the lion”; or if a muḍāf to the like of what was dropped is repeated, as yā Tayma Tayma ʿAdiyyin “O Taym, Taym of ʿAdī!”.

text.original: وَإِلَّا فَيُنَوَّنُ الْمُضَافُ عِوَضًا عَنْهُ إِنْ لَمْ يَكُنِ الْمُضَافُ غَايَةً، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَكُلًّا آتَيْنَاهُ، وَنَحْوُ: حِينَئِذٍ وَيَوْمَئِذٍ، أَيْ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ، وَحِينَ إِذْ كَانَ كَذَا، وَيَوْمَ إِذْ كَانَ كَذَا. وَإِنْ كَانَ غَايَةً، وَهِيَ الْجِهَاتُ السِّتُّ وَحَسْبُ وَلَا غَيْرُ وَلَيْسَ غَيْرُ، مَنْوِيًّا فِيهَا الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ، يُبْنَى عَلَى الضَّمِّ.
text.en: Otherwise the muḍāf takes tanwīn in its place, if the muḍāf is not one of the words of limit (ghāya), as His saying, Most High: wa-kullan ātaynāhu “and to each We gave” [21:79], and as ḥīnaʾidhin “at that time” and yawmaʾidhin “on that day”, that is, kulla wāḥidin “each one”, and ḥīna idh kāna kadhā “at the time when such was” and yawma idh kāna kadhā “on the day when such was”. If it is a word of limit, and these are the six directions, ḥasbu “enough”, lā ghayru and laysa ghayru “no other”, with the muḍāf ilayhi intended in them, it is built on the ḍamma.

lessons.title: The majzūm; when the response takes the fāʾ
body: The majzūm is only one: the muḍāriʿ upon which one of the particles of jazm of lesson 12 has come. When that particle is a word of requital (kalim al-mujāzāt), as in or man, it calls for two sentences, the condition and the response. If both are muḍāriʿ, or the first is a muḍāriʿ and the second has no fāʾ, “the jazm in the muḍāriʿ is necessary”: in taḍrib aḍrib. If the first is past and the second muḍāriʿ, the second may be in jazm or in rafʿ: in ḍarabta aḍrib, or aḍribu.

The response may not take the fāʾ when it is a conjugated past verb with the meaning of the muḍāriʿ, in ḍarabta ḍarabtu, “if you hit, I will hit”, or a muḍāriʿ negated by lam or lammā, in ḍarabta lam aḍrib. These are responses the particle can still work on: it gives the past a future meaning, and lam aḍrib stays a muḍāriʿ in jazm.

The response must take the fāʾ when it is a nominal sentence, in ḍarabta fa-anta maḍrūbun; a past verb that is not conjugated, fa-laysa mina Allāhi fī shayʾin (Q 3:28), fa-ʿasā an takrahū shayʾan (Q 4:19); a past kept in its past meaning, which needs qad, visible or understood, fa-ṣadaqat (Q 12:26), that is, fa-qad ṣadaqat; a muḍāriʿ with the sīn, sawfa, lan or mā, fa-sa-turḍiʿu lahu ukhrā (Q 65:6), fa-lan yuqbala minhu (Q 3:85); or a sentence that makes a request: a command, fa-iḍribhu; a prohibition, fa-lā taḍribhu; a question, fa-hal taḍribuhu; a prayer, fa-yarḥamuka Allāhu.

The grammarians give one reason for the whole list: the fāʾ is needed when the response could not itself stand as a condition after in. A nominal sentence, laysa, a past with qad, a verb with sa- or lan, a command or a question: in cannot work on any of them, so the fāʾ binds the response to the condition. The last example teaches this well: yarḥamuka is a muḍāriʿ in rafʿ, but it is a prayer, so it takes the fāʾ.

Between these lie the plain muḍāriʿ, affirmative or negated by lā. Here both ways are open: without the fāʾ it is in jazm, in taḍrib aḍrib, in taḍrib lā aḍrib; with the fāʾ it is in rafʿ, fa-aḍribu, fa-lā aḍribu. The commentators explain the rafʿ: after the fāʾ a mubtadaʾ is understood, fa-anā aḍribu, and the whole sentence is the response, in jazm in its place (lesson 26). This is the response with the fāʾ that lesson 12 left for here.

the words of requital, which call for a condition and a response
the condition and the response
a sentence that makes a request: command, prohibition, question, prayer

tasks.prompt: Must, may or may not the response take the fāʾ? in ḍarabta ḍarabtu; in ḍarabta fa-anta maḍrūbun; in taḍrib aḍrib.
tasks.answer: In ḍarabta ḍarabtu: may not, the response is a conjugated past with a future meaning. In ḍarabta fa-anta maḍrūbun: must, the response is a nominal sentence. In taḍrib aḍrib: may, the response is a plain muḍāriʿ; without the fāʾ it is in jazm (aḍrib), with it in rafʿ (fa-aḍribu).

tasks.prompt: Why does fa-ṣadaqat in Q 12:26 take the fāʾ, though ṣadaqat is a conjugated past verb?
tasks.arabic: وَإِنْ كَانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِنْ قُبُلٍ فَصَدَقَتْ
tasks.answer: Here the past keeps its past meaning: “then she has told the truth”. Such a past needs qad, visible or understood (fa-qad ṣadaqat), and a response with qad must take the fāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Parse fa-aḍribu in in taḍrib fa-aḍribu, as the commentators do.
tasks.answer: The fāʾ is the fāʾ of the response. After it a mubtadaʾ is understood, anā; aḍribu, a muḍāriʿ in rafʿ, with its hidden fāʿil, is its khabar. The sentence fa-anā aḍribu is the response, in jazm in its place.

tasks.prompt: Why does yarḥamuka Allāhu, a muḍāriʿ, take the fāʾ in in tukrimnī fa-yarḥamuka Allāhu?
tasks.answer: Because it is a prayer, a sentence that makes a request (inshāʾiyya), not a statement; the response that is a prayer must take the fāʾ, whatever its form.

quiz.prompt: How many majzūm does the book count?
options: one: the muḍāriʿ after a particle of jazm
quiz.explanation: Only the verb is ever in jazm.

quiz.prompt: If the condition is past and the response a muḍāriʿ, the response is…
Which response may NOT take the fāʾ?
quiz.explanation: A muḍāriʿ negated by lam or lammā.

quiz.prompt: Fa-laysa mina Allāhi fī shayʾin takes the fāʾ because laysa is…
options: a past verb that is not conjugated
quiz.explanation: Laysa and ʿasā do not conjugate.

quiz.prompt: In fa-sa-turḍiʿu lahu ukhrā (Q 65:6) the fāʾ is required because of…
quiz.explanation: A muḍāriʿ with the sīn, sawfa, lan or mā.

quiz.prompt: Fa-hal taḍribuhu is…
quiz.explanation: A sentence that makes a request.

quiz.prompt: With the fāʾ, the plain muḍāriʿ in the response is…

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَجْزُومُ فَفِعْلٌ مُضَارِعٌ دَخَلَهُ إِحْدَى الْجَوَازِمِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ سَابِقًا. فَإِنْ كَانَتْ كَلِمَ الْمُجَازَاةِ تَقْتَضِي شَرْطًا وَجَزَاءً؛ فَإِنْ كَانَا مُضَارِعَيْنِ، أَوِ الْأَوَّلُ مُضَارِعًا، بِغَيْرِ فَاءٍ، فَالْجَزْمُ فِي الْمُضَارِعِ وَاجِبٌ، وَإِنْ كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ مَاضِيًا وَالثَّانِي مُضَارِعًا جَازَ الْجَزْمُ وَالرَّفْعُ فِي الثَّانِي.
text.en: As for the majzūm, it is a muḍāriʿ verb upon which one of the particles of jazm mentioned before has come. If it is one of the words of requital, it calls for a condition and a response. If both are muḍāriʿ, or the first is muḍāriʿ, without a fāʾ, the jazm in the muḍāriʿ is necessary; and if the first is past and the second muḍāriʿ, jazm and rafʿ are both allowed in the second.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ الْجَزَاءُ مَاضِيًا مُتَصَرِّفًا بِمَعْنَى الْمُضَارِعِ، أَوْ مُضَارِعًا مَنْفِيًّا بِلَمْ أَوْ لَمَّا، فَلَا يَجُوزُ دُخُولُ الْفَاءِ فِيهِ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ ضَرَبْتَ ضَرَبْتُ، أَوْ لَمْ أَضْرِبْ. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْجَزَاءُ جُمْلَةً اسْمِيَّةً، أَوْ مَاضِيَةً غَيْرَ مُتَصَرِّفَةٍ أَوْ بِمَعْنَاهُ، فَلَا بُدَّ حِينَئِذٍ مِنْ قَدْ ظَاهِرَةً أَوْ مُقَدَّرَةً، أَوْ مُضَارِعًا مُقْتَرِنًا بِالسِّينِ أَوْ سَوْفَ أَوْ لَنْ أَوْ مَا، أَوْ فِعْلِيَّةً إِنْشَائِيَّةً كَالْأَمْرِيَّةِ وَالنَّهْيِيَّةِ وَالِاسْتِفْهَامِيَّةِ وَالدُّعَائِيَّةِ، يَجِبُ دُخُولُ الْفَاءِ فِيهِ.
text.en: If the response is a fully conjugated past verb with the meaning of the muḍāriʿ, or a muḍāriʿ negated by lam or lammā, the fāʾ may not come into it, as in ḍarabta ḍarabtu “if you hit, I hit” or lam aḍrib “I did not hit”. If the response is a nominal sentence; or a past [verbal sentence] that is not conjugated, or [conjugated but] with its [past] meaning, in which case qad must be there, visible or understood; or a muḍāriʿ joined with the sīn, sawfa, lan or mā; or a verbal sentence that makes [a request] (inshāʾiyya), as one of command, of prohibition, of question or of prayer: then the fāʾ must come into it.

text.original: نَحْوُ: إِنْ ضَرَبْتَ فَأَنْتَ مَضْرُوبٌ، وَنَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَمَنْ يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ فَلَيْسَ مِنَ اللَّهِ فِي شَيْءٍ، فَإِنْ كَرِهْتُمُوهُنَّ فَعَسَى أَنْ تَكْرَهُوا شَيْئًا، وَإِنْ كَانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِنْ قُبُلٍ فَصَدَقَتْ، وَإِنْ تَعَاسَرْتُمْ فَسَتُرْضِعُ لَهُ أُخْرَى، وَمَنْ يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ الْإِسْلَامِ دِينًا فَلَنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنْهُ، وَنَحْوُ: إِنْ ضَرَبَكَ زَيْدٌ فَاضْرِبْهُ، أَوْ فَلَا تَضْرِبْهُ، أَوْ فَهَلْ تَضْرِبُهُ، وَإِنْ تُكْرِمْنِي فَيَرْحَمُكَ اللَّهُ.
text.en: As in ḍarabta fa-anta maḍrūbun “if you hit, you are hit”; and as His saying, Most High: wa-man yafʿal dhālika fa-laysa mina Allāhi fī shayʾin “and whoever does that has nothing to do with God” [3:28], fa-in karihtumūhunna fa-ʿasā an takrahū shayʾan “if you dislike them, it may be that you dislike a thing” [4:19], wa-in kāna qamīṣuhu qudda min qubulin fa-ṣadaqat “if his shirt was torn from the front, then she has told the truth” [12:26], wa-in taʿāsartum fa-sa-turḍiʿu lahu ukhrā “and if you make difficulties for one another, another woman will suckle [the child] for him” [65:6] and wa-man yabtaghi ghayra al-islāmi dīnan fa-lan yuqbala minhu “and whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted from him” [3:85]; and as in ḍarabaka Zaydun fa-iḍribhu “if Zayd hits you, hit him”, or fa-lā taḍribhu “do not hit him”, or fa-hal taḍribuhu “will you hit him?”, and in tukrimnī fa-yarḥamuka Allāhu “if you honour me, God have mercy on you!”.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ مُضَارِعًا بِغَيْرِهَا، مُثْبَتًا أَوْ مَنْفِيًّا بِلَا، فَيَجُوزُ الْفَاءُ مَعَ الرَّفْعِ، وَحَذْفُهُ مَعَ الْجَزْمِ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ تَضْرِبْ أَضْرِبْ، أَوْ فَأَضْرِبُ، أَوْ لَا أَضْرِبْ، أَوْ فَلَا أَضْرِبُ.
text.en: If it is a muḍāriʿ without these, affirmative or negated by lā, the fāʾ is allowed with rafʿ, and leaving it out with jazm, as in taḍrib aḍrib “if you hit, I hit”, or fa-aḍribu, or lā aḍrib “I do not hit”, or fa-lā aḍribu.

lessons.title: The followers; the adjective; the definite and the pronouns
body: The governed “by following” are five: the adjective, ʿaṭf by particles, emphasis, the badal and the explanatory ʿaṭf. Three rules hold for them all. None comes before what it follows; “their governor is the governor of what they follow”; and their iʿrāb is its iʿrāb. So in jāʾanī al-rajulu al-ʿālimu, al-ʿālimu is in rafʿ not because it is a fāʿil but because it follows the fāʿil, and jāʾa governs both.

The first is the adjective (ṣifa), “a follower that indicates a meaning in what it follows”: learning in the man of al-rajulu al-ʿālimu. There may be more than one: jāʾanī al-rajulu al-ʿālimu al-fāḍilu. An indefinite may be qualified by a sentence that states something, and then the sentence must hold a pronoun of the qualified, jāʾanī rajulun qāma abūhu (lesson 26), though it may be dropped when the context shows it.

An adjective may describe the state of the qualified itself, or the state of something connected with it. The first follows its noun in everything: definiteness, number and gender, besides the iʿrāb. Jāʾanī rajulun ʿālimun; jāʾatnī imraʾatun ṣāliḥatun. The second follows it only “in the first two”, definiteness and indefiniteness: jāʾanī rijālun rākibun ghulāmuhum, “men came to me whose servant was riding”. Rākibun is indefinite like rijālun and in rafʿ like it, but singular, because what rides is the servant. It behaves like a verb with a visible fāʿil (lesson 29): rākibun ghulāmuhum is like rakiba ghulāmuhum.

Since adjectives agree in definiteness, Birgivī stops to define it. “The definite is what is laid down for a particular thing, and the indefinite for a thing that is not particular.” The definite is of six kinds, and the first is the pronouns, in four divisions. The first, the marfūʿ joined to the verb, the tāʾ, alif, wāw and the rest, was taught in lessons 28 and 29.

The second division is the marfūʿ separate pronoun, which stands as a word by itself: huwa, hiya, humā, hum, hunna for the absent; anta, anti, antumā, antum, antunna for the one addressed; anā and naḥnu for the speaker. Each is in rafʿ in its place, as a mubtadaʾ, huwa qāʾimun, or as an emphasis of a joined pronoun, ḍarabta anta (lesson 42).

terms.en: the followers: five words governed by following
the adjective: a follower that shows a meaning in what it follows
the definite and the indefinite: laid down for a particular thing, or not
the separate pronoun, a word by itself

a sentence qualifying an indefinite, with its pronoun

tasks.prompt: What governs al-ʿālimu in jāʾanī al-rajulu al-ʿālimu, and why is it in rafʿ?
tasks.answer: Jāʾa governs it, the governor of what it follows. It is in rafʿ because it follows al-rajulu, the fāʿil, in its iʿrāb; it is not a second fāʿil.

tasks.prompt: Explain each agreement in jāʾanī rijālun rākibun ghulāmuhum.
tasks.answer: Rākibun describes the servant, something connected with the men, not the men themselves. So it follows rijālun only in iʿrāb (rafʿ) and indefiniteness. It is singular, like a verb whose fāʿil (ghulāmuhum) is visible, and masculine because the servant is.

tasks.prompt: Give the separate marfūʿ pronouns for the one addressed, in order.
tasks.answer: Anta (a man), anti (a woman), antumā (two), antum (men), antunna (women).

tasks.prompt: Define the definite and the indefinite as the book does, with an example of each.
tasks.answer: The definite is what is laid down for a particular thing, as Zayd or al-rajul in jāʾanī rajulun fa-akramtu al-rajula. The indefinite is what is laid down for a thing that is not particular, as rajulun, “a man”.

quiz.prompt: How many followers does the book count?
quiz.explanation: Adjective, ʿaṭf by particles, emphasis, badal, explanatory ʿaṭf.

quiz.prompt: The governor of a follower is…
options: the governor of what it follows
quiz.explanation: And its iʿrāb is like that of what it follows.

quiz.prompt: May a follower come before what it follows?
quiz.explanation: “None of them may be put before what it follows.”

quiz.prompt: A sentence qualifying an indefinite must have…
An adjective of the noun's own state agrees with it in…
In jāʾanī rijālun rākibun ghulāmuhum, rākibun is singular because…
options: it describes the servant, like a verb with a visible fāʿil
the adjective never takes the plural
quiz.explanation: An adjective of a connected thing's state follows only in definiteness.

quiz.prompt: Which is a marfūʿ separate pronoun?

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَعْمُولُ بِالتَّبَعِيَّةِ فَخَمْسَةٌ، وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُ شَيْءٍ مِنْهَا عَلَى مَتْبُوعِهَا، وَعَامِلُهَا عَامِلُ مَتْبُوعِهَا، وَإِعْرَابُهَا كَإِعْرَابِهِ. الْأَوَّلُ الصِّفَةُ، وَهِيَ تَابِعٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي مَتْبُوعِهِ مُطْلَقًا، وَيَجُوزُ تَعَدُّدُهَا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي الرَّجُلُ الْعَالِمُ الْفَاضِلُ. وَيَجُوزُ وَصْفُ النَّكِرَةِ بِالْجُمْلَةِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ، وَيَلْزَمُ فِيهَا الضَّمِيرُ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ قَامَ أَبُوهُ، وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ لِقَرِينَةٍ.
text.en: As for what is governed by following, it is five. None of them may be put before what it follows; their governor is the governor of what they follow, and their iʿrāb is like its iʿrāb. The first is the adjective (ṣifa), which is a follower that indicates a meaning in what it follows, without restriction. It may be more than one, as jāʾanī al-rajulu al-ʿālimu al-fāḍilu “the learned, excellent man came to me”. An indefinite may be qualified by a sentence that states [something], and then a pronoun is necessary in it, as jāʾanī rajulun qāma abūhu “a man whose father stood came to me”; it may be dropped because of a context.

text.original: وَيُوصَفُ بِحَالِ الْمَوْصُوفِ وَبِحَالِ مُتَعَلَّقِهِ؛ فَالْأَوَّلُ يَتْبَعُهُ فِي التَّعْرِيفِ وَالتَّنْكِيرِ وَالْإِفْرَادِ وَالتَّثْنِيَةِ وَالْجَمْعِ وَالتَّذْكِيرِ وَالتَّأْنِيثِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ عَالِمٌ، وَجَاءَتْنِي امْرَأَةٌ صَالِحَةٌ، وَالثَّانِي فِي الْأَوَّلَيْنِ فَقَطْ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رِجَالٌ رَاكِبٌ غُلَامُهُمْ.
text.en: [A noun] is qualified by a state of the qualified [itself], or by a state of something connected with it. The first follows it in definiteness and indefiniteness, singular, dual and plural, masculine and feminine, as jāʾanī rajulun ʿālimun “a learned man came to me” and jāʾatnī imraʾatun ṣāliḥatun “a righteous woman came to me”; and the second only in the first two, as jāʾanī rijālun rākibun ghulāmuhum “men came to me whose servant was riding”.

text.original: وَالْمَعْرِفَةُ مَا وُضِعَ لِشَيْءٍ بِعَيْنِهِ، وَالنَّكِرَةُ مَا وُضِعَ لِشَيْءٍ لَا بِعَيْنِهِ. وَالْمَعْرِفَةُ سِتَّةُ أَنْوَاعٍ: الْأَوَّلُ الْمُضْمَرَاتُ، وَهِيَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَقْسَامٍ: الْأَوَّلُ مَرْفُوعٌ مُتَّصِلٌ، وَقَدْ سَبَقَ؛ وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّانِي مَرْفُوعٌ مُنْفَصِلٌ، وَهُوَ: هُوَ، هِيَ، هُمَا، هُمْ، هُنَّ، أَنْتَ، أَنْتِ، أَنْتُمَا، أَنْتُمْ، أَنْتُنَّ، أَنَا، نَحْنُ.
text.en: The definite is what is laid down for a particular thing, and the indefinite is what is laid down for a thing that is not particular. The definite is of six kinds. The first is the pronouns, and they are of four divisions. The first is marfūʿ and joined, which has gone before. The second division is marfūʿ and separate, and it is: huwa, hiya, humā, hum, hunna, anta, anti, antumā, antum, antunna, anā and naḥnu (he, she, they two, they, they [f.], you, you [f.], you two, you [pl.], you [f. pl.], I, we).

lessons.title: The kinds of definite: pronouns, names, demonstratives, relatives
body: The third division of pronouns is one set of letters shared by the manṣūb and the majrūr, both joined: ḍarabahu, ḍarabahā … ḍarabaka … ḍarabanī, ḍarabanā, and lahu, lahā, and so on. In ḍarabanī the pronoun is the yāʾ; the nūn before it only protects the verb's last vowel. The fourth is the manṣūb separate pronoun: iyyāhu, iyyāhā … iyyāka … iyyāya, iyyānā, used where a joined pronoun cannot stand, as when the object comes first: iyyāka naʿbudu (Q 1:5).

The second kind of definite is the proper name (ʿalam): of an individual, as Zayd, or of a genus, as Usāma, a name for the lion, and subḥān, a name for glorification. The name of a genus is definite in its wording, so Usāmatu takes no tanwīn and no lām, though it names any lion. The third is the demonstratives: dhā, its dual dhāni and dhayni; for the feminine tā, dhī, tī, tih, dhih, tihī, dhihī, and tāni and tayni; for the plural of both ulāʾi, with the long or the short alif.

The hā of drawing attention may come at their beginning, hādhā; the kāf of address at their end, dhāka, dhākumā, dhākum, dhākunna; or both, hādhāka. The kāf changes with the one spoken to, not with the thing pointed at: dhākum is one thing shown to many. For what is far one says tilka, ulālika, and dhānnika and tānnika with a doubled nūn. Thamma, hāhunā, hunā and hunālika point to places only.

The fourth kind is the relative noun (mawṣūl). It must have a ṣila, “a sentence that states something and is known to the hearer, with a pronoun in it that refers back to the relative”, though that pronoun may be dropped with a context. The relatives are alladhī; alladhāni, alladhayni; alladhīna, which keeps its form in all three cases; allatī, allatāni, allatayni, and six plurals, allawātī, allāʾī, allāyi, allātī, allāti, allawāʾī; dhā after the mā of question, as mādhā; man, mā, ayyun and ayyatun; and the alif and lām on the participles (lesson 24).

The fifth kind is the noun defined by the lām: for what is already known, jāʾanī rajulun fa-akramtu al-rajula, “a man came to me and I honoured the man”, the one just mentioned; or for the genus, al-rajulu khayrun mina al-marʾati, speaking of men as a kind. With it goes the noun defined by the particle of calling when one person is meant: yā rajulu. The sixth kind is a noun made muḍāf to one of these five “by an iḍāfa of meaning”: ghulāmu Zaydin. The iḍāfa of wording does not define (lesson 20).

terms.en: the proper name: of an individual or of a genus
the demonstrative, with the hā of attention and the kāf of address
the relative noun and the sentence that completes it
the kāf of address, agreeing with the one spoken to
the lām of the known and the lām of the genus

examples.arabic: إِيَّاهُ، إِيَّاهَا، إِيَّاهُمَا، إِيَّاهُمْ، إِيَّاهُنَّ، إِيَّاكَ
examples.en: the manṣūb separate pronouns
the kāf of address following the one spoken to
the lām of the known
the lām of the genus
definite by an iḍāfa of meaning

tasks.prompt: Name the division of each pronoun: iyyāka; the kāf of ḍarabaka; the hāʾ of lahu; anta.
tasks.answer: Iyyāka: manṣūb separate. The kāf of ḍarabaka: manṣūb joined. The hāʾ of lahu: majrūr joined (the same set of letters as the manṣūb joined). Anta: marfūʿ separate.

tasks.prompt: Someone points to one book while speaking to a group of men, and adds the kāf of address. What does he say, and what does each part agree with?
tasks.answer: Dhākum: dhā agrees with the one thing pointed at (singular masculine); the kāf with its -um agrees with the men spoken to (masculine plural).

tasks.prompt: In jāʾanī alladhī ḍaraba Zaydan, find the relative, its ṣila and the pronoun that refers back.
tasks.answer: Alladhī is the relative, the fāʿil of jāʾa. Ḍaraba Zaydan is its ṣila, a sentence that states something. The pronoun that refers back is the fāʿil hidden in ḍaraba.

tasks.prompt: Is the lām for the known or for the genus? jāʾanī rajulun fa-akramtu al-rajula; al-rajulu khayrun mina al-marʾati.
tasks.answer: In the first it is for the known: al-rajula is the man already mentioned. In the second it is for the genus: men as a kind are spoken of.

quiz.prompt: The manṣūb joined and the majrūr joined pronouns are…
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabahu and lahu use the same hāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Iyyāka is a pronoun that is…
Usāma, a name for the lion, is…
In dhākum, the -kum agrees with…
quiz.explanation: The kāf of address follows the one addressed.

quiz.prompt: Which is for what is far?
The ṣila of a relative must be…
options: a statement known to the hearer, with a pronoun back

quiz.prompt: Ghulāmu Zaydin is definite because it is…
options: muḍāf to a definite by an iḍāfa of meaning

text.original: وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّالِثُ مُشْتَرَكٌ بَيْنَ مَنْصُوبٍ مُتَّصِلٍ وَمَجْرُورٍ مُتَّصِلٍ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَهُ، ضَرَبَهَا، ضَرَبَهُمَا، ضَرَبَهُمْ، ضَرَبَهُنَّ، ضَرَبَكَ، ضَرَبَكِ، ضَرَبَكُمَا، ضَرَبَكُمْ، ضَرَبَكُنَّ، ضَرَبَنِي، ضَرَبَنَا، وَنَحْوُ: لَهُ، إِلَى آخِرِهِ. وَالْقِسْمُ الرَّابِعُ مَنْصُوبٌ مُنْفَصِلٌ، وَهُوَ: إِيَّاهُ، إِيَّاهَا، إِيَّاهُمَا، إِيَّاهُمْ، إِيَّاهُنَّ، إِيَّاكَ، إِيَّاكِ، إِيَّاكُمَا، إِيَّاكُمْ، إِيَّاكُنَّ، إِيَّايَ، إِيَّانَا.
text.en: The third division is shared between the manṣūb joined and the majrūr joined, as ḍarabahu, ḍarabahā, ḍarabahumā, ḍarabahum, ḍarabahunna, ḍarabaka, ḍarabaki, ḍarabakumā, ḍarabakum, ḍarabakunna, ḍarabanī and ḍarabanā (he hit him, her, the two of them, them, them [f.], you, you [f.], you two, you [pl.], you [f. pl.], me, us), and as lahu “to him”, to the end. The fourth division is manṣūb and separate, and it is: iyyāhu, iyyāhā, iyyāhumā, iyyāhum, iyyāhunna, iyyāka, iyyāki, iyyākumā, iyyākum, iyyākunna, iyyāya and iyyānā (him, her, … me, us).

text.original: وَالنَّوْعُ الثَّانِي الْعَلَمُ، وَهُوَ قِسْمَانِ: عَلَمُ شَخْصٍ، نَحْوُ زَيْدٍ، وَعَلَمُ جِنْسٍ، نَحْوُ أُسَامَةَ وَسُبْحَانَ. وَالنَّوْعُ الثَّالِثُ أَسْمَاءُ الْإِشَارَةِ، وَهِيَ ذَا لِلْمُذَكَّرِ، وَلِمُثَنَّاهُ ذَانِ وَذَيْنِ، وَلِلْمُؤَنَّثِ تَا وَذِي وَتِي وَتِهْ وَذِهْ وَتِهِي وَذِهِي، وَلِمُثَنَّاهُ تَانِ وَتَيْنِ، وَلِجَمْعِهِمَا أُولَاءِ مَدًّا وَقَصْرًا.
text.en: The second kind is the proper name (ʿalam), and it is of two divisions: the name of an individual, as Zaydin “Zayd”, and the name of a genus, as Usāmata “Usāma [the lion]” and subḥāna “glory”. The third kind is the demonstratives: dhā for the masculine, and for its dual dhāni and dhayni; for the feminine tā, dhī, tī, tih, dhih, tihī and dhihī, and for its dual tāni and tayni; and for the plural of both ulāʾi, with the long and the short alif.

text.original: وَيَلْحَقُ أَوَائِلَهَا حَرْفُ التَّنْبِيهِ، نَحْوُ: هَذَا، وَيَتَّصِلُ بِأَوَاخِرِهَا كَافُ الْخِطَابِ، فَيُقَالُ: ذَاكَ، ذَاكُمَا، ذَاكُمْ، ذَاكُنَّ، وَكَذَا الْبَوَاقِي، وَيُجْمَعُ بَيْنَهُمَا، نَحْوُ: هَذَاكَ. وَيُقَالُ: تِلْكَ، وَأُولَالِكَ، وَذَانِّكَ وَتَانِّكَ مُشَدَّدَتَيْنِ، لِلْبَعِيدِ. وَأَمَّا ثَمَّةَ وَهَهُنَا وَهُنَا وَهُنَالِكَ فَلِلْمَكَانِ خَاصَّةً.
text.en: The particle of drawing attention is put at their beginnings, as hādhā “this”, and the kāf of address is joined to their ends, so one says dhāka, dhākumā, dhākum and dhākunna “that”, and so the rest; and the two may be put together, as hādhāka. One says tilka, ulālika, and dhānnika and tānnika, both with a doubled [nūn], for what is far. As for thammata “there”, hāhunā and hunā “here” and hunālika “there”, they are for place only.

text.original: وَالنَّوْعُ الرَّابِعُ الْمَوْصُولُ، وَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ صِلَةٍ، جُمْلَةٍ خَبَرِيَّةٍ مَعْلُومَةٍ لِلسَّامِعِ، فِيهَا ضَمِيرٌ عَائِدٌ إِلَى الْمَوْصُولِ، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُهُ عِنْدَ قَرِينَةٍ. وَهُوَ الَّذِي لِلْوَاحِدِ، وَلِمُثَنَّاهُ اللَّذَانِ وَاللَّذَيْنِ، وَلِجَمْعِهِ الَّذِينَ فِي الْأَحْوَالِ الثَّلَاثِ، وَالَّتِي لِلْوَاحِدَةِ، وَلِمُثَنَّاهَا اللَّتَانِ وَاللَّتَيْنِ، وَلِجَمْعِهَا اللَّوَاتِي وَاللَّائِي وَاللَّايِ وَاللَّاتِي وَاللَّاتِ وَاللَّوَائِي، وَذَا بَعْدَ مَا لِلِاسْتِفْهَامِ، وَمَنْ وَمَا وَأَيٌّ وَأَيَّةٌ، وَالْأَلِفُ وَاللَّامُ فِي اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ بِمَعْنَى الَّذِي أَوِ الَّتِي.
text.en: The fourth kind is the relative noun (mawṣūl). It must have a ṣila, a sentence that states [something] and is known to the hearer, with a pronoun in it that refers back to the relative; [the pronoun] may be dropped when there is a context. It is alladhī for the singular, for its dual alladhāni and alladhayni, and for its plural alladhīna in all three cases; allatī for the singular feminine, for its dual allatāni and allatayni, and for its plural allawātī, allāʾī, allāyi, allātī, allāti and allawāʾī; dhā after the mā of question; man, mā, ayyun and ayyatun; and the alif and lām in the active and passive participle, in the sense of alladhī or allatī.

text.original: وَالنَّوْعُ الْخَامِسُ الْمُعَرَّفُ بِاللَّامِ، سَوَاءٌ كَانَ لِلْعَهْدِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ فَأَكْرَمْتُ الرَّجُلَ، أَوْ لِلْجِنْسِ، نَحْوُ: الرَّجُلُ خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْمَرْأَةِ، وَبِحَرْفِ النِّدَاءِ إِذَا قُصِدَ بِهِ مُعَيَّنٌ، نَحْوُ: يَا رَجُلُ. وَالنَّوْعُ السَّادِسُ الْمُضَافُ إِلَى أَحَدِ هَذِهِ الْخَمْسَةِ إِضَافَةً مَعْنَوِيَّةً، نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ.
text.en: The fifth kind is what is defined by the lām, whether it is for what is known [from before], as jāʾanī rajulun fa-akramtu al-rajula “a man came to me, and I honoured the man”, or for the genus, as al-rajulu khayrun mina al-marʾati “man is better than woman”; and what is defined by the particle of calling, when a particular one is meant by it, as yā rajulu “O man!”. The sixth kind is what is made muḍāf to one of these five by an iḍāfa of meaning, as ghulāmu Zaydin “Zayd's servant”.

lessons.title: ʿAṭf by particles; emphasis
body: The second follower is ʿaṭf by particles: a follower with one of ten particles between it and what it follows: wa, fa, thumma, ḥattā, aw, immā, am, lā, bal and lākin. The book gives no meanings here; the commentators teach at least the first three: the wāw joins without order, the fāʾ with order and no delay, thumma with order and a delay.

Two pronouns need care. To join a noun to a marfūʿ joined pronoun, the pronoun “must be emphasized by a separate one” first: ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun, “I and Zayd hit”, not ḍarabtu wa-Zaydun. If another word separates them the separate pronoun may be left out: ḍarabtu al-yawma wa-Zaydun. To join a noun to a majrūr pronoun, the word that put it in jarr is repeated: marartu bika wa-bi-Zaydin; al-mālu baynī wa-baynaka. In the second example the repeated word is bayna, a muḍāf, not a particle: the rule is about whatever gives the jarr.

“What is joined is treated like what it is joined to, in what is necessary for it and what is impossible for it”: if the first must hold a pronoun of the mubtadaʾ, so must the second. One particle may join two words to the two governed words of one governor, by agreement: ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran wa-Bakrun Khālidan, Bakrun to Zaydun and Khālidan to ʿAmran, both under ḍaraba. To the governed words of two different governors it is not allowed, except, “in one view”, when the particle of jarr comes first: fī al-dāri Zaydun wa-l-ḥujrati ʿAmrun, where al-ḥujrati is joined to what fī governs and ʿAmrun to the mubtadaʾ.

The third follower is emphasis (taʾkīd), of two kinds. Verbal emphasis is repeating the first word, or, for a joined pronoun, a word of the same meaning; “it runs through all words”: a noun, jāʾanī Zaydun Zaydun; a pronoun, ḍarabta anta; a verb, ḍaraba ḍaraba Zaydun; a whole sentence, Zaydun qāʾimun Zaydun qāʾimun.

Emphasis of meaning is “reserved for definites”, with fixed words: nafsuhu, ʿaynuhu, kilāhumā, kiltāhumā, kulluhu, and ajmaʿu with aktaʿu, abtaʿu, abṣaʿu, which never come before ajmaʿ or without it in eloquent speech. A marfūʿ joined pronoun emphasized by nafs or ʿayn is first emphasized by a separate pronoun: Zaydun ḍaraba huwa nafsuhu. The commentators give the reason: without huwa, nafsuhu would be read as the fāʿil, “his self hit”.

terms.en: ʿaṭf by one of the ten particles
the joined word and what it is joined to
verbal emphasis: repeating the word
emphasis of meaning: nafs, ʿayn, kilā, kull, ajmaʿ

examples.en: joined to a marfūʿ pronoun: the separate pronoun first
joined to a majrūr pronoun: the bāʾ repeated
two words joined to the two governed words of one governor
two governors: allowed in one view, the jārr first
nafs after a joined pronoun: the separate pronoun first

tasks.prompt: Correct each and give the rule: ḍarabtu wa-Zaydun; marartu bika wa-Zaydin.
tasks.answer: Ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun: a noun joined to a marfūʿ joined pronoun needs the separate pronoun first (unless another word separates them, as ḍarabtu al-yawma wa-Zaydun). Marartu bika wa-bi-Zaydin: with a majrūr pronoun the word that gives the jarr is repeated.

tasks.prompt: In ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran wa-Bakrun Khālidan, what is joined to what, and why is it allowed?
tasks.answer: Bakrun is joined to Zaydun (the fāʿil) and Khālidan to ʿAmran (the object), by the one wāw. Both first words are governed by the one governor ḍaraba, so the joining is allowed by agreement.

tasks.prompt: Say what kind of emphasis each is: ḍarabta anta; jāʾa al-qawmu kulluhum; ḍaraba ḍaraba Zaydun.
tasks.arabic: ضَرَبْتَ أَنْتَ — جَاءَ الْقَوْمُ كُلُّهُمْ — ضَرَبَ ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: Ḍarabta anta: verbal, a word of the same meaning for the joined pronoun. Kulluhum: of meaning, with one of its fixed words, after a definite. Ḍaraba ḍaraba Zaydun: verbal, the verb repeated.

tasks.prompt: Why is huwa needed in Zaydun ḍaraba huwa nafsuhu?
tasks.answer: Nafsuhu emphasizes the pronoun hidden in ḍaraba, a marfūʿ joined pronoun; such a pronoun must first be emphasized by a separate one. Without huwa, nafsuhu would be read as the fāʿil of ḍaraba.

quiz.prompt: How many particles of ʿaṭf does the book list?
quiz.explanation: Wa, fa, thumma, ḥattā, aw, immā, am, lā, bal, lākin.

quiz.prompt: To join Zaydun to the tāʾ of ḍarabtu one says…
quiz.explanation: The marfūʿ joined pronoun is first emphasized by a separate one.

quiz.prompt: In al-mālu baynī wa-baynaka, what is repeated?
options: bayna, the word that gives the jarr
quiz.explanation: Joined to a majrūr pronoun, the khāfiḍ is repeated.

quiz.prompt: Joining to the governed words of two different governors is…
options: not allowed, except in one view with the jārr first

quiz.prompt: Verbal emphasis runs through…
quiz.explanation: Ḍaraba ḍaraba Zaydun; Zaydun qāʾimun Zaydun qāʾimun.

quiz.prompt: Emphasis of meaning is reserved for…
quiz.explanation: Nafs, ʿayn, kilā, kiltā, kull, ajmaʿ.

quiz.prompt: Aktaʿu, abtaʿu and abṣaʿu…
options: follow ajmaʿ and are not said without it

text.original: وَالثَّانِي الْعَطْفُ بِالْحُرُوفِ، وَهُوَ تَابِعٌ يَتَوَسَّطُ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ مَتْبُوعِهِ أَحَدُ الْحُرُوفِ الْعَشَرَةِ، وَهِيَ: الْوَاوُ، وَالْفَاءُ، وَثُمَّ، وَحَتَّى، وَأَوْ، وَإِمَّا، وَأَمْ، وَلَا، وَبَلْ، وَلَكِنْ. وَإِذَا عُطِفَ عَلَى الضَّمِيرِ الْمَرْفُوعِ الْمُتَّصِلِ يَجِبُ تَأْكِيدُهُ بِمُنْفَصِلٍ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ أَنَا وَزَيْدٌ، إِلَّا أَنْ يَقَعَ فَصْلٌ فَيَجُوزُ تَرْكُهُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ الْيَوْمَ وَزَيْدٌ. وَإِذَا عُطِفَ عَلَى الضَّمِيرِ الْمَجْرُورِ أُعِيدَ الْخَافِضُ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِكَ وَبِزَيْدٍ، وَالْمَالُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ.
text.en: The second is ʿaṭf by particles, which is a follower between which and what it follows one of the ten particles stands: the wāw, the fāʾ, thumma, ḥattā, aw, immā, am, lā, bal and lākin. When [a noun] is joined by ʿaṭf to a marfūʿ joined pronoun, [the pronoun] must be emphasized by a separate one, as ḍarabtu anā wa-Zaydun “I and Zayd hit”, unless something separates them, and then it may be left out, as ḍarabtu al-yawma wa-Zaydun “I hit today, and Zayd”. When it is joined to a majrūr pronoun, the [particle] that puts in jarr is repeated, as marartu bika wa-bi-Zaydin “I passed by you and by Zayd” and al-mālu baynī wa-baynaka “the wealth is between me and you”.

text.original: وَالْمَعْطُوفُ فِي حُكْمِ الْمَعْطُوفِ عَلَيْهِ فِيمَا يَجِبُ وَيَمْتَنِعُ لَهُ. وَيَجُوزُ عَطْفُ شَيْئَيْنِ بِحَرْفٍ وَاحِدٍ عَلَى مَعْمُولَيْ عَامِلٍ وَاحِدٍ بِالِاتِّفَاقِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا وَبَكْرٌ خَالِدًا، وَلَا يَجُوزُ عَلَى مَعْمُولَيْ عَامِلَيْنِ مُخْتَلِفَيْنِ إِلَّا عِنْدَ تَقَدُّمِ الْجَارِّ عَلَى رَأْيٍ، نَحْوُ: فِي الدَّارِ زَيْدٌ وَالْحُجْرَةِ عَمْرٌو.
text.en: What is joined by ʿaṭf is treated like what it is joined to, in what is necessary for it and what is impossible for it. By agreement two things may be joined by one particle to the two governed words of one governor, as ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran wa-Bakrun Khālidan “Zayd hit ʿAmr, and Bakr Khālid”; it is not allowed [to join] to the two governed words of two different governors, except, in one view, when the [particle] that puts in jarr comes first, as fī al-dāri Zaydun wa-al-ḥujrati ʿAmrun “in the house is Zayd, and [in] the room ʿAmr”.

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ التَّأْكِيدُ، وَهُوَ قِسْمَانِ: لَفْظِيٌّ، وَهُوَ تَكْرِيرُ اللَّفْظِ الْأَوَّلِ، أَوْ مُرَادِفِهِ فِي الضَّمِيرِ الْمُتَّصِلِ، وَيَجْرِي فِي الْأَلْفَاظِ كُلِّهَا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ زَيْدٌ، وَضَرَبْتَ أَنْتَ، وَضَرَبَ ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ، وَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ.
text.en: The third is emphasis (taʾkīd), and it is of two divisions. Verbal (lafẓī), which is repeating the first word, or [using] a word of the same meaning in the joined pronoun; it runs through all words, as jāʾanī Zaydun Zaydun “Zayd, Zayd came to me”, ḍarabta anta “you hit, you”, ḍaraba ḍaraba Zaydun “Zayd hit, hit” and Zaydun qāʾimun Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing, Zayd is standing”.

text.original: وَمَعْنَوِيٌّ مَخْصُوصٌ بِالْمَعَارِفِ، وَهُوَ نَفْسُهُ وَعَيْنُهُ وَكِلَاهُمَا وَكِلْتَاهُمَا وَكُلُّهُ وَأَجْمَعُ وَأَكْتَعُ وَأَبْتَعُ وَأَبْصَعُ، وَهَذِهِ الثَّلَاثَةُ أَتْبَاعٌ لِأَجْمَعَ، وَلَا تَتَقَدَّمُ عَلَيْهِ، وَلَا تُذْكَرُ بِدُونِهِ فِي الْفَصِيحِ. وَإِذَا أُكِّدَ الْمُضْمَرُ الْمَرْفُوعُ الْمُتَّصِلُ بِالنَّفْسِ وَالْعَيْنِ أُكِّدَ أَوَّلًا بِمُنْفَصِلٍ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ ضَرَبَ هُوَ نَفْسُهُ أَوْ عَيْنُهُ.
text.en: And of meaning (maʿnawī), which is reserved for definites: it is nafsuhu “himself”, ʿaynuhu “his very self”, kilāhumā and kiltāhumā “both of them”, kulluhu “all of it”, and ajmaʿu, aktaʿu, abtaʿu and abṣaʿu “all together”. These three [last] are followers of ajmaʿ: they do not come before it, and they are not mentioned without it in eloquent speech. When a marfūʿ joined pronoun is emphasized by nafs or ʿayn, it is first emphasized by a separate [pronoun], as Zaydun ḍaraba huwa nafsuhu aw ʿaynuhu “Zayd, he hit, he himself”.

lessons.title: The badal; the explanatory ʿaṭf; thirty governed words
body: The fourth follower is the badal, “what is meant by the attribution, not what it follows”. The first word only leads in; the speech is really about the second. The commentators put it as the badal standing as if its governor were said again. It has four divisions. The badal of the whole for the whole, when both are true of one thing: jāʾanī Zaydun akhūka, “Zayd, your brother, came to me”. The badal of the part for the whole: ḍarabtu Zaydan raʾsahu, “I hit Zayd, his head”.

The badal of inclusion (ishtimāl) is for any other connection, “such that after the first is mentioned the mind waits and longs for the second”: suliba Zaydun thawbuhu, “Zayd was robbed, his garment”. Told that Zayd was robbed, one waits to hear of what. Note that the part and the inclusion both carry a pronoun of the first, raʾsahu, thawbuhu. The badal of mistake, raʾaytu rajulan ḥimāran, “I saw a man, a donkey”, is the slip of a speaker who corrects himself; “it does not occur in the speech of the eloquent, who bring it with bal”: raʾaytu rajulan bal ḥimāran.

Two limits. An indefinite that is the badal of the whole for a definite must be qualified: bi-l-nāṣiyati nāṣiyatin kādhibatin (Q 96:15–16), “by the forelock, a lying forelock”; the bare nāṣiyatin would add nothing to al-nāṣiya. And a visible noun is not the badal of the whole for a pronoun, except for the absent one: ḍarabtuhu Zaydan, “I hit him, Zayd”, where Zaydan tells who “him” is. The speaker and the one addressed are already as clear as they can be.

The fifth follower is the explanatory ʿaṭf (ʿaṭf al-bayān), “a follower brought to make clear what it follows, and it does not indicate a meaning in it”, as an adjective does: aqsama bi-Allāhi Abū Ḥafṣin ʿUmaru, “Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar swore by God”. Abū Ḥafṣ is the kunya of the caliph ʿUmar; the name ʿUmar makes plain who is meant. The difference from the badal lies in the definitions: in the badal the second word is what is meant, in the explanatory ʿaṭf the first is meant and the second explains it.

So the chapter ends: “the total of the governed words we have mentioned is thirty”. Nine marfūʿ, thirteen manṣūb, two majrūr and one majzūm are governed in their own right; five followers are governed by following. With the sixty governors of the first chapter, the student now has both sides of every iʿrāb: what governs, and what is governed.

terms.en: the follower that is what the attribution really means
the badal of inclusion, for which the mind waits
the badal of mistake, said with bal by the eloquent
the explanatory ʿaṭf, which makes clear what it follows

examples.en: the badal of the whole for the whole
the badal of the part for the whole
the badal of inclusion
an indefinite badal for a definite, qualified (Q 96:15–16)
the explanatory ʿaṭf

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of badal in each: jāʾanī Zaydun akhūka; ḍarabtu Zaydan raʾsahu; suliba Zaydun thawbuhu.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ أَخُوكَ — ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا رَأْسَهُ — سُلِبَ زَيْدٌ ثَوْبُهُ
tasks.answer: Akhūka: the badal of the whole for the whole (Zayd and your brother are one person). Raʾsahu: the badal of the part for the whole. Thawbuhu: the badal of inclusion (the garment is connected with Zayd, and after “Zayd was robbed” the mind waits for it).

tasks.prompt: Why must nāṣiyatin be qualified by kādhibatin in Q 96:15–16?
tasks.answer: Nāṣiyatin is an indefinite standing as the badal of the whole for the definite al-nāṣiya. Such a badal must be qualified; the adjective kādhibatin gives it something the first word did not say.

tasks.prompt: May one say ḍarabtuka Zaydan, with Zaydan as the badal of the kāf? And ḍarabtuhu Zaydan?
tasks.answer: Not ḍarabtuka Zaydan: a visible noun is not the badal of the whole for the pronoun of the one addressed or the speaker. Ḍarabtuhu Zaydan is allowed, since the pronoun is of the absent, and Zaydan makes clear who is meant.

tasks.prompt: Count the thirty governed words of the chapter.
tasks.answer: Governed in their own right: nine marfūʿ, thirteen manṣūb, two majrūr (by a particle and by iḍāfa) and one majzūm, twenty-five in all. Governed by following: five, the adjective, ʿaṭf by particles, emphasis, the badal and the explanatory ʿaṭf.

quiz.prompt: The badal is…
options: a meaning in what it follows
what is meant by the attribution, not what it follows
quiz.explanation: The first word only leads in to it.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabtu Zaydan raʾsahu has a badal of…
quiz.explanation: The head is a part of Zayd.

quiz.prompt: In suliba Zaydun thawbuhu the badal is of…
quiz.explanation: After “Zayd was robbed”, the mind waits for what.

quiz.prompt: The eloquent say the badal of mistake…
A visible noun may be the badal of the whole for a pronoun only when the pronoun is…
In aqsama bi-Allāhi Abū Ḥafṣin ʿUmaru, ʿUmaru is…
quiz.explanation: It makes clear who Abū Ḥafṣ is, and shows no meaning in him.

quiz.prompt: How many governed words does the second chapter count?
quiz.explanation: Twenty-five in their own right and five by following.

text.original: وَالرَّابِعُ الْبَدَلُ، وَهُوَ الْمَقْصُودُ بِالنِّسْبَةِ دُونَ مَتْبُوعِهِ، وَأَقْسَامُهُ أَرْبَعَةٌ: بَدَلُ الْكُلِّ مِنَ الْكُلِّ إِنْ صَدَقَا عَلَى وَاحِدٍ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ أَخُوكَ، وَبَدَلُ الْبَعْضِ مِنَ الْكُلِّ إِنْ كَانَ جُزْءَ الْمُبْدَلِ مِنْهُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا رَأْسَهُ، وَبَدَلُ الِاشْتِمَالِ إِنْ كَانَ بَيْنَهُمَا تَعَلُّقٌ بِغَيْرِهِمَا، بِحَيْثُ تَنْتَظِرُ النَّفْسُ بَعْدَ ذِكْرِ الْأَوَّلِ وَتَتَشَوَّقُ إِلَى الثَّانِي، نَحْوُ: سُلِبَ زَيْدٌ ثَوْبُهُ.
text.en: The fourth is the badal, which is what is meant by the attribution, not what it follows. Its divisions are four. The badal of the whole for the whole, if both are true of one thing, as jāʾanī Zaydun akhūka “Zayd, your brother, came to me”. The badal of the part for the whole, if it is a part of what it stands for, as ḍarabtu Zaydan raʾsahu “I hit Zayd, his head”. The badal of inclusion (ishtimāl), if between them there is a connection other than these, such that after the first is mentioned the mind waits and longs for the second, as suliba Zaydun thawbuhu “Zayd was robbed, his garment”.

text.original: وَبَدَلُ الْغَلَطِ إِنْ كَانَ ذِكْرُ الْمُبْدَلِ مِنْهُ غَلَطًا، نَحْوُ: رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا حِمَارًا، وَلَا يَقَعُ فِي كَلَامِ الْفُصَحَاءِ، بَلْ يُورِدُونَهُ بِبَلْ. وَيَجِبُ وَصْفُ النَّكِرَةِ مِنَ الْمَعْرِفَةِ بَدَلَ الْكُلِّ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: بِالنَّاصِيَةِ نَاصِيَةٍ كَاذِبَةٍ. وَلَا يُبْدَلُ الظَّاهِرُ مِنَ الْمُضْمَرِ بَدَلَ الْكُلِّ إِلَّا مِنَ الْغَائِبِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُهُ زَيْدًا.
text.en: The badal of mistake, if mentioning what it stands for was a mistake, as raʾaytu rajulan ḥimāran “I saw a man, a donkey”; it does not occur in the speech of the eloquent, who bring it with bal “rather”. An indefinite standing as badal of the whole for a definite must be qualified, as His saying, Most High: bi-al-nāṣiyati nāṣiyatin kādhibatin “by the forelock, a lying forelock” [96:15–16]. A visible noun is not put as badal of the whole for a pronoun, except for the absent [pronoun], as ḍarabtuhu Zaydan “I hit him, Zayd”.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ عَطْفُ الْبَيَانِ، وَهُوَ تَابِعٌ جِيءَ بِهِ لِإِيضَاحِ مَتْبُوعِهِ، وَلَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِيهِ، نَحْوُ: أَقْسَمَ بِاللَّهِ أَبُو حَفْصٍ عُمَرُ. فَمَجْمُوعُ مَا ذَكَرْنَا مِنَ الْمَعْمُولَاتِ ثَلَاثُونَ.
text.en: The fifth is the explanatory ʿaṭf (ʿaṭf al-bayān), which is a follower brought to make clear what it follows, and it does not indicate a meaning in it, as aqsama bi-Allāhi Abū Ḥafṣin ʿUmaru “Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar swore by God”. So the total of the governed words we have mentioned is thirty.

parts.title: Chapter three: iʿrāb, its signs and its places

lessons.title: What iʿrāb is; its ten signs
body: The third chapter is on the third of the book's three things (lesson 1): the governing itself, iʿrāb. It is “something that comes from the governor, by which the end of the word with iʿrāb (muʿrab) differs”. Two parts of the definition matter. “From the governor”: no governor, no iʿrāb, which is why the first chapter came first. “The end”: the vowels inside a word, as the kasra of the rāʾ in yaḍribu, belong to ṣarf; iʿrāb is only the change at the end.

Birgivī divides iʿrāb four ways, and the divisions “overlap”: one and the same sign can be described by each of them. The first is by its nature. Iʿrāb is a vowel, a letter, or a dropping. The vowels are three: ḍamma, fatḥa and kasra, jāʾanī Zaydun, raʾaytu Zaydan, marartu bi-Zaydin.

The letters are four: wāw, alif and yāʾ, as in jāʾanī abūhu, raʾaytu abāhu, marartu bi-abīhi, and the nūn, as in yaḍribāni, where the nūn is the sign of rafʿ and the alif the pronoun (lesson 29). The droppings are three: of the vowel, lam yaḍrib; of the last letter, lam yaghzu, where the wāw of yaghzū falls; and of the nūn, lam yaḍribā. “So the total is ten.” Notice that the sukūn of lam yaḍrib is not counted as a sign of its own: the book calls it the dropping of the vowel the verb had.

The second division is by place: what kinds of word take which signs. The iʿrāb is by vowels only, by letters only, by a vowel with dropping, or by letters with dropping. The first of these is either full, with all three vowels, or deficient, with two. Full iʿrāb with three vowels belongs to the singular noun and the broken plural that are fully declined (munṣarif): jāʾanī rajulun wa-rijālun, raʾaytu rajulan wa-rijālan, marartu bi-rajulin wa-rijālin. The next lesson goes through the rest.

terms.en: what comes from the governor and changes the word's end
the word with iʿrāb, whose end changes
full iʿrāb: a different sign for each of three states

examples.en: iʿrāb by letters: wāw, alif, yāʾ

examples.en: the three droppings
full iʿrāb by vowels: the singular and the broken plural
