tasks.prompt: Name the sign of iʿrāb and its kind by nature: jāʾanī abūhu; lam yaḍribā; marartu bi-Zaydin; lam yaghzu.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي أَبُوهُ — لَمْ يَضْرِبَا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ — لَمْ يَغْزُ
tasks.answer: Abūhu: the wāw, a letter (rafʿ). Lam yaḍribā: dropping the nūn (jazm). Bi-Zaydin: the kasra, a vowel (jarr). Lam yaghzu: dropping the last letter, the wāw (jazm).

tasks.prompt: Why does the book count the jazm of lam yaḍrib as a dropping, not as a vowel?
tasks.answer: The sukūn is not a vowel but the absence of one. The verb had a ḍamma in rafʿ (yaḍribu); jazm takes that vowel away. So the sign is the dropping of the vowel.

tasks.prompt: Give the three states of rijāl as the book does, with their signs.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي رِجَالٌ — رَأَيْتُ رِجَالًا — مَرَرْتُ بِرِجَالٍ
tasks.answer: Rafʿ by the ḍamma (rijālun), naṣb by the fatḥa (rijālan), jarr by the kasra (rijālin): full iʿrāb by vowels, since it is a broken plural that is fully declined.

tasks.prompt: What do the words “the end” and “from the governor” in the definition leave out?
tasks.answer: “The end” leaves out the vowels inside the word, which belong to ṣarf, as the kasra of the rāʾ in yaḍribu. “From the governor” leaves out any change that a governor does not cause: a word with no governor has no iʿrāb.

quiz.prompt: Iʿrāb, in the book's definition, comes from…
quiz.explanation: And it changes the end of the muʿrab.

quiz.prompt: Iʿrāb by its nature is…
options: a vowel, a letter or a dropping
quiz.explanation: The first of the four divisions.

quiz.prompt: How many signs does the first division count?
quiz.explanation: Three vowels, four letters, three droppings.

quiz.prompt: In yaḍribāni the sign of iʿrāb is…
quiz.explanation: The alif is the pronoun; the nūn shows the rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: In lam yaghzu the sign of jazm is…
Which letter is NOT one of the four letters of iʿrāb?
Full iʿrāb with three vowels belongs to…
options: the munṣarif singular and broken plural

text.original: وَهُوَ شَيْءٌ جَاءَ مِنَ الْعَامِلِ يَخْتَلِفُ بِهِ آخِرُ الْمُعْرَبِ، وَلَهُ تَقْسِيمَاتٌ أَرْبَعَةٌ مُتَدَاخِلَةٌ. التَّقْسِيمُ الْأَوَّلُ بِحَسَبِ الذَّاتِ وَالْحَقِيقَةِ، فَنَقُولُ: هُوَ إِمَّا حَرَكَةٌ أَوْ حَرْفٌ أَوْ حَذْفٌ. وَالْحَرَكَةُ ثَلَاثَةٌ: ضَمَّةٌ وَفَتْحَةٌ وَكَسْرَةٌ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ.
text.en: It is something that comes from the governor, by which the end of the word with iʿrāb (muʿrab) differs. It has four divisions that overlap. The first division is by its nature and reality, and we say: it is either a vowel, a letter or a dropping. The vowel is three: ḍamma, fatḥa and kasra, as jāʾanī Zaydun “Zayd came to me”, raʾaytu Zaydan “I saw Zayd” and marartu bi-Zaydin “I passed by Zayd”.

text.original: وَالْحَرْفُ أَرْبَعَةٌ: وَاوٌ وَأَلِفٌ وَيَاءٌ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي أَبُوهُ، وَرَأَيْتُ أَبَاهُ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِأَبِيهِ، وَنُونٌ، نَحْوُ: يَضْرِبَانِ. وَالْحَذْفُ ثَلَاثَةٌ: حَذْفُ الْحَرَكَةِ، نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَضْرِبْ، وَحَذْفُ الْآخِرِ، نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَغْزُ، وَحَذْفُ النُّونِ، نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَضْرِبَا. فَالْمَجْمُوعُ عَشَرَةٌ.
text.en: The letter is four: wāw, alif and yāʾ, as jāʾanī abūhu “his father came to me”, raʾaytu abāhu “I saw his father” and marartu bi-abīhi “I passed by his father”; and nūn, as yaḍribāni “they both hit”. The dropping is three: dropping the vowel, as lam yaḍrib “he did not hit”; dropping the last [letter], as lam yaghzu “he did not raid”; and dropping the nūn, as lam yaḍribā “they both did not hit”. So the total is ten.

text.original: وَالتَّقْسِيمُ الثَّانِي بِحَسَبِ الْمَحَلِّ، فَهُوَ إِمَّا بِالْحَرَكَةِ الْمَحْضَةِ، أَوْ بِالْحُرُوفِ الْمَحْضَةِ، أَوْ بِالْحَرَكَةِ مَعَ الْحَذْفِ، أَوْ بِالْحُرُوفِ مَعَ الْحَذْفِ. وَالْأَوَّلُ إِمَّا تَامُّ الْإِعْرَابِ بِالْحَرَكَاتِ الثَّلَاثَةِ: بِالضَّمَّةِ رَفْعًا، وَالْفَتْحَةِ نَصْبًا، وَالْكَسْرَةِ جَرًّا، فَهُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمُفْرَدُ وَالْجَمْعُ الْمُكَسَّرُ الْمُنْصَرِفَانِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ وَرِجَالٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا وَرِجَالًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ وَرِجَالٍ.
text.en: The second division is by place. [The iʿrāb] is either by vowels only, by letters only, by a vowel with dropping, or by letters with dropping. The first has either full iʿrāb with the three vowels, the ḍamma for rafʿ, the fatḥa for naṣb and the kasra for jarr, and that is the singular noun and the broken plural that are fully declined (munṣarif), as jāʾanī rajulun wa-rijālun “a man and men came to me”, raʾaytu rajulan wa-rijālan “I saw a man and men” and marartu bi-rajulin wa-rijālin “I passed by a man and men”.

lessons.title: Which words take which signs: the nine places
body: Deficient iʿrāb has only two signs for three states. With the ḍamma for rafʿ and the fatḥa for naṣb and jarr: the noun that is not fully declined, jāʾanī Aḥmadu, raʾaytu Aḥmada, marartu bi-Aḥmada (next lesson). With the ḍamma for rafʿ and the kasra for naṣb and jarr: the sound feminine plural, muslimātun, muslimātin, bi-muslimātin. A beginner who writes raʾaytu muslimātan has given it the fatḥa it never takes.

By letters, full: the wāw, alif and yāʾ of “the six nouns made muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker, singular and not diminutive”. The commentators name the six: ab, akh, ḥam, han, fam and dhū: abūhu, abāhu, abīhi. Each condition counts: abī, “my father”, does not change; abawāni, a dual, takes the dual's signs; ubayy, a diminutive, takes vowels.

By letters, deficient: the wāw for rafʿ and the yāʾ for naṣb and jarr, in the sound masculine plural, in ulū, “possessors of”, and in ʿishrūna and its sisters: muslimūna, ulū mālin, ʿishrūna; muslimīna, ulī mālin, ʿishrīna. Or the alif for rafʿ and the yāʾ for naṣb and jarr, in the dual, in ithnāni, and in kilā made muḍāf to a pronoun: kilāhumā, kilayhimā. The condition “to a pronoun” matters: before a visible noun kilā keeps its alif in every state.

By a vowel with dropping, which is always full: the muḍāriʿ with no pronoun joined to its end. If it is sound, rafʿ by the ḍamma, naṣb by the fatḥa, jazm by dropping the vowel: yaḍribu, lan yaḍriba, lam yaḍrib. If its end is a weak letter, jazm by dropping that letter: yaghzū, lan yaghzuwa, lam yaghzu.

By letters with dropping, which is always deficient: the muḍāriʿ with a marfūʿ pronoun joined to it, “other than the nūn”: rafʿ by the nūn, naṣb and jazm by dropping it: yaḍribāni, lan yaḍribā, lam yaḍribā; so too yaḍribūna and taḍribīna. The pronoun nūn of yaḍribna is left out, because with it the verb is built and has no iʿrāb (lesson 52). “So the total is nine”, and the table gathers them.

terms.en: deficient iʿrāb: two signs for three states
the six nouns, with iʿrāb by wāw, alif and yāʾ
the sound feminine plural: kasra for naṣb
the dual: alif for rafʿ, yāʾ for naṣb and jarr

examples.arabic: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمَاتٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَاتٍ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمَاتٍ
examples.en: the sound feminine plural: the kasra in naṣb
the wāw for rafʿ
the yāʾ for naṣb
a weak-ended muḍāriʿ: jazm by dropping the last letter

tasks.prompt: Correct the mistake and give the rule: raʾaytu muslimātan.
tasks.answer: Raʾaytu muslimātin. The sound feminine plural has deficient iʿrāb: the ḍamma for rafʿ and the kasra for both naṣb and jarr.

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of abūhu in each and the condition it meets: jāʾanī abūhu; raʾaytu abāhu.
tasks.answer: Abūhu: fāʿil, in rafʿ by the wāw; abāhu: object, in naṣb by the alif. Ab is one of the six nouns, singular, not diminutive, and muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker (here the hāʾ), so its iʿrāb is by letters.

tasks.prompt: Why is the yāʾ of kilayhimā a sign of iʿrāb, but the alif of kilā al-rajulayni is not changed?
tasks.answer: Kilā takes the iʿrāb of the dual (alif in rafʿ, yāʾ in naṣb and jarr) only when it is muḍāf to a pronoun, as kilāhumā, kilayhimā. Muḍāf to a visible noun it keeps its alif in every state.

tasks.prompt: Put yaḍribūna after lan and after lam, and name the sign each time.
tasks.answer: Lan yaḍribū and lam yaḍribū: the nūn, the sign of rafʿ, is dropped for naṣb and for jazm. The wāw stays: it is the pronoun, the fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: The noun that is not fully declined takes in jarr…
The sound feminine plural in naṣb takes…
Which is NOT a condition of the six nouns' iʿrāb by letters?
options: muḍāf to other than the yāʾ of the speaker

quiz.prompt: Ulū mālin is in rafʿ by…
quiz.explanation: Ulū goes with the sound masculine plural.

quiz.prompt: Kilā takes the alif and the yāʾ when it is muḍāf to…
Lam yaghzu shows jazm by…
quiz.explanation: Its end is a weak letter.

quiz.prompt: Yaḍribāni has rafʿ by…
quiz.explanation: Naṣb and jazm by dropping it: lan yaḍribā, lam yaḍribā.

text.original: أَوْ نَاقِصُ الْإِعْرَابِ بِالْحَرَكَتَيْنِ: إِمَّا بِالضَّمَّةِ رَفْعًا وَالْفَتْحَةِ نَصْبًا وَجَرًّا، فَهُوَ غَيْرُ الْمُنْصَرِفِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي أَحْمَدُ، وَرَأَيْتُ أَحْمَدَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِأَحْمَدَ، وَإِمَّا بِالضَّمَّةِ رَفْعًا وَالْكَسْرَةِ نَصْبًا وَجَرًّا، وَهُوَ جَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمَاتٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَاتٍ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمَاتٍ.
text.en: Or it has deficient iʿrāb with two vowels: either with the ḍamma for rafʿ and the fatḥa for naṣb and jarr, and that is what is not fully declined (ghayr al-munṣarif), as jāʾanī Aḥmadu “Aḥmad came to me”, raʾaytu Aḥmada “I saw Aḥmad” and marartu bi-Aḥmada “I passed by Aḥmad”; or with the ḍamma for rafʿ and the kasra for naṣb and jarr, and that is the sound feminine plural, as jāʾanī muslimātun “Muslim women came to me”, raʾaytu muslimātin “I saw Muslim women” and marartu bi-muslimātin “I passed by Muslim women”.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي أَيْضًا إِمَّا تَامُّ الْإِعْرَابِ بِالْحُرُوفِ الثَّلَاثَةِ: بِالْوَاوِ رَفْعًا، وَالْأَلِفِ نَصْبًا، وَالْيَاءِ جَرًّا، فَهُوَ الْأَسْمَاءُ السِّتَّةُ الْمُضَافَةُ إِلَى غَيْرِ يَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ، الْمُفْرَدَةُ الْمُكَبَّرَةُ. وَإِمَّا نَاقِصُ الْإِعْرَابِ بِالْحَرْفَيْنِ: إِمَّا بِالْوَاوِ رَفْعًا وَالْيَاءِ نَصْبًا وَجَرًّا، فَهُوَ جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ وَأُولُو وَعِشْرُونَ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمُونَ وَأُولُو مَالٍ وَعِشْرُونَ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِينَ وَأُولِي مَالٍ وَعِشْرِينَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمِينَ وَأُولِي مَالٍ وَعِشْرِينَ.
text.en: The second too has either full iʿrāb with the three letters, the wāw for rafʿ, the alif for naṣb and the yāʾ for jarr, and that is the six nouns made muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker, singular and not diminutive; or deficient iʿrāb with two letters: either with the wāw for rafʿ and the yāʾ for naṣb and jarr, and that is the sound masculine plural, ulū “possessors of” and ʿishrūna “twenty” and its sisters, as jāʾanī muslimūna wa-ulū mālin wa-ʿishrūna “Muslims, men of wealth and twenty came to me”, raʾaytu muslimīna wa-ulī mālin wa-ʿishrīna “I saw Muslims, men of wealth and twenty” and marartu bi-muslimīna wa-ulī mālin wa-ʿishrīna “I passed by Muslims, men of wealth and twenty”.

text.original: أَوْ بِالْأَلِفِ رَفْعًا وَالْيَاءِ نَصْبًا وَجَرًّا، فَهُوَ الْمُثَنَّى وَاثْنَانِ وَكِلَا مُضَافًا إِلَى مُضْمَرٍ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمَانِ وَاثْنَانِ وَكِلَاهُمَا، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَيْنِ وَاثْنَيْنِ وَكِلَيْهِمَا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمَيْنِ وَاثْنَيْنِ وَكِلَيْهِمَا.
text.en: Or with the alif for rafʿ and the yāʾ for naṣb and jarr, and that is the dual, ithnāni “two”, and kilā “both” made muḍāf to a pronoun, as jāʾanī muslimāni wa-ithnāni wa-kilāhumā “two Muslims, two, both of them, came to me”, raʾaytu muslimayni wa-ithnayni wa-kilayhimā “I saw two Muslims, two, both of them” and marartu bi-muslimayni wa-ithnayni wa-kilayhimā “I passed by two Muslims, two, both of them”.

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ لَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا تَامَّ الْإِعْرَابِ، وَهُوَ قِسْمَانِ؛ لِأَنَّ مَحْذُوفَهُ إِمَّا حَرَكَةٌ أَوْ حَرْفٌ. فَالْأَوَّلُ الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ الَّذِي لَمْ يَتَّصِلْ بِآخِرِهِ ضَمِيرٌ وَهُوَ صَحِيحٌ، فَرَفْعُهُ بِالضَّمَّةِ، وَنَصْبُهُ بِالْفَتْحَةِ، وَجَزْمُهُ بِحَذْفِ الْحَرَكَةِ، نَحْوُ: يَضْرِبُ، وَلَنْ يَضْرِبَ، وَلَمْ يَضْرِبْ. وَالثَّانِي الْمُضَارِعُ الْمَذْكُورُ إِنْ كَانَ آخِرُهُ حَرْفَ عِلَّةٍ، فَرَفْعُهُ بِالضَّمَّةِ، وَنَصْبُهُ بِالْفَتْحَةِ، وَجَزْمُهُ بِحَذْفِ الْآخِرِ، نَحْوُ: يَغْزُو، وَلَنْ يَغْزُوَ، وَلَمْ يَغْزُ.
text.en: The third has only full iʿrāb, and it is of two divisions, because what is dropped from it is either a vowel or a letter. The first is the muḍāriʿ verb to whose end no pronoun is joined, when it is sound: its rafʿ is by the ḍamma, its naṣb by the fatḥa and its jazm by dropping the vowel, as yaḍribu “he hits”, lan yaḍriba “he will not hit” and lam yaḍrib “he did not hit”. The second is that muḍāriʿ if its end is a weak letter: its rafʿ is by the ḍamma, its naṣb by the fatḥa and its jazm by dropping the last [letter], as yaghzū “he raids”, lan yaghzuwa “he will not raid” and lam yaghzu “he did not raid”.

text.original: وَالرَّابِعُ لَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا نَاقِصَ الْإِعْرَابِ، وَهُوَ الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ الَّذِي اتَّصَلَ بِآخِرِهِ ضَمِيرٌ مَرْفُوعٌ غَيْرُ النُّونِ، فَرَفْعُهُ بِالنُّونِ، وَنَصْبُهُ وَجَزْمُهُ بِحَذْفِهِ، نَحْوُ: يَضْرِبَانِ، وَلَنْ يَضْرِبَا، وَلَمْ يَضْرِبَا. فَالْمَجْمُوعُ تِسْعَةٌ.
text.en: The fourth has only deficient iʿrāb, and it is the muḍāriʿ verb to whose end a marfūʿ pronoun other than the nūn is joined: its rafʿ is by the nūn, and its naṣb and jazm by dropping it, as yaḍribāni “they both hit”, lan yaḍribā “they both will not hit” and lam yaḍribā “they both did not hit”. So the total is nine.

lessons.title: The fully declined noun and the diptote
body: The fully declined noun (munṣarif) is “what jarr and tanwīn come upon”, as Zaydin. The noun not fully declined, the diptote, is “a noun given iʿrāb by vowels that jarr and tanwīn do not come upon”: it takes no tanwīn, and the fatḥa stands for its jarr (last lesson). The Kāfiya, which the Ottoman student reads after this book, teaches the same words through nine causes; Birgivī simply lists them, in two kinds: those known by hearing, and those by rule.

Known by hearing: the number words of distribution, uḥād and mawḥad, “one by one”, thunāʾ and mathnā, thulāth and mathlath, rubāʿ and marbaʿ, as in mathnā wa-thulātha wa-rubāʿa (Q 4:3); ukhar, “others”, as an adjective; jumaʿ, kutaʿ, butaʿ and buṣaʿ, the plural emphasis words that go with ajmaʿ (lesson 42); and the names ʿUmar, Zufar, Zuḥal and Quzaḥ.

By rule: a name on a pattern reserved for the verb, as a man named Ḍuriba, Shammara or Istakhraja, or beginning with a letter of the muḍāriʿ and not taking the tāʾ, as Yazīd and Yashkur; every afʿal of preference or of adjective, afḍal, abyaḍ; a foreign name used as a name from its first coming into Arabic, if it has more than three letters or a vowel on the middle one, Qālūn, Ibrāhīm, Shatar, while a short one like Nūḥ is declined; and every feminine with an alif, short or long, ḥublā, ḥamrāʾ.

So too every name with the tāʾ of the feminine, in the wording, Fāṭima, and Ḥamza too, though a man's name, because the tāʾ is in the word; or understood, in a name of more than three letters, Zaynab, or of three with a vowel on the middle, Qadam as a woman's name. A three-letter feminine name with a sukūn in the middle, Hind, may be declined or not. Further: a name compounded of two nouns, neither governing the other, Baʿlabakk, Ḥaḍramawt; a word with an added alif and nūn, as a name, ʿImrān, or as an adjective that does not take the tāʾ, sakrān, raḥmān; and every plural on faʿālil or faʿālīl, masājid, maṣābīḥ.

Two last rules. A diptote may be declined for the necessity of verse or to match the words around it: salāsilan and qawārīran (Q 76:4, 15), in the reading of those who give them tanwīn. And every diptote takes its kasra again when it is muḍāf or has the lām of definiteness: marartu bi-l-aḥmari, “I passed by the red one”, bi-aḥmarinā, “by our red one”.

terms.en: the fully declined noun, with jarr and tanwīn
the diptote: no tanwīn, the fatḥa for jarr
the added alif and nūn, as in ʿImrān and sakrān
the foreign noun, a diptote as a name of more than three letters

examples.en: names with the tāʾ in the wording: diptotes
plurals on faʿālil and faʿālīl
declined to match the words around (Q 76:4, 15)
with the lām or in iḍāfa: the kasra returns

grid.caption: Diptotes, by hearing and by rule (pp. 83–84)
head: Kind
The book's examples

tasks.prompt: Fully declined or not? Zayd; Aḥmad; Hind; Ḥamza; Ibrāhīm.
tasks.answer: Zayd: declined. Aḥmad: not declined (a name on the pattern afʿal, reserved for the verb). Hind: either (a three-letter feminine name with a sukūn in the middle). Ḥamza: not declined (a name with the tāʾ in its wording, even for a man). Ibrāhīm: not declined (a foreign name of more than three letters).

tasks.prompt: Say “I passed by mosques” and “I passed by the mosques”, and explain the difference.
tasks.answer: Marartu bi-masājida: a plural on faʿālil is a diptote, so the fatḥa stands for its jarr and it has no tanwīn. Marartu bi-l-masājidi: with the lām of definiteness the diptote takes the kasra again.

tasks.prompt: Why is Qadam a diptote as a woman's name, but declined as a man's?
tasks.answer: As a woman's name it is a feminine name of three letters with a vowel on the middle one, and its tāʾ is understood; such a name is not declined. Named for a man, the feminine is gone, and the book says it is declined.

tasks.prompt: Why is sakrān a diptote? Would an adjective like it that takes the tāʾ be one?
tasks.answer: Sakrān ends in an added alif and nūn and is an adjective that does not take the tāʾ (its feminine is not sakrāna). An adjective with added alif and nūn that does take the tāʾ does not meet the book's condition, so it is declined.

quiz.prompt: The munṣarif is what…
Mathnā, “two by two”, is a diptote…
quiz.explanation: With uḥād, thulāth, rubāʿ and the rest.

quiz.prompt: Yazīd is a diptote because it is a name…
options: beginning with a letter of the muḍāriʿ
quiz.explanation: And it does not take the tāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Ḥamza, a man's name, is…
options: fully declined: it is a man's name
a diptote: the tāʾ is in its wording
quiz.explanation: The tāʾ of the feminine in the word decides.

quiz.prompt: Hind may be…
quiz.explanation: Three letters, a sukūn in the middle.

quiz.prompt: Masājid is a diptote as…
A diptote takes the kasra when…
options: it is muḍāf or has the lām

text.original: وَالْمُرَادُ بِالْمُنْصَرِفِ مَا دَخَلَهُ الْجَرُّ وَالتَّنْوِينُ، نَحْوُ زَيْدٍ، وَبِغَيْرِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ اسْمٌ مُعْرَبٌ بِالْحَرَكَةِ لَا يَدْخُلُهُ الْجَرُّ وَالتَّنْوِينُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى نَوْعَيْنِ: سَمَاعِيٌّ، نَحْوُ أُحَادَ وَمَوْحَدَ وَثُنَاءَ وَمَثْنَى وَثُلَاثَ وَمَثْلَثَ وَرُبَاعَ وَمَرْبَعَ، وَأُخَرَ صِفَاتٍ، وَجُمَعَ وَكُتَعَ وَبُتَعَ وَبُصَعَ جُمُوعًا، وَعُمَرَ وَزُفَرَ وَزُحَلَ وَقُزَحَ أَعْلَامًا.
text.en: By the fully declined (munṣarif) is meant what jarr and tanwīn come upon, as Zaydin “Zayd”; and by the not fully declined, a noun given iʿrāb by vowels that jarr and tanwīn do not come upon. It is of two kinds. Known by hearing, as uḥāda and mawḥada “one by one”, thunāʾa and mathnā “two by two”, thulātha and mathlatha “three by three”, rubāʿa and marbaʿa “four by four”, and ukhara “others”, as adjectives; jumaʿa, kutaʿa, butaʿa and buṣaʿa “all together”, as plurals; and ʿUmara, Zufara, Zuḥala and Quzaḥa, as names.

text.original: وَقِيَاسِيٌّ، وَهُوَ كُلُّ عَلَمٍ عَلَى وَزْنٍ مَخْصُوصٍ بِالْفِعْلِ، كَضُرِبَ وَشَمَّرَ وَاجْتَمَعَ وَانْقَطَعَ وَاسْتَخْرَجَ، أَوْ فِي أَوَّلِهِ إِحْدَى زَوَائِدِ الْمُضَارِعِ غَيْرَ قَابِلٍ لِلتَّاءِ، نَحْوُ يَزِيدَ وَيَشْكُرَ، وَكُلُّ أَفْعَلِ التَّفْضِيلِ وَالصِّفَةِ، نَحْوُ أَفْضَلَ وَأَبْيَضَ، وَكُلُّ اسْمٍ أَعْجَمِيٍّ اسْتُعْمِلَ فِي أَوَّلِ نَقْلِهِ إِلَى الْعَرَبِ عَلَمًا، وَهُوَ زَائِدٌ عَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ أَوْ مُتَحَرِّكُ الْأَوْسَطِ، نَحْوُ قَالُونَ وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ وَشَتَرَ.
text.en: And by rule: every name on a pattern reserved for the verb, as ḍuriba, shammara, ijtamaʿa, inqaṭaʿa and istakhraja, or with one of the added letters of the muḍāriʿ at its beginning and not taking the tāʾ, as Yazīda and Yashkura; every afʿal of preference and of adjective, as afḍala “better” and abyaḍa “white”; and every foreign noun used as a name when it was first carried over to the Arabs, when it has more than three [letters] or a vowel on its middle [letter], as Qālūna, Ibrāhīma and Shatara.

text.original: وَكُلُّ مُؤَنَّثٍ بِالْأَلِفِ، مَقْصُورَةً أَوْ مَمْدُودَةً، نَحْوُ حُبْلَى وَحَمْرَاءَ، وَكُلُّ عَلَمٍ فِيهِ تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ لَفْظًا، نَحْوُ فَاطِمَةَ وَحَمْزَةَ، أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، وَهُوَ زَائِدٌ عَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ، نَحْوُ زَيْنَبَ، أَوْ مُتَحَرِّكُ الْأَوْسَطِ عَلَمًا لِمُؤَنَّثٍ، نَحْوُ قَدَمَ اسْمِ امْرَأَةٍ، وَلَوْ سُمِّيَ بِهِ مُذَكَّرٌ صُرِفَ، وَلَوْ كَانَ عَلَمُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ ثُلَاثِيًّا سَاكِنَ الْأَوْسَطِ يَجُوزُ صَرْفُهُ وَمَنْعُهُ، نَحْوُ هِنْدٍ.
text.en: Every feminine with an alif, short or long, as ḥublā “pregnant” and ḥamrāʾa “red”; every name with the tāʾ of the feminine, in the wording, as Fāṭimata and Ḥamzata, or understood, when it has more than three [letters], as Zaynaba, or has a vowel on its middle [letter], as the name of a female, as Qadama, the name of a woman; if a male is named by it, it is fully declined; and if the name of a female has three letters with a sukūn on the middle, it may be declined or not, as Hindin.

text.original: وَكُلُّ عَلَمٍ مُرَكَّبٍ مِنَ اسْمَيْنِ لَيْسَ أَحَدُهُمَا عَامِلًا فِي الْآخَرِ، وَالثَّانِي صَوْتًا مُتَضَمِّنًا لِمَعْنَى الْحَرْفِ، نَحْوُ بَعْلَبَكَّ وَحَضْرَمَوْتَ، وَكُلُّ مَا فِيهِ أَلِفٌ وَنُونٌ زَائِدَتَانِ، عَلَمًا أَوْ وَصْفًا لَا يَدْخُلُهُ التَّاءُ، نَحْوُ عِمْرَانَ وَسَكْرَانَ وَرَحْمَنَ، وَكُلُّ جَمْعٍ عَلَى وَزْنِ فَعَالِلَ أَوْ فَعَالِيلَ، نَحْوُ مَسَاجِدَ وَمَصَابِيحَ.
text.en: Every name compounded of two nouns, neither of which governs the other, and the second of which is not a sound containing the meaning of a particle, as Baʿlabakka and Ḥaḍramawta; everything with an added alif and nūn, as a name, or as an adjective that the tāʾ does not come upon, as ʿImrāna, sakrāna “drunk” and raḥmāna “merciful”; and every plural on the pattern faʿālil or faʿālīl, as masājida “mosques” and maṣābīḥa “lamps”.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ صَرْفُهُ لِضَرُورَةِ الشِّعْرِ أَوْ لِلتَّنَاسُبِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: سَلَاسِلًا، وَقَوَارِيرًا. وَكُلُّ مَا لَا يَنْصَرِفُ إِذَا أُضِيفَ إِلَى شَيْءٍ، أَوْ دَخَلَهُ لَامُ التَّعْرِيفِ، انْصَرَفَ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِالْأَحْمَرِ، أَوْ أَحْمَرِنَا.
text.en: It may be fully declined for the necessity of verse or for matching [the words around it], as His saying, Most High: salāsilan “chains” [76:4] and qawārīran “glass vessels” [76:15]. Everything not fully declined becomes fully declined when it is made muḍāf to something or the lām of definiteness comes upon it, as marartu bi-al-aḥmari “I passed by the red one” or aḥmarinā “our red one”.

parts.title: The kinds and the quality of iʿrāb

lessons.title: Iʿrāb by kind and by quality; the understood iʿrāb begins
body: The third division is by kind, and the kinds are four: rafʿ and naṣb, shared by the noun and the verb; jarr, for the noun alone; and jazm, for the verb alone. Then each kind is given its signs, gathered from the last two lessons: rafʿ has four, naṣb five, jarr three and jazm three. The same sign may serve two kinds: the kasra is the sign of jarr, and of naṣb in the sound feminine plural; the fatḥa is the sign of naṣb, and of jarr in the diptote; the yāʾ serves both naṣb and jarr.

The fourth division is by quality, and it is three: verbal (lafẓī), “which appears in the wording”; understood (taqdīrī); and of place (maḥallī). Birgivī defines only the last two, “so that it is known that everything other than them is verbal”. This is the part of the book a student uses most when he parses: before he says that a word is in rafʿ, he must say whether the rafʿ is seen, understood, or only in its place.

The understood iʿrāb “does not appear in the wording, but is understood at the end because of something there that prevents it, other than real iʿrāb”. It is found only in a muʿrab word, as the verbal is; a mabnī word has no iʿrāb to understand. It is in seven places. The first: a singular word ending in alif, even when the alif is dropped because two sukūns meet, as in ʿaṣan. If it is a noun, all three states are understood, al-ʿaṣā, ʿaṣan; if a verb, its rafʿ and naṣb are understood and its jazm is verbal, yakhshā, lan yakhshā, lam yakhsha. The commentators give the reason: an alif cannot carry any vowel.

The second: a word made muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker, except the dual. In a sound masculine plural only the rafʿ is understood: jāʾanī muslimiyya, “whose origin is muslimūya”: the wāw of rafʿ became a yāʾ and merged with the pronoun; in naṣb and jarr the yāʾ of iʿrāb is there to be seen. In anything else, all three states are understood: jāʾanī ghulāmī wa-rijālī wa-muslimātī, since the yāʾ needs a kasra before it, and that kasra takes the place of every sign.

terms.en: verbal iʿrāb, which appears in the wording
understood iʿrāb, prevented from showing at the end
iʿrāb of place, given to the place a word fills
the yāʾ of the speaker, “my”

examples.en: a noun ending in alif: all three states understood
a verb ending in alif: its jazm verbal
a sound plural with the yāʾ of the speaker: the rafʿ understood
with the yāʾ of the speaker: all understood

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of iʿrāb shown by each sign, and the word that takes it that way: the kasra of muslimātin after raʾaytu; the fatḥa of Aḥmada after bi-; the alif of muslimāni.
tasks.answer: The kasra of raʾaytu muslimātin is naṣb, in the sound feminine plural. The fatḥa of marartu bi-Aḥmada is jarr, in the diptote. The alif of muslimāni is rafʿ, in the dual.

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of al-ʿaṣā in raʾaytu al-ʿaṣā, and of yakhshā in lan yakhshā.
tasks.answer: Al-ʿaṣā is the object, in naṣb by an understood fatḥa on the alif, which cannot carry a vowel. Yakhshā after lan is in naṣb by an understood fatḥa, for the same reason.

tasks.prompt: Why is lam yakhsha's jazm verbal, while its rafʿ is understood?
tasks.answer: In rafʿ and naṣb the sign would be a vowel on the alif, which cannot show. Jazm in a weak-ended verb is the dropping of the last letter, and the alif is in fact dropped: lam yakhsha. So the jazm appears in the wording.

tasks.prompt: In which state is the iʿrāb of muslimiyya understood, and in which does it show?
tasks.answer: In rafʿ it is understood: the origin is muslimūya, and the wāw of rafʿ has become a yāʾ merged with the pronoun. In naṣb and jarr it shows, since the yāʾ of iʿrāb is there in the wording.

quiz.prompt: Jarr belongs to…
quiz.explanation: And jazm to the verb only.

quiz.prompt: How many signs has naṣb?
quiz.explanation: Fatḥa, kasra, alif, yāʾ, dropping the nūn.

quiz.prompt: The fatḥa is a sign of jarr in…
Understood iʿrāb is found…
In al-ʿaṣā, which states are understood?
In lam yakhsha, the jazm is…
Jāʾanī ghulāmī: the rafʿ of ghulāmī is…
quiz.explanation: With the yāʾ of the speaker, all three states are understood.

text.original: وَالتَّقْسِيمُ الثَّالِثُ بِحَسَبِ النَّوْعِ، فَهُوَ أَرْبَعَةٌ: رَفْعٌ وَنَصْبٌ مُشْتَرَكَانِ بَيْنَ الِاسْمِ وَالْفِعْلِ، وَجَرٌّ مُخْتَصٌّ بِالِاسْمِ، وَجَزْمٌ مُخْتَصٌّ بِالْفِعْلِ. وَعَلَامَةُ الرَّفْعِ أَرْبَعَةٌ: ضَمَّةٌ، وَوَاوٌ، وَأَلِفٌ، وَنُونٌ. وَعَلَامَةُ النَّصْبِ خَمْسَةٌ: فَتْحَةٌ، وَكَسْرَةٌ، وَأَلِفٌ، وَيَاءٌ، وَحَذْفُ النُّونِ. وَعَلَامَةُ الْجَرِّ ثَلَاثَةٌ: كَسْرَةٌ، وَفَتْحَةٌ، وَيَاءٌ. وَعَلَامَةُ الْجَزْمِ ثَلَاثَةٌ: حَذْفُ الْحَرَكَةِ، وَحَذْفُ الْآخِرِ، وَحَذْفُ النُّونِ.
text.en: The third division is by kind, and it is four: rafʿ and naṣb, shared between the noun and the verb; jarr, reserved for the noun; and jazm, reserved for the verb. The signs of rafʿ are four: ḍamma, wāw, alif and nūn. The signs of naṣb are five: fatḥa, kasra, alif, yāʾ and dropping the nūn. The signs of jarr are three: kasra, fatḥa and yāʾ. The signs of jazm are three: dropping the vowel, dropping the last [letter] and dropping the nūn.

text.original: وَالتَّقْسِيمُ الرَّابِعُ بِحَسَبِ الصِّفَةِ، فَهُوَ ثَلَاثَةٌ: لَفْظِيٌّ يَظْهَرُ فِي اللَّفْظِ، وَتَقْدِيرِيٌّ، وَمَحَلِّيٌّ؛ فَلْنَذْكُرِ الْأَخِيرَيْنِ حَتَّى يُعْلَمَ أَنَّ مَا عَدَاهُمَا لَفْظِيٌّ.
text.en: The fourth division is by quality, and it is three: verbal (lafẓī), which appears in the wording; understood (taqdīrī); and of place (maḥallī). So let us mention the last two, so that it is known that everything other than them is verbal.

text.original: فَالتَّقْدِيرِيُّ مَا لَا يَظْهَرُ فِي اللَّفْظِ، بَلْ يُقَدَّرُ فِي آخِرِهِ لِمَانِعٍ فِيهِ غَيْرِ الْإِعْرَابِ الْحَقِيقِيِّ، وَلَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا فِي الْمُعْرَبِ كَاللَّفْظِيِّ، وَذَلِكَ فِي سَبْعَةِ مَوَاضِعَ: الْأَوَّلُ مُفْرَدٌ آخِرُهُ أَلِفٌ وَإِنْ حُذِفَ لِالْتِقَاءِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ اسْمًا فَإِعْرَابُهُ فِي الْأَحْوَالِ الثَّلَاثِ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: الْعَصَا وَعَصًا، وَإِنْ كَانَ فِعْلًا فَرَفْعُهُ وَنَصْبُهُ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ وَجَزْمُهُ لَفْظِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: يَخْشَى، وَلَنْ يَخْشَى، وَلَمْ يَخْشَ.
text.en: The understood is that which does not appear in the wording, but is understood at the end [of the word] because of something there that prevents it, other than real iʿrāb. Like the verbal, it is only in what has iʿrāb, and that is in seven places. The first is a singular whose end is an alif, even if it is dropped because two sukūns meet. If it is a noun, its iʿrāb in all three cases is understood, as al-ʿaṣā and ʿaṣan “a stick”; and if it is a verb, its rafʿ and naṣb are understood and its jazm is verbal, as yakhshā “he fears”, lan yakhshā “he will not fear” and lam yakhsha “he did not fear”.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي مَا أُضِيفَ إِلَى يَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ غَيْرَ التَّثْنِيَةِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ جَمْعَ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ فَرَفْعُهُ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ فَقَطْ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمِيَّ، أَصْلُهُ مُسْلِمُويَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ غَيْرَهُ فَالْكُلُّ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي غُلَامِي وَرِجَالِي وَمُسْلِمَاتِي.
text.en: The second is what is made muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker, other than the dual. If it is a sound masculine plural, only its rafʿ is understood, as jāʾanī muslimiyya “my Muslims came to me”, whose origin is muslimūya; and if it is something else, all [three] are understood, as jāʾanī ghulāmī wa-rijālī wa-muslimātī “my servant, my men and my Muslim women came to me”.

lessons.title: Understood iʿrāb: the reported word; the ends in yāʾ and wāw
body: The third place of understood iʿrāb is a word whose end carries a reported (maḥkī) iʿrāb: its last letter is already taken up by the vowel it had in the words it was taken from, so the vowel the governor brings cannot show. It may be a sentence turned into a name, as Taʾabbaṭa Sharran, “he carried evil under his arm”, the nickname of a poet: one says jāʾa Taʾabbaṭa Sharran and raʾaytu Taʾabbaṭa Sharran without change.

Or it may be a single word repeated after the speaker, “in the speech of the Ḥijāzī”. When someone says ḍarabtu Zaydan, he answers man Zaydan, “who is Zayd?”, keeping the naṣb he heard, though Zayd there is a khabar. Told a-laka tamratāni, “have you two dates?”, he says daʿnī ʿan tamratāni, “spare me your ‘two dates’”, keeping the alif after ʿan, which gives jarr.

So too a compound name whose second part is governed by a word with no iʿrāb, as men named In Zaydun, Hal Zaydun or Man Zaydun: the whole is reported. ʿAbd Allāh and Maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu are different: their first part takes verbal iʿrāb from the governor, jāʾa ʿAbdu Allāhi, raʾaytu ʿAbda Allāhi, and only the second is taken up with its own iʿrāb. And a reported binā, as khamsata ʿashara used as a name, “according to the better-known view”, stays as it is in every state.

The fourth place is a word ending in a yāʾ after a kasra, even when the yāʾ is dropped because two sukūns meet, as in qāḍin. In a noun the rafʿ and the jarr are understood, al-qāḍī, qāḍin, and the naṣb shows on the yāʾ. In a verb with no marfūʿ pronoun at its end only the rafʿ is understood: yarmī, tarmī, armī, narmī. The fifth place is a verb ending in a wāw after a ḍamma, with the same rule: yaghzū, taghzū, aghzū, naghzū; its naṣb and jazm show (lesson 45). The commentators give the reason for both: a ḍamma or a kasra is heavy on a yāʾ or a wāw, while the light fatḥa can be spoken.

reporting a word or sentence with its own vowels
a compound name

tasks.prompt: Why does Taʾabbaṭa Sharran not change in jāʾa Taʾabbaṭa Sharran and raʾaytu Taʾabbaṭa Sharran?
tasks.answer: It is a sentence turned into a name, and it is reported: its last letter keeps the vowel it had in the sentence. The rafʿ of the fāʿil and the naṣb of the object are understood, not shown.

tasks.prompt: Explain the naṣb of Zaydan in man Zaydan, said in answer to ḍarabtu Zaydan.
tasks.answer: Man is the mubtadaʾ and Zaydan its khabar, which should be in rafʿ. But the Ḥijāzī reports the word as he heard it, in naṣb; its rafʿ is understood, prevented by the reported iʿrāb.

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of al-qāḍī in jāʾa al-qāḍī and in marartu bi-l-qāḍī.
tasks.answer: In jāʾa al-qāḍī it is the fāʿil, in rafʿ by an understood ḍamma on the yāʾ. In marartu bi-l-qāḍī it is in jarr by an understood kasra on the yāʾ. Both vowels are heavy on the yāʾ, so they are not spoken.

tasks.prompt: How do ʿAbd Allāh and a man named Man Zaydun differ in their iʿrāb?
tasks.answer: In ʿAbd Allāh the first part takes verbal iʿrāb from the governor: jāʾa ʿAbdu Allāhi, raʾaytu ʿAbda Allāhi. In Man Zaydun the first part, man, has no iʿrāb, and the whole name is reported, so its iʿrāb is understood in every state.

quiz.prompt: A reported (maḥkī) iʿrāb is one where the word's end…
options: keeps the vowel it had where it was taken from
quiz.explanation: So the governor's vowel cannot show.

quiz.prompt: Taʾabbaṭa Sharran is…
options: a sentence turned into a name
quiz.explanation: Its iʿrāb is understood in all three states.

quiz.prompt: Man Zaydan, after ḍarabtu Zaydan, is the way of…
In ʿAbd Allāh, the first part takes…
quiz.explanation: Jāʾa ʿAbdu Allāhi, raʾaytu ʿAbda Allāhi.

quiz.prompt: In a noun ending in yāʾ after kasra, which state shows?
quiz.explanation: The light fatḥa can be spoken on the yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: In yaghzū, what is understood?
quiz.explanation: Lan yaghzuwa and lam yaghzu show.

quiz.prompt: The commentators' reason for understanding the ḍamma on yarmī is…
options: the impossibility of any vowel on a yāʾ
quiz.explanation: The alif cannot carry a vowel at all; the yāʾ and wāw only find the ḍamma and kasra heavy.

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ مَا فِي آخِرِهِ إِعْرَابٌ مَحْكِيٌّ، إِمَّا جُمْلَةً مَنْقُولَةً إِلَى الْعَلَمِيَّةِ، نَحْوُ: تَأَبَّطَ شَرًّا، أَوْ مُفْرَدًا فِي قَوْلِ الْحِجَازِيِّ، نَحْوُ: مَنْ زَيْدًا، لِمَنْ قَالَ: ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا، وَدَعْنِي عَنْ تَمْرَتَانِ، لِمَنْ قَالَ: أَلَكَ تَمْرَتَانِ.
text.en: The third is that at whose end there is a reported (maḥkī) iʿrāb: either a sentence carried over to be a name, as Taʾabbaṭa Sharran “Taʾabbaṭa Sharran [he carried evil under his arm]”; or a single word, in the speech of the Ḥijāzī, as man Zaydan “who is Zayd?”, said to one who said ḍarabtu Zaydan “I hit Zayd”, and daʿnī ʿan tamratāni “spare me your ‘two dates’”, said to one who said a-laka tamratāni “do you have two dates?”.

text.original: وَكَذَا كُلُّ عَلَمٍ مُرَكَّبٍ جُزْؤُهُ الثَّانِي مَعْمُولٌ لِمَا لَا إِعْرَابَ لَهُ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ زَيْدٌ، وَهَلْ زَيْدٌ، وَمَنْ زَيْدٌ، بِخِلَافِ نَحْوِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ وَمَضْرُوبٍ غُلَامُهُ؛ فَإِنَّ إِعْرَابَ الْجُزْءِ الْأَوَّلِ مِنْهُمَا لَفْظِيٌّ بِحَسَبِ الْعَامِلِ، وَالثَّانِي مَشْغُولٌ بِإِعْرَابِ الْحِكَايَةِ، أَوْ بِنَاءٌ مَحْكِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ عَلَمًا، عَلَى الْأَشْهَرِ.
text.en: So too every compound name whose second part is governed by what has no iʿrāb, as in Zaydun, hal Zaydun and man Zaydun [as names]; unlike ʿAbdi Allāhi “ʿAbd Allāh” and maḍrūbin ghulāmuhu “[one named] Maḍrūbun Ghulāmuhu”, for the iʿrāb of the first part of these is verbal, according to the governor, and the second is taken up with the iʿrāb of reporting. Or [at its end there is] a reported binā, as khamsata ʿashara “fifteen” as a name, according to the better-known [view].

text.original: وَالرَّابِعُ مَا فِي آخِرِهِ يَاءٌ مَكْسُورٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَإِنْ حُذِفَ لِالْتِقَاءِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ اسْمًا فَرَفْعُهُ وَجَرُّهُ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: الْقَاضِي وَقَاضٍ، وَإِنْ كَانَ فِعْلًا فَرَفْعُهُ فَقَطْ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ إِنْ لَمْ يَلْحَقْ بِآخِرِهِ ضَمِيرٌ مَرْفُوعٌ، نَحْوُ: يَرْمِي وَتَرْمِي وَأَرْمِي وَنَرْمِي. وَالْخَامِسُ فِعْلٌ آخِرُهُ وَاوٌ مَضْمُومٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا، فَرَفْعُهُ فَقَطْ أَيْضًا تَقْدِيرِيٌّ إِنْ لَمْ يَلْحَقْ بِآخِرِهِ ضَمِيرٌ، نَحْوُ: يَغْزُو وَتَغْزُو وَأَغْزُو وَنَغْزُو.
text.en: The fourth is that at whose end there is a yāʾ with a kasra before it, even if it is dropped because two sukūns meet. If it is a noun, its rafʿ and jarr are understood, as al-qāḍī and qāḍin “a judge”; and if it is a verb, only its rafʿ is understood, if no marfūʿ pronoun is joined to its end, as yarmī, tarmī, armī and narmī “he, you, I, we throw”. The fifth is a verb whose end is a wāw with a ḍamma before it: only its rafʿ too is understood, if no pronoun is joined to its end, as yaghzū, taghzū, aghzū and naghzū “he, you, I, we raid”.

lessons.title: Understood iʿrāb before a sukūn and in pause; iʿrāb of place
body: The sixth place is a noun whose iʿrāb is by letters, when a sukūn meets it, that is, when the next word begins with a hamza of joining. With the six nouns all three states are then understood: Abū al-Qāsimi, Abā al-Qāsimi, Abī al-Qāsimi are spoken abu l-qāsim, aba l-qāsim, abi l-qāsim, the long letter shortened before the sukūn, so the wāw, alif and yāʾ of iʿrāb are written but not heard.

In the sound masculine plural it depends on the letter before the sign. If that letter has a fatḥa, as in muṣṭafawna and muṣṭafayna, the wāw is given a ḍamma and the yāʾ a kasra, and the iʿrāb is heard in all three states: muṣṭafawu al-qawmi, muṣṭafayi al-qawmi. If not, the wāw and yāʾ fall away in speech and the iʿrāb is understood: ḍāribū al-qawmi, ḍāribī al-qawmi. In the dual the rafʿ is understood, ghulāmā ibnika, but the yāʾ of naṣb and jarr takes a kasra and is heard: ghulāmayi ibnika.

The seventh place is the word paused on with a sukūn, when its iʿrāb is by vowels. If it has no tanwīn of full declension, or ends in the tāʾ of the feminine, all three states are understood in pause: Aḥmad, ḍāribah, ḍāribāt. If it has that tanwīn, its rafʿ and jarr are understood, “but not its naṣb”, as Zayd: in naṣb one pauses on an alif, Zaydā, which shows the case.

The iʿrāb of place (maḥallī) is in two places. The first is a muʿrab noun whose end is taken up with another iʿrāb, not a reported one: in marartu bi-Zaydin, Zayd is in jarr in its wording and in naṣb in its place, as an object (lesson 33); in aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin it is in rafʿ in its place as the fāʿil of the maṣdar; in murra bi-Zaydin in rafʿ in its place as the deputy (lesson 27).

The second place is the built word (mabnī), “that whose vowel and sukūn are not by a governor”, while the muʿrab is “that whose vowel and sukūn are by a governor”. The mabnī never changes, so whatever iʿrāb it has is only in its place. The last three lessons are on it.

terms.en: the hamza of joining, dropped in connected speech
pausing on a word with a sukūn
the tanwīn of the fully declined noun
the built word, whose end is not set by a governor

examples.en: the six nouns before a sukūn: understood
a fatḥa before the wāw: the wāw takes ḍamma, the iʿrāb heard
no fatḥa before it: the wāw falls in speech, the iʿrāb understood
the dual in naṣb: the yāʾ takes kasra, heard

tasks.prompt: Is the iʿrāb heard or understood? jāʾanī Abū al-Qāsimi; raʾaytu ghulāmayi ibnika; jāʾanī ḍāribū al-qawmi.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ — رَأَيْتُ غُلَامَيِ ابْنِكَ — جَاءَنِي ضَارِبُو الْقَوْمِ
tasks.answer: Abū al-Qāsimi: understood, the wāw is shortened before the sukūn. Ghulāmayi ibnika: heard, the yāʾ of naṣb takes a kasra. Ḍāribū al-qawmi: understood, the wāw falls in speech, since the letter before it has no fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Why is the iʿrāb of muṣṭafawu al-qawmi heard, but that of ḍāribū al-qawmi not?
tasks.answer: In muṣṭafawna the letter before the wāw has a fatḥa, so before the sukūn the wāw is given a ḍamma and is spoken. In ḍāribūna the letter before it has a ḍamma, so the wāw falls away in speech and the iʿrāb is only understood.

tasks.prompt: Pause on Zaydun, Zaydan and Zaydin, and say where the iʿrāb is understood.
tasks.answer: Zayd, Zaydā, Zayd. In rafʿ and jarr the pause is on a sukūn, and the iʿrāb is understood. In naṣb one pauses on an alif, so the naṣb still shows.

tasks.prompt: Give both the verbal and the place iʿrāb of Zayd in marartu bi-Zaydin and in murra bi-Zaydin.
tasks.answer: In both, Zayd is in jarr in its wording, by the bāʾ. In marartu bi-Zaydin it is in naṣb in its place, as the object of the intransitive verb reached through the bāʾ. In murra bi-Zaydin it is in rafʿ in its place, as the deputy of the fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾanī Abū al-Qāsimi, the iʿrāb of Abū is…
quiz.explanation: The wāw is shortened before the sukūn.

quiz.prompt: Muṣṭafawu al-qawmi has its iʿrāb heard because…
options: a fatḥa comes before the wāw
quiz.explanation: The wāw is given a ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: In the dual before a sukūn, which state is understood?
quiz.explanation: Ghulāmā ibnika; but ghulāmayi ibnika is heard.

quiz.prompt: Paused on, Aḥmad has…
Paused on, which state of Zayd still shows?
quiz.explanation: One pauses Zaydā, on an alif.

quiz.prompt: In aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin, Zayd is in rafʿ in its place as…
quiz.explanation: Its end is taken up by the jarr of the iḍāfa.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسُ اسْمٌ إِعْرَابُهُ بِالْحُرُوفِ مُلَاقٍ لِسَاكِنٍ بَعْدَهُ، أَيْ كَلِمَةٍ فِي أَوَّلِهَا هَمْزَةُ وَصْلٍ؛ وَإِنْ كَانَ مِنَ الْأَسْمَاءِ السِّتَّةِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ فَإِعْرَابُهُ فِي الْأَحْوَالِ الثَّلَاثِ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ، وَرَأَيْتُ أَبَا الْقَاسِمِ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِأَبِي الْقَاسِمِ.
text.en: The sixth is a noun whose iʿrāb is by letters, meeting a sukūn after it, that is, a word that begins with a hamza of joining. If it is one of the six nouns mentioned, its iʿrāb in all three cases is understood, as jāʾanī Abū al-Qāsimi “Abū al-Qāsim came to me”, raʾaytu Abā al-Qāsimi “I saw Abū al-Qāsim” and marartu bi-Abī al-Qāsimi “I passed by Abū al-Qāsim”.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ جَمْعَ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ مَا قَبْلَ حَرْفِ الْإِعْرَابِ مَفْتُوحًا، نَحْوُ: مُصْطَفَوْنَ وَمُصْطَفَيْنَ، فَتُحَرَّكُ الْوَاوُ بِالضَّمَّةِ وَالْيَاءُ بِالْكَسْرَةِ، فَيَكُونُ لَفْظِيًّا فِي الْأَحْوَالِ الثَّلَاثِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي مُصْطَفَوُ الْقَوْمِ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُصْطَفَيِ الْقَوْمِ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُصْطَفَيِ الْقَوْمِ؛ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَفْتُوحًا يُحْذَفَانِ، فَيَكُونُ تَقْدِيرِيًّا فِي الْأَحْوَالِ الثَّلَاثِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي ضَارِبُو الْقَوْمِ، وَرَأَيْتُ ضَارِبِي الْقَوْمِ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِضَارِبِي الْقَوْمِ.
text.en: If it is a sound masculine plural, then if the letter before the letter of iʿrāb has a fatḥa, as muṣṭafawna and muṣṭafayna “chosen ones”, the wāw is given a ḍamma and the yāʾ a kasra, and it is verbal in all three cases, as jāʾanī muṣṭafawu al-qawmi “the chosen ones of the people came to me”, raʾaytu muṣṭafayi al-qawmi and marartu bi-muṣṭafayi al-qawmi; and if it does not have a fatḥa, they are dropped, and it is understood in all three cases, as jāʾanī ḍāribū al-qawmi “those hitting the people came to me”, raʾaytu ḍāribī al-qawmi and marartu bi-ḍāribī al-qawmi.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ تَثْنِيَةً فَرَفْعُهُ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ، وَفِي نَصْبِهِ وَجَرِّهِ تُحَرَّكُ الْيَاءُ بِالْكَسْرِ، فَيَكُونُ لَفْظِيًّا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي غُلَامَا ابْنِكَ، وَرَأَيْتُ غُلَامَيِ ابْنِكَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِغُلَامَيِ ابْنِكَ. وَالسَّابِعُ الْمَوْقُوفُ عَلَيْهِ بِالْإِسْكَانِ مِمَّا كَانَ إِعْرَابُهُ بِالْحَرَكَةِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ غَيْرَ مُنَوَّنٍ بِتَنْوِينِ التَّمَكُّنِ، أَوْ كَانَ فِي آخِرِهِ تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ، فَأَحْوَالُهُ الثَّلَاثُ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: أَحْمَدْ، وَضَارِبَةْ، وَضَارِبَاتْ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مُنَوَّنًا بِغَيْرِهَا فَرَفْعُهُ وَجَرُّهُ تَقْدِيرِيٌّ دُونَ نَصْبِهِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدْ.
text.en: If it is a dual, its rafʿ is understood, and in its naṣb and jarr the yāʾ is given a kasra, and it is verbal, as jāʾanī ghulāmā ibnika “your son's two servants came to me”, raʾaytu ghulāmayi ibnika and marartu bi-ghulāmayi ibnika. The seventh is what is paused on with a sukūn, of what has its iʿrāb by vowels. If it has no tanwīn of full declension, or has the tāʾ of the feminine at its end, all three of its cases are understood, as Aḥmad, ḍāribah and ḍāribāt; and if it has such tanwīn, its rafʿ and jarr are understood, but not its naṣb, as Zayd.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَحَلِّيُّ فَفِي مَوْضِعَيْنِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الِاسْمُ الْمُعْرَبُ الْمُشْتَغِلُ آخِرُهُ بِإِعْرَابٍ غَيْرِ مَحْكِيٍّ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ، فَإِنَّهُ يُحْكَمُ عَلَى مَحَلِّ زَيْدٍ بِالنَّصْبِ عَلَى الْمَفْعُولِيَّةِ، وَكَذَا: أَعْجَبَنِي ضَرْبُ زَيْدٍ، وَمُرَّ بِزَيْدٍ، فَزَيْدٌ مَرْفُوعُ الْمَحَلِّ عَلَى الْفَاعِلِيَّةِ فِي الْأَوَّلِ، وَالنَّائِبِيَّةِ فِي الثَّانِي. وَالثَّانِي الْمَبْنِيُّ، وَهُوَ مَا كَانَ حَرَكَتُهُ وَسُكُونُهُ لَا بِعَامِلٍ، بِخِلَافِ الْمُعْرَبِ، فَهُوَ مَا كَانَ حَرَكَتُهُ وَسُكُونُهُ بِعَامِلٍ.
text.en: As for that of place, it is in two places. One of them is the noun with iʿrāb whose end is taken up with an iʿrāb that is not reported, as marartu bi-Zaydin “I passed by Zayd”, for the place of Zayd is judged to be in naṣb as an object; and likewise aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin “Zayd's hitting pleased me” and murra bi-Zaydin “Zayd was passed by”, for Zayd is marfūʿ in its place, as fāʿil in the first and as deputy in the second. The second is the built word (mabnī), which is that whose vowel and sukūn are not by a governor, unlike the muʿrab, which is that whose vowel and sukūn are by a governor.

lessons.title: The mabnī: built in origin and built by what comes upon it; the compounds
body: The mabnī is of two kinds. Some words are built in origin (mabnī al-aṣl): the particle, the past verb, the imperative without the lām for the Baṣrans (lesson 24), and the sentence. Nothing made them built; that is what they are. Others are nouns, whose origin is iʿrāb, built because of something that has come upon them (mabnī al-ʿāriḍ); the grammarians' usual reason is that such a noun has come to resemble a particle. The second kind is again of two: those whose binā is necessary and never leaves them (lāzim), and those built only in some uses.

Never free of binā are: the pronouns, the demonstratives and the relatives (lessons 40–41), except ayyun and ayyatun, “which have iʿrāb”; the nouns of verbs (lesson 22); words on the pattern faʿāli, as a maṣdar, fajāri, “wickedness”, as an adjective in calling, yā fasāqi, “O wicked woman!”, or as a woman's name, Ḥadhāmi, “among the people of the Ḥijāz”, while others decline it as a diptote; and the sounds: words that imitate a sound, ghāqi, the crow's caw, or call to beasts, nakh, said to make a camel kneel.

Built too are some compounds: two words, neither governing the other, made one noun. If the second is a sound, both are built, the first on fatḥa and the second on kasra: Sībawayhi. If not, the first part is built, on fatḥa if it ends in a sound letter, Baʿlabakka, Ḥaḍramawta, on sukūn if it ends in a weak one, Maʿdī Kariba; and the second part takes the iʿrāb of a diptote (lesson 46): jāʾa Baʿlabakku, raʾaytu Baʿlabakka, marartu bi-Baʿlabakka.

If the two are not made one noun, but the second contains a particle, as the numbers from eleven to nineteen contain the wāw (aḥada ʿashara is “one and ten”), both parts are built on fatḥa, or the first on sukūn if it ends in a weak letter: aḥada ʿashara, iḥdā ʿashrata, thalāthata ʿashara, thalātha ʿashrata, ḥādiya ʿashara … tāsiʿata ʿashrata. So too huwa jārī bayta bayta, “he is my neighbour, house to house”, and bayna bayna, “in between”.

The one exception is twelve. When the first part is ithnā, only the second is built; the first takes the iʿrāb of the dual and drops its nūn: jāʾanī ithnā ʿashara rajulan, raʾaytu ithnay ʿashara rajulan, marartu bi-ithnay ʿashara rajulan. A student who has learned the dual in lesson 45 can see why: ithnā behaves like a dual muḍāf.

terms.en: built in origin: the particle, the past, the imperative, the sentence
a noun built by something that comes upon it
the sounds: words that imitate a sound or call beasts
a compound of two words made one

examples.en: the pattern faʿāli as an adjective in calling: built
a compound whose second part is a sound: both built
the first part built on fatḥa, the second a diptote
two words with a particle understood between them: both built

examples.arabic: جَاءَنِي اثْنَا عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَرَأَيْتُ اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا
examples.en: twelve: the first part with iʿrāb, the second built

tasks.prompt: Built in origin, or built by what came upon it? qad; ḍaraba; hādhā; alladhī; iḍrib.
tasks.answer: Built in origin: qad (a particle), ḍaraba (a past verb), iḍrib (the imperative without the lām, for the Baṣrans). Built by what came upon them, necessarily: hādhā (a demonstrative) and alladhī (a relative), nouns whose origin is iʿrāb.

tasks.prompt: Which relatives have iʿrāb, according to the book?
tasks.answer: Ayyun and ayyatun. All the other relatives are built.

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of Baʿlabakk as fāʿil, object and after bi-, and explain.
tasks.answer: Jāʾa Baʿlabakku, raʾaytu Baʿlabakka, marartu bi-Baʿlabakka. The first part, baʿla, is built on fatḥa because it ends in a sound letter; the second part takes the iʿrāb of a diptote: ḍamma in rafʿ, fatḥa in naṣb and in jarr.

tasks.prompt: Why is the first part of twelve not built, while that of thirteen is?
tasks.answer: With every other number from eleven to nineteen both parts are built on fatḥa, as the second contains the wāw. With ithnā the book makes an exception: the first part takes the iʿrāb of the dual (ithnā in rafʿ, ithnay in naṣb and jarr) and drops its nūn; only ʿashara is built.

quiz.explanation: The pronoun is a noun built by what came upon it.

quiz.explanation: The second is a sound; the first is built on fatḥa.

quiz.explanation: It ends in a weak letter.

text.original: وَالْمَبْنِيُّ عَلَى نَوْعَيْنِ: مَبْنِيُّ الْأَصْلِ، وَمَبْنِيُّ الْعَارِضِ. وَالْأَوَّلُ أَرْبَعَةٌ: الْحَرْفُ، وَالْمَاضِي، وَالْأَمْرُ بِغَيْرِ اللَّامِ عِنْدَ الْبَصْرِيِّينَ، وَالْجُمْلَةُ. وَالثَّانِي أَيْضًا عَلَى نَوْعَيْنِ: لَازِمٌ وَغَيْرُ لَازِمٍ.
text.en: The mabnī is of two kinds: built in origin, and built by something that comes upon it. The first is four: the particle, the past [verb], the imperative without the lām according to the Baṣrans, and the sentence. The second too is of two kinds: necessary and not necessary.

text.original: وَاللَّازِمُ مَا لَا يَنْفَكُّ عَنِ الْبِنَاءِ، وَهُوَ الْمُضْمَرَاتُ، وَأَسْمَاءُ الْإِشَارَاتِ، وَالْمَوْصُولَاتُ غَيْرَ أَيٍّ وَأَيَّةٍ، فَإِنَّهُمَا مُعْرَبَانِ، وَأَسْمَاءُ الْأَفْعَالِ، وَقَدْ سَبَقَتْ، وَمَا كَانَ عَلَى فَعَالِ: مَصْدَرًا، كَفَجَارِ، أَوْ صِفَةً، نَحْوُ: يَا فَسَاقِ، أَوْ عَلَمًا لِلْمُؤَنَّثِ، نَحْوُ: حَذَامِ عِنْدَ أَهْلِ الْحِجَازِ، وَالْأَصْوَاتُ، وَهُوَ كُلُّ لَفْظٍ حُكِيَ بِهِ صَوْتٌ، كَغَاقِ، أَوْ صُوِّتَ بِهِ لِلْبَهَائِمِ، كَنَخْ.
text.en: The necessary is that which is never free of binā: the pronouns; the demonstratives; the relatives, except ayyin and ayyatin, which have iʿrāb; the verb-nouns, which have gone before; what is on the pattern faʿāli, as a maṣdar, as fajāri “wickedness”, or as an adjective, as yā fasāqi “O wicked woman!”, or as the name of a female, as Ḥadhāmi “Ḥadhām”, among the people of the Ḥijāz; and the sounds, which are every word by which a sound is imitated, as ghāqi “caw”, or by which beasts are called, as nakh [said to make a camel kneel].

text.original: وَبَعْضُ الْمُرَكَّبَاتِ، وَهُوَ كُلُّ كَلِمَتَيْنِ لَيْسَ إِحْدَاهُمَا عَامِلَةً فِي الْأُخْرَى جُعِلَتَا اسْمًا وَاحِدًا؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ الثَّانِي صَوْتًا بُنِيَا، وَكُسِرَ الثَّانِي وَفُتِحَ الْأَوَّلُ، نَحْوُ سِيبَوَيْهِ، وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ صَوْتًا بُنِيَ الْأَوَّلُ عَلَى الْفَتْحِ إِنْ كَانَ آخِرُهُ حَرْفًا صَحِيحًا، نَحْوُ بَعْلَبَكَّ وَحَضْرَمَوْتَ، وَعَلَى السُّكُونِ إِنْ كَانَ آخِرُهُ حَرْفَ عِلَّةٍ، نَحْوُ مَعْدِي كَرِبَ، وَأُعْرِبَ الثَّانِي غَيْرَ مُنْصَرِفٍ عَلَى اللُّغَةِ الْفَصِيحَةِ.
text.en: And some compounds, which are every two words, neither of which governs the other, made into one noun. If the second is a sound, both are built, the second with a kasra and the first with a fatḥa, as Sībawayhi “Sībawayh”. If it is not a sound, the first is built on the fatḥa if its end is a sound letter, as Baʿlabakka and Ḥaḍramawta, and on the sukūn if its end is a weak letter, as Maʿdī Kariba “Maʿdī Karib”; and the second has the iʿrāb of what is not fully declined, in the eloquent dialect.

text.original: وَإِنْ لَمْ يُجْعَلَا اسْمًا وَاحِدًا وَلَكِنْ تَضَمَّنَ الثَّانِي حَرْفًا؛ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنِ الْأَوَّلُ لَفْظَ اثْنَيْنِ بُنِيَا عَلَى الْفَتْحِ إِنْ كَانَ آخِرُهُمَا حَرْفًا صَحِيحًا، وَعَلَى السُّكُونِ إِنْ كَانَ حَرْفَ عِلَّةٍ، نَحْوُ: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ، وَإِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ، وَثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ، وَثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ، وَحَادِي عَشَرَ، وَحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ، إِلَى تِسْعَ عَشْرَةَ، وَتَاسِعَةَ عَشْرَةَ، وَنَحْوُ: هُوَ جَارِي بَيْتَ بَيْتَ، وَبَيْنَ بَيْنَ. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ لَفْظَ اثْنَيْنِ بُنِيَ الثَّانِي، وَأُعْرِبَ الْأَوَّلُ وَحُذِفَ نُونُهُ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي اثْنَا عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَرَأَيْتُ اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِاثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا.
text.en: If they are not made one noun but the second contains [the meaning of] a particle: if the first is not the word ithnān “two”, both are built on the fatḥa if their end is a sound letter, and on the sukūn if it is a weak letter, as aḥada ʿashara and iḥdā ʿashrata “eleven”, thalāthata ʿashara and thalātha ʿashrata “thirteen”, ḥādī ʿashara and ḥādiyata ʿashrata “eleventh”, up to tisʿa ʿashrata “nineteen” and tāsiʿata ʿashrata “nineteenth”; and as huwa jārī bayta bayta “he is my neighbour, house to house” and bayna bayna “in between”. If the first is the word ithnān, the second is built, and the first has iʿrāb and its nūn is dropped, as jāʾanī ithnā ʿashara rajulan “twelve men came to me”, raʾaytu ithnay ʿashara rajulan “I saw twelve men” and marartu bi-ithnay ʿashara rajulan “I passed by twelve men”.

lessons.title: More words always built; the cut-off adverbs; the munādā
body: Also never free of binā are some of the words of allusion (kināyāt). Kam asks, and then puts the word after it in naṣb as a tamyīz: kam rajulan, “how many men?”; or it states, “in the sense of making many”, and then it is muḍāf to the word after it: kam rajulin, “how many a man!”. Kadhā stands for a number and takes a tamyīz in naṣb, ʿindī kadhā dirhaman, “I have so many dirhams”; kayta and dhayta stand for speech, “such and such”. And the words with the meaning of the in of condition or of the question, as man and mā, again “except ayyun and ayyatun”.

So too some adverbs: amsi, qaṭṭu, ʿawḍu, mudh, mundhu, idh, idhā, lammā, matā, annā, ayyāna, kayfa, ḥaythu, ladā, ladun, ladu, and the kāf, ʿalā and ʿan when they are nouns. The last three are particles of jarr (lesson 4) that sometimes serve as nouns, as when min comes before ʿan in min ʿan yamīnī, “from my right side”; as nouns they are built.

The binā that is not necessary belongs to words built only in some uses. First, the adverbs cut off from the iḍāfa with the muḍāf ilayhi still intended (lesson 38): qablu, baʿdu, taḥtu, quddāmu, khalfu, warāʾu, lā ghayru, laysa ghayru, ḥasbu; and al-āna, “now”. Made muḍāf, the same words have iʿrāb: min qabli dhālika; cut off, they are built on ḍamma.

Second, the single definite munādā, the one called: it is “built on what it is put in rafʿ by”: on the ḍamma, yā Zaydu; on the alif, yā muslimāni; on the wāw, yā muslimūna. If it is muḍāf, like a muḍāf, or an indefinite with no one meant, it is in naṣb “by an understood verb”, the commentators' “I call”: yā ʿAbda Allāhi, yā khayran min Zaydin, yā rajulan. Compare yā rajulu (lesson 41): there one particular man is meant, so the word is definite and built.

Two more cases. With the alif of calling for help or of lament at its end, the munādā is built on fatḥa: yā Zaydāh, “alas, Zayd!”. With a lām at its beginning it must be in jarr: yā la-Zaydin, “help, Zayd!”, where the lām is the particle of jarr.

terms.en: the words of allusion: kam, kadhā, kayta, dhayta
kam that asks (naṣb after it) and kam that states (jarr after it)
the one called; the single definite one is built
cut off from the iḍāfa, its muḍāf ilayhi intended

tasks.prompt: Parse the word after kam in kam rajulan and in kam rajulin.
tasks.answer: In kam rajulan, kam asks “how many?”, and rajulan is its tamyīz, in naṣb. In kam rajulin, kam states that there are many, “how many a man!”, and is muḍāf to rajulin, which is in jarr as muḍāf ilayhi.

tasks.prompt: Why is qablu built in min qablu, but has iʿrāb in min qabli dhālika?
tasks.answer: Qabl is built only when it is cut off from the iḍāfa with its muḍāf ilayhi intended; then it is built on ḍamma. When it is made muḍāf, as qabli dhālika, it has iʿrāb, here jarr after min.

tasks.prompt: Give the state of each munādā and the reason: yā Zaydu; yā ʿAbda Allāhi; yā muslimūna.
tasks.arabic: يَا زَيْدُ — يَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ — يَا مُسْلِمُونَ
tasks.answer: Yā Zaydu: single and definite, built on the ḍamma, its sign of rafʿ. Yā ʿAbda Allāhi: muḍāf, in naṣb by an understood verb. Yā muslimūna: single and definite, built on the wāw, the sign of rafʿ of the sound masculine plural.

tasks.prompt: How do yā rajulu and yā rajulan differ?
tasks.answer: In yā rajulu one particular man is meant, so the calling makes it definite and it is built on ḍamma. In yā rajulan no particular man is meant: it is indefinite and in naṣb by an understood verb.

quiz.prompt: Kam that asks puts the word after it in…
Kam rajulin means…
quiz.explanation: Kam that states, in the sense of making many.

quiz.prompt: Kayta and dhayta stand for…
Qablu and baʿdu are built when…
options: cut off from the iḍāfa, their muḍāf ilayhi intended

quiz.prompt: Yā muslimāni is built on…
quiz.explanation: On what it would be put in rafʿ by.

quiz.prompt: Yā khayran min Zaydin is in naṣb because the munādā is…
quiz.explanation: Khayran governs min Zaydin, as a muḍāf governs.

quiz.prompt: Yā la-Zaydin is in jarr because of…
quiz.explanation: The lām of calling for help is a particle of jarr.

text.original: وَبَعْضُ الْكِنَايَاتِ، وَهُوَ كَمْ: يَكُونُ لِلِاسْتِفْهَامِ فَيَنْصِبُ مَا بَعْدَهُ عَلَى التَّمْيِيزِ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رَجُلًا، وَلِلْخَبَرِيَّةِ بِمَعْنَى التَّكْثِيرِ فَيُضَافُ إِلَى مَا بَعْدَهُ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رَجُلٍ؛ وَكَذَا لِلْعَدَدِ، يَنْصِبُ مَا بَعْدَهُ عَلَى التَّمْيِيزِ، نَحْوُ: عِنْدِي كَذَا دِرْهَمًا؛ وَكَيْتَ وَذَيْتَ لِلْحَدِيثِ. وَالْكَلِمَاتُ الْمُتَضَمِّنَةُ بِمَعْنَى إِنْ وَالِاسْتِفْهَامِ غَيْرَ أَيٍّ وَأَيَّةٍ.
text.en: And some of the words of allusion (kināyāt), which are kam: it is for question, and then it puts what comes after it in naṣb as a tamyīz, as kam rajulan “how many men?”; and for stating, in the sense of making many, and then it is made muḍāf to what comes after it, as kam rajulin “how many a man!”; and likewise kadhā, for number, which puts what comes after it in naṣb as a tamyīz, as ʿindī kadhā dirhaman “I have so many dirhams”; and kayta and dhayta “such and such”, for speech. And the words that contain the meaning of in and of the question, except ayyin and ayyatin.

text.original: وَبَعْضُ الظُّرُوفِ، نَحْوُ: أَمْسِ، وَقَطُّ، وَعَوْضُ، وَمُذْ، وَمُنْذُ، وَإِذْ، وَإِذَا، وَلَمَّا، وَمَتَى، وَأَنَّى، وَأَيَّانَ، وَكَيْفَ، وَحَيْثُ، وَلَدَى، وَلَدُنْ، وَلَدُ، وَالْكَافِ، وَعَلَى، وَعَنِ الِاسْمِيَّةِ. وَغَيْرُ اللَّازِمِ مَا قُطِعَ عَنِ الْإِضَافَةِ مَنْوِيًّا فِيهِ الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ، نَحْوُ: قَبْلُ، وَبَعْدُ، وَتَحْتُ، وَقُدَّامُ، وَخَلْفُ، وَوَرَاءُ، وَلَا غَيْرُ، وَلَيْسَ غَيْرُ، وَحَسْبُ، وَالْآنَ.
text.en: And some adverbs, as amsi “yesterday”, qaṭṭu “ever”, ʿawḍu “ever”, mudh and mundhu “since”, idh and idhā “when”, lammā “when”, matā “when?”, annā “how?, where?”, ayyāna “when?”, kayfa “how?”, ḥaythu “where”, ladā, ladun and ladu “with”, and the kāf, ʿalā and ʿani when they are nouns. The not necessary is what is cut off from the iḍāfa with the muḍāf ilayhi intended in it, as qablu “before”, baʿdu “after”, taḥtu “below”, quddāmu “in front”, khalfu and warāʾu “behind”, lā ghayru and laysa ghayru “no other”, ḥasbu “enough”; and al-āna “now”.

text.original: وَالْمُنَادَى الْمُفْرَدُ الْمَعْرِفَةُ، فَإِنَّهُ مَبْنِيٌّ عَلَى مَا يُرْفَعُ بِهِ إِنْ لَمْ يَلْحَقْ بِآخِرِهِ أَلِفُ الِاسْتِغَاثَةِ أَوِ النُّدْبَةِ، وَلَا بِأَوَّلِهِ لَامٌ، نَحْوُ: يَا زَيْدُ، وَيَا مُسْلِمَانِ، وَيَا مُسْلِمُونَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مُضَافًا أَوْ مُشَابِهًا بِهِ أَوْ نَكِرَةً يُنْصَبُ بِفِعْلٍ مُقَدَّرٍ، نَحْوُ: يَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ، وَيَا خَيْرًا مِنْ زَيْدٍ، وَيَا رَجُلًا، وَإِنْ لَحِقَ بِآخِرِهِ أَلِفٌ بُنِيَ عَلَى الْفَتْحِ، نَحْوُ: يَا زَيْدَاهْ، وَإِنِ اتَّصَلَ بِأَوَّلِهِ لَامٌ يَجِبُ جَرُّهُ، نَحْوُ: يَا لَزَيْدٍ.
text.en: And the single definite one called (munādā): it is built on what it is put in rafʿ by, if the alif of calling for help or of lament is not joined to its end, nor a lām to its beginning, as yā Zaydu “O Zayd!”, yā muslimāni “O two Muslims!” and yā muslimūna “O Muslims!”. If it is muḍāf, or like a muḍāf, or indefinite, it is put in naṣb by an understood verb, as yā ʿAbda Allāhi “O ʿAbd Allāh!”, yā khayran min Zaydin “O one better than Zayd!” and yā rajulan “O a man!”. If an alif is joined to its end, it is built on the fatḥa, as yā Zaydāh “alas, Zayd!”; and if a lām is joined to its beginning, it must be in jarr, as yā la-Zaydin “help, Zayd!”.

lessons.title: Necessary and allowed binā; lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata
body: The badal of a munādā, and a word joined to it without the lām, take the munādā's own rule, as if the yā were said again: yā rajulu Zaydu, yā Zaydu wa-ʿAmru. The particles of calling are yā, ayā, hayā, ay and the hamza, and wā is only for lament. The commentators add how they are used: the hamza and ay for one who is near, ayā and hayā for one who is far, yā for both.

The ism of the lā that denies the genus is built (lesson 10) when it is single, not muḍāf; indefinite; joined to lā; and lā is not repeated: lā rajula. And the muḍāriʿ is built when the nūn of the feminine plural or the nūn of emphasis is joined to it: yaḍribna, taḍribna, hal yaḍribanna, hal taḍribanna. This is the muḍāriʿ that lesson 45 left out of the nine places. “The binā of these words is necessary.”

Allowed, not necessary, is the binā of adverbs made muḍāf to a sentence or to idh, which may be built on fatḥa: yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum (Q 5:119), in the reading with yawma, though it stands where a rafʿ is expected (the reading of Ḥafṣ has yawmu); and ḥīnaʾidhin, yawmaʾidhin. So too mithl and ghayr before mā, an and anna; the grammarians' usual example is innahu la-ḥaqqun mithla mā annakum tanṭiqūna (Q 51:23), where mithla, an adjective of ḥaqqun in rafʿ, is built on fatḥa.

With a repeated lā, each joined to a single indefinite ism, as lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi, “there is no might and no strength except through God”, the book allows five ways: both built on fatḥa; both in rafʿ; the first built and the second in naṣb; the first built and the second in rafʿ; and the first in rafʿ and the second built. “These are five ways allowed in examples like it.” The first, which every Muslim says, is the best known.

Last, the adjective of the built ism of lā, single and joined to it, may be built with it on fatḥa, lā rajula ẓarīfa, “no witty man”, or given iʿrāb, in rafʿ or in naṣb: lā rajula ẓarīfun, lā rajula ẓarīfan. With this the book ends: the student who holds its sixty governors, its thirty governed words and its rules of iʿrāb and binā is ready for the Kāfiya.

terms.en: the particles of calling: yā, ayā, hayā, ay, the hamza; wā for lament
lament: calling one mourned, with wā
a word whose binā is necessary in that use
a word that may be built or given iʿrāb

tasks.prompt: Give the state of Zaydu in yā rajulu Zaydu and of ʿAmru in yā Zaydu wa-ʿAmru.
tasks.arabic: يَا رَجُلُ زَيْدُ — يَا زَيْدُ وَعَمْرُو
tasks.answer: Zaydu is the badal of the munādā rajulu, and ʿAmru is joined to the munādā Zaydu without the lām; both take the rule of the munādā itself, as if yā were repeated, and are built on ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: Which conditions make the ism of lā built? Test them on lā rajula and lā ghulāma rajulin.
tasks.answer: It must be single (not muḍāf), indefinite, joined to lā, and lā not repeated. Lā rajula meets them all, so rajula is built on fatḥa. In lā ghulāma rajulin the ism is muḍāf, so it is not built: it is in naṣb (lesson 37).

tasks.prompt: Why is yaḍribna built, while yaḍribūna has iʿrāb?
tasks.answer: The book makes the muḍāriʿ built when the nūn of the feminine plural or of emphasis is joined to it, so yaḍribna is built. Yaḍribūna has a wāw pronoun joined to it; its nūn is the sign of rafʿ, dropped in naṣb and jazm (lesson 45).

tasks.prompt: Write the five ways of lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata that the book allows.
tasks.answer: Lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata (both built); lā ḥawlun wa-lā quwwatun (both in rafʿ); lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwatan (built, then naṣb); lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwatun (built, then rafʿ); lā ḥawlun wa-lā quwwata (rafʿ, then built).

tasks.prompt: Give the three ways of the adjective in lā rajula ẓarīf…
tasks.answer: Built with the ism on fatḥa: lā rajula ẓarīfa. With iʿrāb in rafʿ: lā rajula ẓarīfun. With iʿrāb in naṣb: lā rajula ẓarīfan.

quiz.prompt: In yā Zaydu wa-ʿAmru, ʿAmru is…
options: built on ḍamma, with the munādā's rule
quiz.explanation: A word joined without the lām takes the munādā's rule.

quiz.prompt: Which particle is only for lament?
Lā rajula is built because its ism is…
options: single, indefinite, joined, lā not repeated

quiz.prompt: Hal yaḍribanna is built because of…
quiz.explanation: And the nūn of the feminine plural in yaḍribna.

quiz.prompt: An adverb muḍāf to a sentence may be…
How many ways does the book allow in lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata?
quiz.explanation: “Five ways allowed in examples like it.”

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five ways?
quiz.explanation: After a first in rafʿ, the second is in rafʿ or built, not in naṣb.

text.original: وَالْبَدَلُ وَالْمَعْطُوفُ الْخَالِي عَنِ اللَّامِ حُكْمُهُ حُكْمُ الْمُنَادَى، نَحْوُ: يَا رَجُلُ زَيْدُ، وَيَا زَيْدُ وَعَمْرُو. وَحُرُوفُ النِّدَاءِ: يَا، وَأَيَا، وَهَيَا، وَأَيْ، وَالْهَمْزَةُ، وَوَا مُخْتَصٌّ بِالنُّدْبَةِ. وَاسْمُ لَا لِنَفْيِ الْجِنْسِ إِذَا كَانَ مُفْرَدًا نَكِرَةً مُتَّصِلَةً بِلَا غَيْرِ مُكَرَّرَةٍ، نَحْوُ: لَا رَجُلَ. وَالْمُضَارِعُ الْمُتَّصِلُ بِهِ نُونُ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ أَوْ نُونُ التَّأْكِيدِ، نَحْوُ: يَضْرِبْنَ، وَتَضْرِبْنَ، وَهَلْ يَضْرِبَنَّ، وَهَلْ تَضْرِبَنَّ. وَهَذِهِ الْأَلْفَاظُ يَجِبُ بِنَاؤُهَا.
text.en: The badal, and what is joined by ʿaṭf without the lām, have the rule of the munādā, as yā rajulu Zaydu “O man, Zayd!” and yā Zaydu wa-ʿAmru “O Zayd and ʿAmr!”. The particles of calling are yā, ayā, hayā, ay and the hamza; and wā is reserved for lament. And the ism of the lā that denies the genus, when it is a single indefinite joined to lā, which is not repeated, as lā rajula “no man”. And the muḍāriʿ to which the nūn of the feminine plural or the nūn of emphasis is joined, as yaḍribna, taḍribna, hal yaḍribanna and hal taḍribanna. The binā of these words is necessary.

text.original: وَأَمَّا جَائِزَةُ الْبِنَاءِ فَالظُّرُوفُ الْمُضَافَةُ إِلَى الْجُمْلَةِ وَإِذْ، فَإِنَّهَا يَجُوزُ بِنَاؤُهَا عَلَى الْفَتْحِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: يَوْمَ يَنْفَعُ الصَّادِقِينَ صِدْقُهُمْ، وَحِينَئِذٍ وَيَوْمَئِذٍ، وَكَذَلِكَ مِثْلُ وَغَيْرُ مَعَ مَا وَأَنْ وَأَنَّ.
text.en: As for those whose binā is allowed: the adverbs made muḍāf to a sentence, and to idh, may be built on the fatḥa, as His saying, Most High: yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum “the day their truthfulness profits the truthful” [5:119], and ḥīnaʾidhin and yawmaʾidhin; and likewise mithlu “like” and ghayru “other than” with mā, an and anna.

text.original: وَاسْمُ لَا الْمُكَرَّرَةِ الْمُتَّصِلُ بِهَا، الْمُفْرَدُ النَّكِرَةُ، نَحْوُ: لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ، فَإِنَّهُ يَجُوزُ بِنَاؤُهُمَا عَلَى الْفَتْحِ، وَرَفْعُهُمَا، وَفَتْحُ الْأَوَّلِ مَعَ نَصْبِ الثَّانِي وَرَفْعِهِ، وَرَفْعُ الْأَوَّلِ مَعَ فَتْحِ الثَّانِي، وَهَذِهِ خَمْسَةُ أَوْجُهٍ تَجُوزُ فِي أَمْثَالِهِ. وَصِفَةُ اسْمِ لَا الْمَبْنِيِّ، الْمُفْرَدَةُ الْمُتَّصِلَةُ بِهِ، فَإِنَّهُ يَجُوزُ بِنَاؤُهَا عَلَى الْفَتْحِ، نَحْوُ: لَا رَجُلَ ظَرِيفَ، وَإِعْرَابُهَا رَفْعًا وَنَصْبًا، نَحْوُ: لَا رَجُلَ ظَرِيفٌ وَظَرِيفًا.
text.en: And the ism of a repeated lā joined to it, a single indefinite, as lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi “there is no might and no strength except through God”: both may be built on the fatḥa; both may be in rafʿ; the first may have a fatḥa with the second in naṣb or in rafʿ; and the first may be in rafʿ with a fatḥa on the second. These are five ways allowed in examples like it. And the adjective of the built ism of lā, single and joined to it: it may be built on the fatḥa, as lā rajula ẓarīfa “no witty man”, or given iʿrāb in rafʿ and naṣb, as lā rajula ẓarīfun wa-ẓarīfan “no man [is] witty”.
